Teaching case · Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Growth & Retention

Tinka Devsthan Systems: Three Trees and One Number

1. The night before

At a quarter to eleven on Sunday night, 11 October 2026, Kanchan Barnwal was still at the Bailey Road office in Patna, because the building's power had held and her flat's had not. On her screen were three spreadsheets, each named some version of FY28 growth model, each built by someone she trusted, each giving a different answer. The board of Tinka Devsthan Systems met at ten next morning to approve one.

The Gaya Pitrupaksh Mela had ended the previous day, and fifteen days of pind-daan bookings were still settling through the ledgers. The most important coefficient in all three spreadsheets — how often a devotee who books a slot also buys a prasad box — was being rewritten underneath the models.

Kanchan, vice-president for product for twenty months and head of growth for five, had asked for the growth-model exercise in January, expecting it to end the arguments. Instead it had given every argument a spreadsheet, and they disagreed by more than three times.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2022

Tinka Devsthan Systems was founded in Patna in March 2020 by Damodar Keshri, a former Infosys delivery manager whose family had managed a small Shiva temple in Nalanda district for four generations. His first proposition was to sell trusts a software licence for slot management, as Zoho sells a CRM. Trusts do not buy software: committees meet quarterly, surpluses are earmarked, and accounts are scrutinised by the Bihar State Board of Religious Trusts under the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950.

By late 2021 it had pivoted to a share of the devotee's convenience fee. Tinka Darshan Desk published a trust's slot grid; a devotee paid ₹22 to hold a slot, mostly over UPI; the trust kept ₹9, Tinka the rest less costs. Tinka Puja Register took paid archana and sankalp bookings, for which a devotee supplies gotra and nakshatra. Rasoi Prasad Line couriered sealed boxes, packed at a Gaya facility called Rasoi Bhog Kendra, to devotees who could not travel.

The decision that still shapes everything was taken in September 2022, when Damodar signed an exclusive channel agreement with the Zameen Devalaya Parishad, a federation of trusts in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh. The Parishad delivered 164 trusts in fourteen months. In exchange it took 22 per cent of Tinka's share of the fee at member trusts and — the clause nobody weighted — the right to approve any change to the devotee-facing fee there. The agreement runs to 31 March 2028, and 164 of the 268 trusts live today, or 61.2 per cent, sit inside it. Price is therefore not a lever Kanchan can model.

3. The industry

India's large shrines had solved slot booking for themselves. Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams, the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board and the Shri Saibaba Sansthan Trust each run their own darshan systems at a scale no vendor will displace; Ujjain's Mahakaleshwar temple books its Bhasma Aarti directly. The addressable market was the long tail: some 2,500 registered trusts in Bihar alone, plus Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh and the Mithila belt into Nepal, where a Janakpur trust had been in conversation since Vivah Panchami 2025.

Around that tail larger players circled: MakeMyTrip sold pilgrimage packages, IRCTC ran Bharat Gaurav pilgrim trains, Blinkit and Zepto stocked puja samagri in Patna itself. The sharpest direct competitor was Zameen Teerth Network, a Noida aggregator buying temple partnerships with guaranteed minimums Tinka could not match.

Regulation pressed from three sides. Prasadam from a religious institution is exempt from GST, but Tinka's platform fee on that supply is not obviously exempt, and the auditors had flagged the treatment as unsettled: if the fee is held taxable and cannot be passed on, the ₹95 contribution per box becomes ₹80.51. Sankalp data is personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; the Gaya facility runs under FSSAI's BHOG scheme; and revenue-sharing at a registered trust needs the Religious Trusts Board's sanction — three sanctions had been pending since June.

4. How the model came to disagree with itself

Exhibit 1 gives the trailing twelve months to September 2026: ₹960.65 lakh, of which ₹747.50 lakh came from 29,32,000 bookings and ₹213.15 lakh from trust licences. That much nobody disputed.

Four dates explain the rest. In September 2025, during Pitru Paksha, nine Gaya trusts recorded 37,000 confirmed slots and 12,580 prasad boxes: attach of 34.0 per cent. The company concluded that prasad, not slots, was the engine. A quieter measurement across all live trusts in January–February 2026 found 3,88,000 slots and 42,680 boxes — 11.0 per cent. In April 2026 an investor update reported "412 temple trusts onboarded". In August 2026 Kusum Poddar's finance team, reconciling for the data room, reported that 203 trusts had ever generated an invoice. Product's dashboard showed 268. Nobody had lied: partnerships counted a signed memorandum, product a published grid, finance collected money, and each believed it was the company's number. 5. The people

Kanchan Barnwal, vice-president, product and growth, Patna. She owns the model the board will see, and believes the devotee is the unit that compounds. Unsaid: her tree is the lowest of the three, and presenting it may cost the round.

Damodar Keshri, founder and chief executive, Patna. He has told the lead investor that FY28 revenue will be ₹30 crore, and wants a model that supports the sentence. Unsaid: he agreed ₹30 crore in August, before any tree existed.

Rakesh Mahto, head of trust partnerships, in Gaya three weeks a month. His team's variable pay is keyed to memoranda signed; trusts, he argues, are the only durable asset, since a devotee who books at a trust that leaves is lost with it. Unsaid: 144 of his 412 memoranda never produced a grid.

Kusum Poddar, finance head, Mumbai. She will not certify a data-room model on any trust count but the paying one, and wants ₹30 crore built on ₹4.73 lakh a trust, which conveniently works. Unsaid: her own renewal analysis, Exhibit 5, undermines that forecast.

Dharmendra Ranjan, engineering lead, Bengaluru. His June rebuild of the analytics pipeline changed what "slots offered" counts; the resulting jump in conversion was celebrated at an all-hands. Unsaid: he flagged the change in a commit message and nowhere else.

Richa Sharan, head of prasad fulfilment, Patna and Gaya. With 46 packers on rolls and 180 on mela contracts, she insists the business is not a subscription but a calendar of eleven occasions a year. Unsaid: the Gaya facility cannot pack more than 14,000 boxes a day, which no model mentions.

Devika Rauniyar, diaspora growth lead, Chicago, ten and a half hours behind Patna. Her 9,400 devotees in the United States pay 3.75 times Indian prices for a couriered prasad box — ₹2,400 against ₹640 — and she wants a dedicated pod. Her package is $145,000, or ₹127.60 lakh at ₹88 to the dollar, 12.76 times the ₹10 lakh a Patna analyst costs. Unsaid: her repeat rate rests on eleven months and 1,100 orders.

Durgesh Ambastha, board member for the lead investor, Mumbai. He asked for "one model, six drivers, no scenarios" and will read whatever arrives as the team's view. Unsaid: his fund's reserves are already provisioned against a ₹30 crore FY28 case.

Exhibit 3 sets the three trees side by side. Each is built from company data and each is defensible; together they span ₹10.26 crore to ₹50.56 crore for the same year and company.

7. Voices

"A devotee is not an asset; the trust is. When Teerth Network took a Bodh Gaya trust from us in May, we lost 14,000 devotees in a week. Model the trusts."

Rakesh Mahto, partnerships review, 29 September 2026

"I will sign off on 203 — the number of trusts that have sent us money. If the model says 412, my name goes nowhere near the data room."

Kusum Poddar, email from Mumbai, 2 October 2026, 11.04 pm IST

"You are all forecasting per month. There is no per month. There is Pitru Paksha, Chhath, Shravani Mela, and forty weeks of nothing in which I pay 46 packers. Your 21 lakh boxes need over 150 peak days at the Kendra; we have 41."

Richa Sharan, operations call, 6 October 2026

"Eleven months of data, I know. But the model has no row for me, and I am asked to hit a number inside it."

Devika Rauniyar, 7.30 pm IST call, 7 October 2026

"I said thirty crore in August because a founder who answers 'I do not know' does not get a Series B. Find me a tree that gets there honestly."

Damodar Keshri, to Kanchan, 10 October 2026

8. The options as Kanchan currently sees them

Ship Tree A at ₹30.27 crore, on the paying-trust denominator, disclosed in a footnote. It matches what Damodar has said, is built from audited collections, and Kusum will sign it. It also requires 92.4 lakh bookings that Richa's arithmetic says cannot be packed or passed through a mela gate, and turns Exhibit 5's two largest lapsed trusts into non-events.

Ship Tree B at ₹18.25 crore. Honest about the devotee and the 2.932 bookings one actually makes — and it collapses the raise. It also rests on a devotee count that is itself three numbers, and its ₹32.76 carries licence fees and averages a business that is 65.6 per cent mela.

Ship all three as a range, ₹10.26 to ₹50.56 crore. Truthful, and Durgesh has already written down how he will read three trees.

Forecast nothing; commit to ninety days of definition work — one trust count, one denominator, one attach rate re-measured across this Pitru Paksha and Chhath — and ask the lead for a bridge.

None of the four touches the possibility that the framing is the error. Each assumes the FY28 number exists and the argument is how to find it. Yet the hiring plan, Rakesh's variable pay, Devika's pod and the Parishad renegotiation are already keyed to ₹30 crore: the model is not predicting the business, it is authorising commitments that will reshape it. And the lever a growth model normally reaches for — price — is unavailable at 61.2 per cent of live trusts until the exclusive lapses on the last day of the forecast year.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 10 am on Monday, 12 October 2026, and Durgesh's fund has indicated primary capital conditional on a board-approved FY28 plan by 31 October. Cash stands at ₹6.20 crore against net monthly burn of ₹64 lakh — 9.7 months, to end July 2027. Headcount is 118, 74 of them in Bihar; Richa's 180 mela-contract packers come off rolls on 31 October. Chhath in mid-November is the last large window before the plan year begins. The Parishad's fee-approval right runs to 31 March 2028, three Religious Trusts Board sanctions are pending, and the GST question on the platform fee over exempt prasadam would take ₹59.41 lakh off the prasad line.

At twenty past midnight Kanchan did the one calculation nobody had done. Taking Rakesh's 640 trusts, Richa's ceiling, Kusum's ₹4.73 lakh and the 27.4 per cent that had arrived that afternoon, she found she could build, in four minutes each, two further trees: one at ₹11 crore, one at ₹41 crore, using only numbers the company had measured. She closed the laptop without saving either.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 2, state what a "trust" is in each of the three counts, choose the one the FY28 model should use, and say what each choice loses.

2. Exhibit 4 gives four conversion rates for one numerator. If the board asks whether conversion is improving, what is the honest answer, and what would make the question answerable?

3. Exhibits 5 and 6 rest on a handful of events — fourteen renewals, one fortnight at nine trusts. How much forecast weight can such evidence bear, and how would you build a model that carries its uncertainty?

4. Trees A and C imply booking volumes differing by 2.23 times, and only Tree C counts days and pilgrims. Does that make Tree C right? Argue each tree as the correct root for this business.

5. The Parishad agreement of 2022 bought 164 trusts and sold the pricing lever until 31 March 2028. Evaluate that trade with what is now known, and say how a 2022 model could have made the cost visible.

6. It is Monday morning. What does Kanchan put in front of the board, and what does she say when Durgesh asks for one number? If she cannot give one, what does she offer that a board can act on?

Outside, the last Pitru Paksha traffic moved south on the Gaya road, and somewhere in the settlement files a coefficient was changing.
exp20v2-growth.model:
Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation — Growth & Retention

Building a Growth Model

Can I connect the inputs to the growth number in a spreadsheet? A driver-based model turns spend, conversion rates and retention into the one number a board asks about — mechanically enough that anyone can trace the answer back to its inputs.

Devika's cell

On the second Monday of September 2026, Devika Ranganathan, VP of Growth at Nagad Money — a four-year-old savings app headquartered in Gurugram — opened a blank spreadsheet and stared at a single cell. In eleven days she would stand before the board and ask for an incremental ₹17.5 lakh a month in growth budget, taking monthly performance-marketing spend from ₹63 lakh to ₹80.5 lakh. At the previous review, the CFO, Rohan Deshmukh, had asked a question she hadn't answered cleanly: “If I give you seventeen and a half lakh more a month, how many more transacting users do I get, and does it move the AUM number I report to investors?” Devika had answered in adjectives — “meaningfully more,” “a healthy lift” — and Rohan had written nothing down. Nagad Money closed August 2026 with 4,20,000 transacting users and ₹1,850 crore in assets under management, growing at a pace the board considered too slow for the Series C story it was telling. What Devika lacked, walking into that meeting, was a spreadsheet that could take a rupee of spend in one cell and walk it, formula by formula, to a rupee of AUM in another — one where Rohan could change one assumption and watch every downstream number move.

The idea

A growth model is a spreadsheet, or a chain of formulas inside one, that connects the inputs a team can actually change — spend, conversion rates at each funnel stage, retention, average deposit size — to the single output number leadership tracks, through nothing but arithmetic. Every downstream cell is a multiplication or subtraction of cells upstream; nowhere does the modeller simply assert a number. The idea has no single inventor, but its modern shape owes most to two sources that converged in the early 2010s: consumer growth teams at companies such as Facebook and Uber formalised the funnel-to-output chain that Dave McClure had sketched as “AARRR” — Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue — in 2007; and FP&A (financial planning and analysis) had already built driver-based budget models connecting units sold to revenue through price and volume, decades before growth teams pointed the same technique at users instead of dollars. The sentence Devika could say without sounding glib was this: a growth model is a spreadsheet that turns the things you can change into the one number the board asks about, mechanically enough that anyone in the room can trace the answer back to its inputs.

How it actually works

Building one starts, counter to instinct, not with the inputs but with the output: Devika first had to agree with Rohan on the single metric the model would end in — net new AUM added per month — because a model built toward “growth” in the abstract cannot know which of a dozen possible outputs to optimise. With the output fixed, the next step lays out the causal chain that produces it as a sequence of stages, each a subset of the one before: spend, to paid installs, to organic and referral installs, to activated users (completed KYC and set up a first savings instruction), to transacting users (a first auto-debit actually executed), to the rupee amount each deposited. Every arrow between stages needs a rate, and this is the step practitioners most often skip: the rate has to come from the company's own trailing actuals, not a benchmark deck, because a model built on someone else's activation rate confidently produces the wrong number. With the chain and its rates in place, the model multiplies forward — installs times activation rate gives activated users, activated users times transaction rate gives transacting users — and a second, easily forgotten layer sits on top: retention. A model that only adds new users without subtracting the ones who churn measures gross growth, not the net growth a board cares about.

Fig. 1 — The base-case driver chain, September 2026: every number is produced by the one before it.

The worked example

Table 1 lays out Devika's base model, built from Nagad Money's trailing actuals. Spend of ₹63,00,000 bought 1,80,000 paid installs at a blended cost per install of ₹35 (₹63,00,000 ÷ 1,80,000). Referral and organic search added 70,000 more installs at near-zero marginal cost, for 2,50,000 installs in total. Of those, 20 per cent completed KYC and set up a first savings instruction within seven days — the activation rate — giving 50,000 activated users (20% × 2,50,000). Of the activated users, 60 per cent saw a first auto-debit actually execute within thirty days — the transaction rate — giving 30,000 transacting users (60% × 50,000). Each deposited an average of ₹2,500 in that first month, so the cohort's gross new AUM was ₹7,50,00,000, or ₹7.5 crore (30,000 × ₹2,500). Against that gross figure sits the existing base: 4,20,000 transacting users churn at 2 per cent a month, losing 8,400 users (2% × 4,20,000) who, Devika's cohort data showed, skewed to the smallest balances — an average of ₹6,000 each, against a base average closer to ₹44,000. That churn removed ₹5,04,00,000, or ₹5.04 crore (8,400 × ₹6,000). Net new AUM for September was therefore ₹7.5 crore minus ₹5.04 crore, or ₹2.46 crore — a monthly AUM growth rate of just 0.13 per cent (₹2.46 crore ÷ ₹1,850 crore), even though the user base itself grew a healthier 5.14 per cent (21,600 net new users, or 30,000 gross additions minus 8,400 churned, ÷ 4,20,000).

That gap — 5.14 per cent in users, 0.13 per cent in AUM — is the finding a growth model exists to surface. Devika ran a second pass, changing one input: activation rising from 20 to 24 per cent, spend held flat. Activated users rose to 60,000 (24% × 2,50,000), transacting users to 36,000 (60% × 60,000), gross new AUM to ₹9 crore, and net new AUM to ₹3.96 crore (₹9 crore − ₹5.04 crore) — 0.21 per cent AUM growth, still slow but nearly double. Blended cost per transacting user fell from ₹210 (₹63,00,000 ÷ 30,000) to ₹175 (₹63,00,000 ÷ 36,000), for no extra spend. She then checked what the ₹17.5 lakh spend increase alone would buy, activation held at 20 per cent: 50,000 more paid installs, 3,00,000 installs total, 60,000 activated, 36,000 transacting — the identical number the activation fix reached, at a recurring ₹17.5 lakh a month, roughly ₹292 per incremental transacting user, against an onboarding fix costing one product team a quarter, once.

Fig. 2 — The activation-rate fix, spend unchanged: every downstream figure recomputes from one changed input.

Nuances a learner must become aware of

A model describes, it does not explain

Knowing activation is 20 per cent says nothing about why — a confusing screen, a slow OTP, or a channel that brings in low-intent users. The model says where to look; it never says what you will find.

It is not a forecast

The two get used interchangeably, but the model recomputes correctly whatever rates it is fed; a forecast additionally claims those rates hold into a future period — a judgment the arithmetic itself cannot make.

It is easily confused with a growth loop model

A funnel model runs input to output once per cohort; a loop model treats an output, such as a referred install, as a new input to the same funnel, compounding round after round.

Blended rates hide mix shift

Devika's 20 per cent activation rate averaged paid and organic installs; if organic activates at 35 per cent and paid at 12, a shift in the mix moves the blended number even when neither underlying rate changes.

Stocks and flows must not be mixed

Churn (2 per cent) is measured against the stock of existing users (4,20,000); activation (20 per cent) against a single cohort's installs (2,50,000). Applying one rate's base to the other's flow produces numbers that look plausible and are wrong.

Resolution is a judgment call

Nagad Money's model runs monthly and blended; a more mature team might run it weekly, by channel, or by segment. Finer resolution catches what the blended version hides, at the cost of a slower build.

A model cannot tell you which output matters

Nothing in the arithmetic says whether the board should track transacting users or AUM; that is a business judgment the model executes once given — and Devika's finding, that 5.1 per cent user growth coexists with 0.13 per cent AUM growth, was visible only because she tracked both.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and stage

The shape of the chain changes with the business. A consumer product like Nagad Money runs a single-sided funnel — install, activate, transact — where top-of-funnel volume is cheap and the constraint sits downstream. A B2B product replaces installs with leads and KYC with a sales cycle: marketing-qualified lead, to sales-qualified lead, to closed-won account, to expansion revenue, where cycle length and deal size usually bind more than volume, since one enterprise account can outweigh a thousand installs. A marketplace needs two funnels, supply and demand, multiplied through a liquidity rate — the odds a demand-side visit finds a matching listing — so growth on one side without the other adds cost without output. Stage matters too: an early-stage model is one funnel with rates borrowed from a few thin months of data, useful for ordering decisions by rough size, while a company at Nagad Money's scale runs nested models — one per channel, one per segment — reconciled monthly against finance's actuals.

Common mistakes

Reporting a blended rate as uniform

Symptom: a team says “our activation rate is 20 per cent” as a single fact, when three channels sit at 9, 18 and 34. Misunderstanding: managing an average instead of a mix. Diagnostic: split any headline rate by source for one cohort before repeating it in a room.

Counting gross additions and calling it growth

Symptom: the team reports “30,000 new transacting users” with visible pride while the net figure, after churn, is 21,600. Misunderstanding: growth without a churn term measures activity, not outcome. Diagnostic: check whether the ending-base difference matches the gross additions claimed.

Never running a second pass

Symptom: the model is a static set of numbers, shown once and shelved until the next deck. Misunderstanding: an unresensitised model is a report, not a decision tool. Diagnostic: before the meeting, ask what happens to the output if the input about to be funded moves by the amount actually proposed.

What good looks like

Three weeks later, Kabir Grover, who ran Nagad Money's lending product, handled an almost identical decision differently from the start. Before asking for budget, he built the chain backward from the metric finance actually tracked — net new disbursed loan book, not applications — gathered ninety days of his own team's rates, and ran three passes ahead of the meeting: one on spend, one on approval-rate improvement, one on average ticket size. He walked in with a single slide showing which lever moved the number most per rupee of effort, and asked for budget against that lever specifically. Nobody needed to ask what a ten per cent change would do — the model already said so.

What Devika decided

Devika's model changed what she asked for. Instead of the ₹17.5 lakh spend increase, she brought both passes side by side: spend and the activation fix produced the identical 6,000 additional transacting users, but one cost ₹17.5 lakh every month and the other cost one product team a quarter's work, once. She asked for engineering time, not ad budget — and told Rohan plainly that neither lever, alone, would move AUM growth much past 0.2 per cent a month, because new users deposited ₹2,500 against a base averaging ₹44,000. That admission made the model credible: it showed the board where the next question needed to go. What Devika needs next is to turn “average deposit is too small” into its own driver-based decision — which is what monetisation as a growth lever and growth plateaus and saturation cover next.

Two questions worth sitting with:

If your team's headline growth number improved next month, would you know which of your model's inputs moved to cause it?

Is the metric your model ends in the one your organisation actually needs to grow?

Building a Growth Model

A spreadsheet in which every downstream cell is arithmetic on cells upstream, ending in the number leadership is accountable for. Its value is not the forecast; it is that certain arguments become impossible to win.

1. Two spreadsheets, eleven days apart

On 2 October 2026, Tejaswini Bapat, VP of Growth at Hindola Learning Systems in Jaipur, was given a number and eleven weeks. Hindola sold vernacular vocational courses by subscription and closed September with 1,80,000 paying subscribers at a blended ₹349 of net revenue each per month, after store commission and GST: ₹6.282 crore of monthly recurring revenue, an annualised ₹75.38 crore. The board, preparing a Series C, had fixed an exit-March-2027 target of ₹10 crore MRR. Nilanjana Dutta, the CFO, framed it so adjectives would not answer: “I am asking which cells have to move, and by how much.”

Tejaswini had the inputs. Marketing ran at ₹1.40 crore a month at ₹28 a paid install, buying 5,00,000 installs; organic and referral added 2,00,000, for 7,00,000. Twenty-two per cent started the seven-day trial — 1,54,000 — and 15 per cent of trials converted: 23,100 new paying subscribers. Nine per cent of the opening base cancelled, 16,200, for a net addition of 6,900, or 3.83 per cent. Arranged as a model rather than a scorecard, those figures proved the target unreachable on that plan, for ever.

In Nagpur, on 13 October, Pranit Salunkhe faced a different shape. Hukum Procurement Cloud sold indirect-procurement software to mid-market manufacturers and closed the September quarter with 1,200 accounts and ₹72 crore of annual recurring revenue, ₹6 lakh an account. Farzana Merchant, the Chief Revenue Officer, wanted five more account executives at a fully loaded ₹9 lakh per rep per quarter; Pranit wanted the same money for a squad letting customers add seats and modules unassisted. Both were assertions, because Hukum’s plan was targets rather than arithmetic.

2. The idea, and what it was invented against

A growth model is a chain of formulas connecting the inputs a team can change — spend, unit costs, conversion rates, retention, price, capacity — to a single output metric, in which no downstream figure is asserted. Three consequences are the whole of the idea: any output traces to its inputs; any input can be moved and the output recomputed; and any claim that an initiative will accelerate growth must name the cell it moves.

Two parents met late. Driver-based planning is old financial practice: revenue as price times volume, built so a committee could vary one assumption. Finance lacked a vocabulary for pre-revenue behaviour; that came from the consumer internet, where Dave McClure’s 2007 sketch of Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral and Revenue gave growth teams stages to put rates between. A growth plan had been a narrative defended by conviction; it became a spreadsheet defended by its rates.

Those who agree on mechanics disagree on purpose. The forecasting school will sign that a model missing next quarter by more than ten per cent is a bad model; it will not sign that the model’s value survives a bad forecast. The constraint school will sign that a model naming the binding constraint is valuable even when its forecast is poor, and will not sign that the output is a prediction for a board. The instrumentation school will sign that most of the benefit is realised in the building, and not that borrowed benchmarks are useful.

3. Mechanics: building the chain

Expert practice inverts the beginner’s instinct. Start with the output cell and agree it with whoever is accountable, because a model built toward growth in the abstract cannot know which output to end in; Tejaswini and Nilanjana fixed MRR at 31 March 2027. Only then is the chain laid backwards, each stage a subset of the one above.

Every rate must come from trailing actuals: Hindola’s 22 and 15 per cent came from ninety days of its own cohorts, where a benchmark would have been confidently wrong. Then flows must be separated from stocks. The 23,100 conversions are a flow produced within the month; the 9 per cent cancellation rate is a rate on the stock of 1,80,000 that existed at the opening. Apply one to the other and the figures look plausible and are wrong.

Fig. 1 — Flows multiply forward, the stock term subtracts, and their ratio fixes a ceiling.

The roll-forward writes itself: closing base equals opening base, less churn on the opening base, plus the new cohort. Churn scales with the base and the cohort does not, so the base converges on flow divided by churn rate: 23,100 ÷ 0.09 = 2,56,667 subscribers, which at ₹349 is ₹8.96 crore of MRR. Hindola’s plan, run for ever, asymptotes ₹1.04 crore short of the target. That is not a forecast; it is a division.

The sensitivity pass follows: change one input, recompute the chain. Two second-order effects surface. Marginal channel cost is not constant — to spend ₹2.10 crore Hindola bought thinner inventory, and cost per install rose from ₹28 to ₹35, giving 6,00,000 paid installs: 20 per cent more volume for 50 per cent more money. And mix and retention are not independent, since the cheapest installs are the least intentional.

4. When the model applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as checkable claims. One: the output is produced by countable events. Hindola passes; Hukum passes with a caveat, since expansion arrives through conversations recorded inconsistently and enters as an ARR rate. Two: the rates are stable over the horizon. Hindola passes over a quarter and fails over four, because cost per install is seasonal and trial-start moves with mix; Hukum fails across a pricing change. Three: the inputs are movable. Hindola’s cost per install is set by an auction.

It misleads when the binding constraint sits outside the chain, when rates have no stable meaning before product-market fit, and when the output is a stock whose composition the team does not control.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product companies meet the seam problem first. Hukum’s procurement suite and its invoice-matching module share a sales team and a customer base, so one chain double-counts: an account won for procurement that later takes invoice matching is new-logo in one model and expansion in another. Mature companies nominate one company model, call anything sold to an existing account expansion, and accept that the product accounts will not reconcile.

Two-sided markets break the single chain: the middle rate belongs to the ratio between the sides, not the product. Hansa Freight Exchange, a Visakhapatnam load-matching marketplace, posted 36,000 loads in a month and matched 62 per cent — 22,320 loads — at an average freight value of ₹28,000: gross merchandise value of ₹62.496 crore and, at a 6.5 per cent take rate, revenue of ₹4.06 crore. When demand spend lifted postings 40 per cent to 50,400 with truck supply unchanged, the fill rate fell to 48 per cent: 24,192 matched loads, ₹67.74 crore of GMV, ₹4.40 crore of revenue — an 8.4 per cent gain from a 40 per cent input increase. A supply pass instead, postings held at 36,000 and fill rate raised to 71 per cent, gave 25,560 matched loads, ₹71.57 crore of GMV and ₹4.65 crore: 14.5 per cent.

Fig. 2 — Demand added to a supply-constrained exchange becomes unmatched postings.

Hardware plus software adds a capacity term no funnel rate captures. Hridaya Imaging Devices in Mysuru placed 120 diagnostic units in the December quarter at ₹11 lakh each, ₹13.2 crore of hardware revenue, taking its installed base from 860 units to 980. Software attached to 55 per cent of new placements, 66 units, on top of 430 already attached: 496 subscribing units at ₹42,000 a quarter, ₹2.08 crore of recurring revenue, an attach rate across the closing base of 50.6 per cent. The chain must also carry the plant’s limit of 135 units a quarter.

In regulated products a regulator’s rule sits in the chain as a hard rate that product work improves only within limits. AI-native products put variable cost inside the chain. Hetu Resolution Cloud, billing ₹9 per automated resolution against an inference cost of ₹3.40, handled 18 lakh conversations a month at 64 per cent auto-resolution: 11,52,000 resolutions, ₹1.04 crore of revenue, ₹39.17 lakh of cost, 62.2 per cent gross margin. At 72 per cent: 12,96,000 resolutions, ₹1.17 crore of revenue, ₹44.06 lakh of cost — margin unchanged at 62.2 per cent, because on consumption pricing a product gain scales revenue and cost together. On per-seat pricing it would have raised margin outright.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent modeller

The model describes; it never explains. Hindola knows trial-to-paid is 15 per cent. Nothing says whether the loss is a payment failure, a price objection or a dull first lesson. The tell-tale sign is a team that states a rate to one decimal and cannot name the screen where it is lost.

Growth rates decay mechanically, even when nothing changes. With cohort and churn rate held constant, Hindola grows 3.83 per cent in month one, 3.36 in month two, 2.96 in month three and 2.06 in month six, because the churn term scales with a base that is growing while the cohort does not. The tell-tale sign is a plan extrapolating last month’s percentage.

Fig. 3 — One recursion, four input sets. Three curves flatten below the target; the fourth crosses in month six.

The ceiling is the first thing to compute, not the last. Flow over churn gives the asymptote in one cell: 2,56,667 subscribers on the base plan, 3,08,000 at 7.5 per cent churn, 2,93,333 at ₹2.10 crore of spend. It settles in seconds whether a target is reachable. The comfortable reading, that any target yields to time, is false wherever churn exceeds zero.

A blended rate hides a mix that moves with nobody touching the product. Hindola’s 22 per cent trial-start rate blends 17.2 per cent on 5,00,000 paid installs with 34 per cent on 2,00,000 organic ones. Push paid spend up and the blend falls although neither rate changed. The tell-tale sign is asking for a rate split by source before repeating it.

Churn is a function of tenure, and blending it couples acquisition to retention. Hindola’s 16,200 cancellations decompose exactly into 22 per cent of the 23,100 newest subscribers (5,082) and 7.086 per cent of the 1,56,900 older ones (11,118). That changes Pass A: at 26,400 new subscribers cancellations become 5,808 plus 10,884, or 16,692, so net additions fall from the 10,200 the flat-rate model claimed to 9,708 — 5.39 per cent growth, not 5.67.

Marginal cost curves, so a spend scenario is never a multiplication. Pass A buys 20 per cent more installs for 50 per cent more money only because cost per install rose from ₹28 to ₹35. The tell-tale sign is output scaling exactly with spend.

Referral is a loop term, and treating it as a constant understates the ceiling. Hindola’s 2,00,000 organic installs are roughly 1.11 per paying subscriber per month. Make organic endogenous and the recursion becomes base × 0.9467 plus 16,500, whose ceiling is 3,09,375 subscribers — ₹10.80 crore of MRR, 52,708 subscribers and ₹1.84 crore above the constant-organic answer. Over six months the loop is nearly invisible, ₹7.55 crore against ₹7.44 crore; over four years it is the whole argument.

A model nobody else can open is not a model. Nothing in the arithmetic decides whether Hindola is run on subscribers, MRR or contribution after acquisition cost; that judgement belongs to whoever is accountable, which is why an expert settles the output cell first, then hands the file over. The test is whether the CFO changes an input herself.

7. Product type and company stage

The real differences lie in the middle of the chain. Consumer subscription puts a cheap, high-volume top of funnel above a narrow conversion step and a churn rate that dominates past a year. Business software replaces installs with leads and conversion with a sales cycle, and adds net revenue retention: this year’s revenue from last year’s customers over what they paid. Enterprise selling stretches the cycle until the closing quarter is near random, so enterprise models are annual and built on pipeline coverage. Marketplaces need two chains and an endogenous middle; hardware a capacity ceiling; AI products a variable-cost row. Everything else is identical. Stage changes resolution, not method: seed-stage, one chain ranking decisions by order of magnitude; at this scale, nested by channel and segment and reconciled monthly to finance.

8. Three worked examples

Hukum, four quarters out. Retention and expansion run at 101.0 per cent of opening ARR in the base and Pass A and 103.6 under Pass B, with ₹6.72 crore or ₹10.08 crore of new ARR quarterly. Rolling from ₹72 crore, after four quarters the base reaches ₹102.21 crore, Pass A ₹115.85 crore, Pass B ₹111.31 crore, Pass C ₹125.49 crore. Pass A buys ₹13.64 crore of extra ARR for ₹5.64 crore of extra spend, ₹2.42 per rupee; Pass B buys ₹9.10 crore for a one-time ₹1.10 crore, ₹8.27 per rupee. Because expansion applies to a compounding base while new-logo ARR is a fixed addition, Pass B overtakes Pass A in the thirteenth quarter, ₹222.99 crore against ₹221.14 crore.

Fig. 4 — Retention and expansion change the multiplier; new logos change the constant.

Hridaya, funded past the wall. The model was arithmetically sound and missing one row. The plan for the December quarter was 175 placements, ₹19.25 crore of hardware revenue at ₹11 lakh a unit, against a plant that could build 135. It built 135, recognised ₹14.85 crore and missed by ₹4.40 crore. Forty placements’ worth of demand generation at ₹1.10 lakh each, ₹44 lakh, bought orders that became backlog, and the attach on those units — 22 subscriptions at ₹42,000 a quarter, ₹9.24 lakh of quarterly recurring revenue — moved right by a quarter. A model fails most often not because a rate is wrong but because a constraint is absent.

Haldi Meals Network, and the blended rate that broke. Haldi, a Surat ready-meals brand, forecast the March-2027 quarter on 4,20,000 customers and a blended monthly active rate of 38 per cent: 1,59,600 actives, 2.4 orders each — 3,83,040 orders — at an average order value of ₹310, or ₹11.87 crore a month. The 38 per cent averaged first-month cohorts at 61 per cent with post-six-month cohorts at 19, and held only while acquisition kept the mix young. When Haldi cut discount spend the mix aged, the blended rate fell to 26 per cent, and revenue arrived as 1,09,200 actives, 2,62,080 orders and ₹8.12 crore: ₹3.75 crore, or 31.6 per cent, below plan.

The rebuild applied a retention curve cohort by cohort: of a 60,000-customer cohort, 36,600 active in month one, then 26,400, 20,400, 16,800, 13,800 and 11,400, summing to 1,25,400 active-months, 3,00,960 orders and 5.016 orders per acquired customer over six months. At ₹310 and a 22 per cent contribution margin that is ₹1,554.96 of revenue and ₹342.09 of contribution per customer against an acquisition cost of ₹640: the unit economics had never worked, so the fix was not analytical. Haldi took average order value to ₹395 and contribution margin to 29 per cent, and by retiring discount-led channels brought acquisition cost to ₹480: ₹1,981.32 of six-month revenue, ₹574.58 of contribution per customer, paying back inside six months with ₹94.58 to spare.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Borrowed rates. Sign: a rate nobody can point to a query for. Diagnostic: which cohort and date range? Hindola’s first draft used a benchmark 25 per cent trial-start rate against its own 22: 21,000 extra trial starts and 3,150 extra paying subscribers a month, overstating the March base by 15,125 through the 9 per cent churn recursion.

The frozen model. Sign: last modified the day before the last board meeting. Diagnostic: what happened when last quarter’s actuals were entered?

The missing constraint. Sign: no row has a maximum. Diagnostic: what limit does this plan hit first? Hridaya’s ₹4.40 crore miss is the price.

Precision as authority. Sign: outputs to four figures from inputs known to one. Diagnostic: what is the range, and the output at both ends?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Forecast accuracy against constraint identification. The forecasting position is that a model whose predictions are unreliable cannot allocate capital, and a team shrugging off a 30 per cent miss wants budget without accountability; Haldi is its evidence. The constraint position replies that Haldi failed because its model was built to predict rather than expose structure. For the forecasting school to be wrong, capital would have to be allocable on relative answers.

One model or many. The single-model school holds that resolution is the enemy of use: a company chain ten people understand beats forty channel chains one analyst maintains. The nested school points at Hindola’s 17.2-against-34 per cent split: the blend conceals the very effect that weakens the spend increase.

Whether loops belong in the model. The funnel position is that endogenous terms make a model unfalsifiable: once organic installs depend on the base, the ceiling rests on a coefficient estimated from noisy data, and Hindola’s moved ₹1.84 crore on one. The loop position is that omitting it understates compounding products and biases companies towards paid acquisition. An honest practitioner shows both ceilings.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds the chain and presents the output. Someone who has internalised it agrees the output cell before opening the file, and computes the ceiling in the first ten minutes, because it is one division that can end the project. They treat every rate as a range with a source, and argue hardest about the assumed ones, because that is where the decision lives.

12. What the two protagonists did

Tejaswini presented Table 2 rather than a plan. ₹10 crore in March sits only in the 35,000-conversion column, which at flat spend means lifting trial-to-paid from 15 to 22.7 per cent, and at current conversion means ₹3.01 crore a month instead of ₹1.40 crore — while the churn work, which barely moves March, lifts the ceiling from ₹8.96 crore to ₹10.75 crore. She asked the board to fund both, hold spend at ₹1.40 crore, and restate the March commitment at ₹9.15 crore: the 30,000-conversion, 7.5-per-cent-churn cell.

Pranit asked for the expansion squad plus two account executives rather than five — not because Pass B beat Pass A in the quarter, but because Pass A’s advantage is rented at ₹1.41 crore a quarter while Pass B’s is owned for ₹1.10 crore once, and because the model showed the rep request was a marketing request in a sales costume. Farzana’s objection was honest: expansion rates are the least reliable numbers here, and Pass B rests on a 2.3-point lift nobody has yet shown.

Discussion questions.

1. Hindola’s ceiling is ₹8.96 crore of MRR on current inputs and ₹10.80 crore once organic installs depend on the base. Which belongs in the investor materials?

2. With tenure-split churn, Pass A and Pass B grow almost identically. On what grounds other than arithmetic should Tejaswini choose?

3. If Farzana is right that the expansion rate is too poorly measured to plan on, what should Pranit do with the model?

13. Going deeper

  • Growth loops vs funnels — whether the chain is endogenous.
  • Forecasting demand and revenue — the model as a commitment.
  • Growth experimentation process — moving a weak rate.
  • Monetisation as a growth lever — price and mix are inputs.
  • Growth plateaus and saturation — the ceiling formula is the plateau.
  • Scaling: one to n — volume against rates.
  • Modelling and stress-testing growth loops — the disputed coefficient.
  • Acquisition channels and economics — the cost curve’s source.
  • Activation and onboarding optimisation — the deciding rate.
  • Engagement loops and habit — first-month cancellation.
  • Retention strategy — the ceiling’s denominator.
  • Resurrection and win-back — an omitted flow.
  • Virality and the viral coefficient — 1.11 installs per subscriber.

Ujjwal Yatra Systems: Building a Growth Model Before the Chhath Rush

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 29 September 2026, Tanuja Thakur sat in the second-floor office above a sweet shop in Muzaffarpur, with the ceiling fan turning slowly and a blank spreadsheet open on her laptop. The board of Ujjwal Yatra Systems would meet on Friday, 9 October. Ashutosh Choudhary, the founder, had told her that the board would release a pool of ₹1.5 crore for the six months from October to March, and that he wanted one recommendation on how to spend it, not a menu.

Three proposals were already circulating. Each had a champion, and each champion had a persuasive story. Tanuja, the head of product, had a different worry. Nobody had connected any of the stories to a number. Before the board met, she wanted a model that showed which lever moved revenue most for each rupee spent, and she had nine days to build it. Diwali and Chhath, Bihar's busiest travel weeks, were six weeks away.

2. Company background

Ujjwal Yatra Systems was founded in 2019 to serve a segment the large ticketing platforms treated as an afterthought: private bus operators running intercity routes out of north Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand. Most owned between five and thirty buses. Many still sold seats through agents at bus stands and reconciled cash at night; double-sold seats were common.

The company's product, Charcha Bus Book, gave an operator a seat-inventory app, a passenger booking page and a daily settlement report. Passengers paid by UPI, with payments processed through Razorpay under RBI rules for payment aggregators. Ujjwal earned a commission of 5 per cent on the ticket value of each booking and charged operators nothing to join. Passenger data fell under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

The competitive map was crowded at the top. redBus and AbhiBus dominated metro-to-metro routes, MakeMyTrip and Paytm resold bus tickets inside larger travel apps, and state transport corporations such as the Bihar State Road Transport Corporation ran their own booking. Ujjwal's advantage was local: Maithili- and Hindi-first screens and a team that answered the phone in Muzaffarpur. It employed 46 people, twenty-two in the field.

3. The situation

At the end of September, 640 operators were active on Charcha Bus Book, meaning each had taken at least one booking in the previous thirty days. Each averaged 300 bookings a month at an average ticket of ₹640. Exhibit 1 shows the unit economics. At a 5 per cent take rate, each active operator produced ₹9,600 of monthly revenue, and the network produced ₹61.44 lakh a month on ₹12.29 crore of ticket value.

Growth came from two engines. The first was operator acquisition. Exhibit 2 shows the July to September funnel: field agents contacted 1,500 operators, 450 agreed to a demonstration, 180 signed, and 120 went live with a first booking within thirty days. That is 40 new active operators a month. The second was attrition. Roughly 2 per cent of active operators went quiet every month, usually after a settlement dispute or a season in which their buses were pulled for weddings.

Until now the company had steered by instinct and a monthly total. Tanuja's first insight, working in the spreadsheet, was that the business was a stock with an inflow and a leak. Each month's operator count equalled the previous month's count, less 2 per cent, plus 40. Left alone, that arithmetic carried 640 operators to about 795 by March and monthly revenue to ₹76.34 lakh. The proposals were bets on different inputs.

The distributed team saw it differently. Nitin Karn, the engineering lead in Bengaluru, thought new operators were a distraction while settlement reports still broke every second week. Abhay Mishra, a data scientist in Toronto, warned that six months of history was too short to trust any churn estimate to the decimal.

Figure A: The decision window and the six-month horizon.

4. The people

Ashutosh Choudhary, founder and chief executive, Muzaffarpur. He wants the pool spent where it makes the company most fundable by mid-2027.

Harsh Kamat, head of field sales, Patna. His twenty-two agents are the acquisition engine. He wants more of them and argues that operators in Purnia, Gorakhpur and Ranchi are being won by rivals every week.

Nitin Karn, engineering lead, Bengaluru. He wants the money for product reliability and for a referral programme with a partner association, Ghosla Operator Circle, a Patna body of about two hundred operators that had offered to promote Charcha Bus Book to its members.

Abhay Mishra, data scientist, Toronto. He wants the model to carry ranges and not single numbers, and he wants the chosen plan to be reversible if the data disagree.

Tanuja has authority over the analysis, not the budget.

5. The options

Option A: field expansion. Spend ₹1.10 crore to hire and equip a second field team of twelve, lifting acquisition from 40 to 70 new active operators a month. The upside is visible coverage before the festival season. The cost is that new operators inherit the same 2 per cent churn.

Option B: passenger demand. Spend ₹1.50 crore, the whole pool, on Chhath-season campaigns across Google, Meta and regional radio to push passengers to operators' booking pages, lifting bookings per operator from 300 to 345. The upside is immediate revenue from an existing base. The cost is that the lift is an assumption, and nothing remains once the campaign ends.

Option C: retention and referral. Spend ₹70 lakh on a rebuilt settlement report and inventory tools, and on a referral scheme through Ghosla Operator Circle. Monthly churn falls from 2.0 to 1.2 per cent and referrals add 15 operators a month to the existing 40. The upside is a compounding effect on the operator base. The cost is that the churn improvement is a projection that engineering has not yet shown, and the results arrive slowly.

Tanuja read Exhibit 3 as follows. Option B produced the most six-month revenue, ₹63.26 lakh over the base, but it also cost the most,. Option A produced the largest operator base and the largest run-rate gain, ₹16.44 lakh a month. Dividing spend by the extra month-6 run-rate gives a payback in months: A takes 110 ÷ 16.44, about 6.7 months; B takes 150 ÷ 11.46, about 13.1 months; C takes 70 ÷ 11.55, about 6.1 months. Exhibit 4 mattered because of Abhay's caution. The churn input alone was uncertain by a wide margin: if it rose to 3 per cent, the base plan lost 39 operators, wiping out more than the whole 33-operator gain that a better settlement report promised. New-operator inflow, by contrast, was measured directly in the funnel.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, explain in your own words how the four inputs combine to produce network revenue, and why the operator count behaves as a stock with an inflow and a leak.

2. Which inputs in Exhibit 3 are measured, which are assumed, and how does that change how far you trust each option's output?

3. Exhibit 4 shows that churn alone can move the outcome in either direction. What would you need to observe by December to decide whether Option C's 1.2 per cent is realistic?

4. If the board will approve only one option on 9 October, which would you recommend, and what decision rule would you attach to any money not yet spent?

7. A note for the learner

A growth model is a driver-based forecast: it links what a team controls to the number the board cares about, so that a debate about opinions becomes a debate about assumptions. The strongest answers here do three things. They separate measured inputs from assumed ones, they test sensitivity before choosing, and they treat the model as a tool for staging the spend rather than justifying it.

One defensible path is Option C now, with a gate. It has the shortest payback at about 6.1 months and the lowest spend, and it acts on the input, churn, that leaks value from every operator Ujjwal ever wins. It also keeps ₹80 lakh of the ₹1.5 crore pool unspent. Tanuja should tell the board that this reserve is released in December, only if referrals have delivered at least the 15 additional operators a month the model assumes and churn has fallen below 1.6 per cent, roughly halfway from 2.0 towards 1.2. If both conditions hold, the reserve funds part of Option A, whose acquisition inflow can then be bought against a healthier leak. If not, the model has protected the company from spending on operators who would have left.

Option B is the weakest choice on this evidence: its lift is unproven, it costs the most, and while all three paybacks run past the six-month horizon, its 13.1 months is by far the longest. Option A is credible, but buying 70 operators a month into a 2 per cent leak costs more than the headline suggests. Acquisition is not wrong; a model, honestly built, shows the order in which to pull the levers. Tanuja should share the spreadsheet with the board, every assumption on one tab.

Retention Strategy: Bending a Curve You Can Trust

Two corporate-travel software firms, one billing by usage and one by contract, read the same word off four different instruments.

1. Two desks, two definitions of one word

On 14 September 2026 Milind Gadgil, VP of Growth at Chalan Travel Cloud in Kolhapur, held a ₹2.40 crore FY27 programme budget and two proposals he could not fund together.

Chalan sells corporate travel booking plus expense management to Indian mid-market employers of 240 to 3,000 staff, billed on usage: ₹300 per active seat a month plus ₹25 per billable action — a trip booked or a report filed. Because revenue is metered, seat-level retention is revenue. Milind’s benchmark was the April 2025 cohort of 24,000 seats, observed seventeen months. One proposal, at ₹1.40 crore, attacked the worst-retaining segment; the other, at ₹1.00 crore, a healthier one.

Two days later in Solapur, Smita Inamdar, Chief Customer Officer at Waraq Expense Cloud, faced the inverse problem. Waraq sells expense management alone on annual contracts: 60 employer accounts on 1 April 2025 carrying ₹14.40 crore of ARR. FY26 net revenue retention landed at exactly 100.0 per cent, which two directors read as product health. Beneath that flat line lay a seat decay Smita could not price, since an annual contract lets a dying account pay in full for eleven months.

Retention is not one quantity but four — logo survival, revenue survival, binary activity, usage intensity — and they diverge predictably. Which to bend is settled by how revenue is metered and how long the contract hides the truth.

2. The idea, and the four camps that will not agree

A retention curve plots, for one cohort begun at roughly one date, the share still active at each later interval; retention strategy matches interventions to the stage where loss occurs. Underneath sits the hazard rate h(t): the probability that a unit surviving to period t−1 leaves during t. A curve is the cumulative product of one minus the hazard; every live dispute concerns the hazard.

The idea answered a failure. Through the 2000s growth teams reported downloads, signups and total actives — aggregates that rise weekly while a product loses most of what it just bought. Cohort tables in Mixpanel and Amplitude fixed the accounting; interpretation stayed open, and four camps now answer differently.

The habit-formation camp, associated with Reforge and practitioners such as Casey Winters, holds that the hazard falls with tenure because users form habits, so flattening evidences a durable core and investment belongs early. It will not sign that a flat tail is statistical.

The heterogeneity camp, whose lineage runs through Peter Fader and Bruce Hardie’s shifted-beta-geometric models, holds that individual hazards may be constant while aggregates flatten anyway, because high-propensity churners leave first. It signs that aggregates flatten under constant individual hazard given heterogeneous propensities, refuses flattening as evidence of habit, and prescribes better cohort selection over lifecycle campaigns.

The intensity camp argues that a binary active/inactive definition destroys the information you need, the curve worth bending being one of usage depth. The contractual camp holds that only revenue retention clears an audit, and will not call decay inside a renewing account a retention problem before renewal.

3. Mechanics: the cohort table, and why a naive one lies

Chalan’s cohort was keyed on a behavioural event, not a billing date: a seat entered on the day it both booked a trip and filed its first report, since a seat that books but never files behaves like one that never onboarded. Retention meant at least one billable action in the month. Milind’s analytics lead, Bhakti Ghatge, held the team to one convention: every percentage below is a share of the original cohort, and every rate labelled “period survival” is the ratio of two consecutive retained counts. Conflating them is the commonest error in growth reporting.

Censoring, and the cohort table you may not build

The employer side is too small for monthly tables. Chalan signed 96 employer accounts across 2025; the data cut was 31 August 2026. An account signed in November 2025 has been observed three quarters, not six: it is right-censored. A naive table counts the 24 accounts that churned against all 96 and reports six-quarter retention of 75.0 per cent — meaningless, since it credits 72 censored accounts with surviving a window most never entered. Kaplan–Meier instead computes survival one interval at a time against the population genuinely at risk.

Left-censoring inflates every early number

Chalan re-instrumented its pipeline in November 2024, and seats already transacting carried no first-action timestamp, so a cohort built from “first observed activity” dated all of them to November 2024. That cohort of 31,000 seats retained 20,820 at month one, 67.2 per cent, Chalan’s best published figure. Bhakti separated it: 6,660 of the 7,400 pre-instrumentation seats were retained, 90.0 per cent, while 14,160 of the 23,600 genuinely new seats were retained, 60.0 per cent — exactly the rate the clean April 2025 cohort later produced. A quarter of celebration rested on a logging change.

4. When the curve is the right object, and when it misleads

First, the interval must match the product’s usage frequency. Chalan’s field seats travel weekly, so monthly is defensible; its back-office seats file two or three claims a year, so a monthly-active definition guarantees a collapsing curve. Measured quarterly, back-office retention in months ten to twelve is 3,264 of 9,600 seats, 34.0 per cent, against 7.5 per cent monthly. Most of the churn Milind was about to spend ₹1.40 crore on was a cadence mismatch.

Second, the cohort must be homogeneous enough for its aggregate to mean something. If segment shapes differ, the aggregate is a mix index; Chalan fails decisively, and Waraq, with 60 accounts, cannot run the test at all. Third, the metric must move with revenue. For Chalan it does; for Waraq it does not, and here the curve misleads, since an account can lose 70 per cent of its active seats and pay in full until renewal. Smita’s seat curve leads by up to eleven months — good for intervention, useless for forecasting.

5. Hard edges: multi-product, two-sided, regulated, agentic

Chalan sells two modules, and a seat can be alive on one and dead on the other. Retention read as “any billable action” hides the book’s most important pattern: employers who adopted expense but abandoned travel booking. An expert builds a cross-module matrix and treats module abandonment as churn even while the seat counts as retained. The supply side is two-sided: inventory comes through airline, hotel and IRCTC rail aggregators, and on the thin-inventory Kolhapur–Solapur corridor employees book directly instead — churn for a supply reason no campaign can touch.

Regulation creates churn cliffs that are not churn. When RBI card-tokenisation norms required corporate cards to be re-tokenised, affected seats had to re-authorise, and those that did not dropped out of the active count in one month; a team reading the curve without the regulatory calendar calls it a product failure. GST input-credit rules give the mirror artefact: quarter-end pushes for GSTIN-valid invoices make March spike, inflating Q4 retention and depressing Q1.

The AI-native case breaks the instrument outright. Chalan is piloting an agent that books an approved itinerary without the employee opening the app: value rises, sessions fall, and every metric built on human interaction reads the improvement as churn. The repair is to define retention on outcomes — trips completed, claims settled — and accept that the metric’s history breaks there. At the organisational seam, mature companies rarely hold the single source of truth they claim: Growth owns the seat curve, Customer Success logo retention, Finance NRR. What works is one canonical cohort table all three reconcile to.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A flattening curve is not evidence of habit. The tell is an aggregate that flattens while no segment does. The obvious reading — users settled in — fails whenever the population is heterogeneous; hold the month-zero mix constant and recompute first.

Retention and engagement decay in opposite directions. Among Chalan’s survivors, mean monthly actions rose from 3.47 at month one to 3.96 at month twelve while every segment’s own intensity fell — Simpson’s paradox on a growth dashboard.

Table 5 — Billable actions among retained seats. The closing row's per-seat figures are weighted averages, not sums.

The aggregate average is total actions over retained seats: 50,016 ÷ 14,400 = 3.47, and 28,512 ÷ 7,200 = 3.96. Billable volume nevertheless fell by 21,504 actions, 43.0 per cent, because the seat count halved.

The worst curve is rarely the best lever. The tell is a catastrophic curve with a low ceiling: back-office seats cannot retain monthly because they do not travel monthly. Fixing an unfixable segment is the most expensive diligence a growth team can buy.

Involuntary retention reads as loyalty. At Waraq, 48 of the 54 surviving accounts — 88.9 per cent — showed falling monthly active seats while paying in full. The tell is renewal strength with usage weakness; missed, it arrives as one churn wave.

Interval choice is a strategic decision disguised as a reporting one. The tell is a team that borrowed Day-1 retention from a social app. Choosing before reading the usage-frequency distribution predetermines which segments look broken.

Cohort entry must be behavioural, and the behaviour must be the value moment. The tell is a cohort keyed on signup or contract date. Chalan’s book-and-file rule cost a third of its nominal signups and made every downstream number honest.

Censoring cuts both ways. Left-censoring inflates early retention, right-censoring deflates late retention; the tells are a cohort starting at an instrumentation change, and a twelve-month figure on a nine-month book. Small cohorts compound both: Chalan’s Q6 interval rests on 25 accounts, where one more churn moves cumulative survival 2.9 points, from 66.9 to 64.0 per cent.

Engagement correlates with retention mostly by selection, and a curve tells you when, never why. People who were going to stay also open the app more, so the tell is a feature that moved an engagement metric without moving the retention point it targeted. Only a pilot separates lever from symptom.

7. Product type, and company stage

For consumer products the unit is the individual and the interval short, so curves are statistically rich and interventions cheap. For B2B the unit is contested: Chalan’s is the seat, Waraq’s the account, and that difference reorders every downstream priority. For enterprise the renewal cycle dominates and the instrument is net revenue retention — a revenue quantity, not a behavioural one.

Table 6 — Waraq, FY26 revenue retention for the 60 accounts live on 1 April 2025. Bracketed figures are reductions; rates are shares of opening ARR.

Logo retention is 54 of 60 accounts, 90.0 per cent. The gap between the first two is the story: expansion inside a few retained accounts, one Kolhapur auto-components employer above all, paid for six lost logos. A metric letting one good outcome conceal six bad ones, Smita told her board, is for reporting, not managing.

Platforms carry a supply-side curve beside the demand-side one, and supply usually leads. Hardware-plus-software retains on the device replacement cycle, which swamps lifecycle work. AI products face the instrumentation break above plus one new failure: an agent that performs the task retains the account while eroding the user’s competence. Stage matters simply: below a thousand paying units cohorts are too small to segment; between one and ten thousand segmentation becomes necessary; above that the constraint is organisational.

8. Three worked cases, one a failure

Chalan. Option A, at ₹1.40 crore, would lift back-office month-twelve retention from 7.5 to 12.5 per cent, taking retained seats from 720 to 1,200 at an unchanged 1.20 actions per seat, so 1,440 actions. At ₹300 a seat and ₹25 an action: ₹3,60,000 plus ₹36,000, or ₹3,96,000 a month against a base of ₹2,37,600 — incrementally ₹1,58,400 a month per cohort. Option B, at ₹1.00 crore, would lift mid-office month-twelve retention from 30.0 to 36.0 per cent, seats from 2,880 to 3,456 and intensity from 2.60 to 2.75 actions, so 9,504 actions: ₹10,36,800 plus ₹2,37,600, or ₹12,74,400 against a base of ₹10,51,200 — incrementally ₹2,23,200 a month.

Waraq. Smita’s 100.0 per cent NRR and 85.0 per cent GRR sit against seat decay in 48 of 54 accounts. Because no seat behaviour touches revenue before renewal, her programme cannot be justified on this year’s numbers; it is insurance on next year’s GRR. She ranked accounts on trailing-90-day active seats over contracted seats, and found the six that churned had all crossed below 40 per cent two quarters before renewal — converting an unprovable programme into a monitored one.

Chirag Travel Desk, where a bent curve became a worse curve. Suyash Pendse, founder of Chirag Travel Desk in Ahilyanagar, ran 2025’s cleanest-looking retention win: ₹75 cashback for every expense report filed through the app. Across a 12,000-seat cohort, month-six monthly-active retention rose from 3,720 seats to 5,760, or 31.0 per cent to 48.0 per cent, and reports per active seat from 2.4 to 3.6. Two things were wrong. Employees split single trips across several reports, so distinct trips per active seat fell from 1.6 to 1.5 while report volume climbed; and the cashback cost 5,760 × 3.6 = 20,736 reports a month at ₹75, or ₹15,55,200 monthly — ₹93,31,200 over six months. The finance heads who had bought claim-cycle reduction watched queues lengthen. Renewals fell from 44 of 50 accounts, 88.0 per cent, to 37 of 50, 74.0 per cent.

The recovery was definitional. Suyash withdrew the cashback, redefined retention as one trip-linked report per quarter, and rebuilt the roadmap around approval-cycle time. Monthly-active retention settled at 4,080 of 12,000 seats, 34.0 per cent — below the gamed 48.0 and above the original 31.0 — and renewals recovered to 46 of 50, 92.0 per cent. If a definition can be satisfied without the customer getting value, someone will satisfy it that way.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Managing the blended active count. Sign: total actives rise while each new cohort’s month-one figure slips. Diagnostic: plot the last three cohorts separately. Cost: a year of spend into a known leak.

Censoring errors. Sign: retention improves in the month the pipeline changed. Diagnostic: publish the observation window and risk set. Cost: Chalan’s 7.2 phantom points.

Gameable definitions. Sign: retention and value metrics diverge, as Chirag’s reports and trips did. Diagnostic: ask how to satisfy the definition most cheaply without delivering value. Cost: ₹93,31,200 and seven logos.

Trusting contract revenue as engagement. Sign: strong renewals, falling active-seat ratios. Diagnostic: cut retention by trailing-90-day actives over contracted seats. Cost: a renewal cohort lost at once.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The unresolved question is whether individual hazards fall with tenure at all. The habit-formation position rests on evidence from high-frequency consumer products, where cohorts are large enough to control for mix; it would be wrong if, with mix held constant, individual hazards proved flat — which is what Chalan found, and Chalan is a weekly-to-quarterly product, not a daily one. The heterogeneity position rests on the accuracy of models assuming constant hazards and beta-distributed propensities; it would be wrong if interventions timed to tenure points produced durable lifts selection cannot explain. Both hold in their own frequency regime, and the boundary is unmapped.

The second disagreement is whether usage intensity belongs inside the retention metric or beside it. The intensity camp points to Table 5: a binary definition misses both the within-segment decay and the mix-driven aggregate rise. The contractual camp answers that intensity is unauditable and cannot be forecast, and that a company managing to it ends up explaining why revenue fell while engagement rose. Both have survived practice, which argues for two metrics rather than a synthesised third.

The third is stage allocation. One school holds that activation dominates because the largest single loss is always the first interval — 9,600 of Chalan’s 24,000 seats were gone by month one. The other holds that late-stage defence is underpriced, a month-twelve seat being worth more and costing less to keep. Table 7 favours the second, but only because Chalan’s activation problem sat in a low-ceiling segment.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks three questions before looking at a curve: what event defines entry, what interval defines activity, what the observation window is. They state once whether a percentage is of the cohort or of the prior period, and never mix the two. They disaggregate before concluding, and treat an aggregate that behaves unlike its parts as a finding. They know which retention quantity their revenue depends on, and they budget for exit interviews alongside experiments, because a curve locates a loss and never explains it.

12. What each protagonist decided

Milind funded Option B at ₹1.00 crore, held the remaining ₹1.40 crore, and spent ₹4 lakh of it re-cutting back-office retention quarterly first. His reasoning: Option B had twice the payback, and Option A’s case rested on a curve whose shape was partly an artefact of the interval he had chosen. Smita funded no seat-engagement programme in FY26; she made the trailing-90-day active-seat ratio a standing item in every quarterly review, and committed to funding in FY27 if the ratio predicted the next renewal cohort as well as it explained the last.

Three questions. First: Chalan’s evidence that hazards are flat within segments comes from a weekly-to-quarterly product — how far should it generalise, and what product would settle it? Second: if Waraq’s seat ratio does predict FY27 renewals, has Smita shown that engagement causes retention, or only that both are caused by something she has not named? Third: Chirag’s recovery lowered reported retention and raised renewals — under what governance is a growth team rewarded for that trade?

13. Going deeper

Retention curves and the PMF signal supplies the question assumed answered here: whether the curve flattens at all. Retention strategy by segment and lifecycle continues Table 3 directly. Activation and onboarding optimisation is the first interval, where Chalan lost 9,600 seats; Engagement loops and habit is the mid-term lever set and the habit camp’s home ground. Engagement and retention in consumer apps covers the high-frequency regime where this page’s conclusions are least likely to hold; Repeat purchase and loyalty for goods is the same arithmetic without a subscription. Resurrection and win-back addresses the population treated here as gone, and Growth loops vs funnels, Building a growth model and Acquisition channels and economics connect the curve to the system around it.

Lipi Weave Cloud: The Renewal Nobody Owned

A case on retention strategy in an Indian small-business software company

1. The Night Before

On the evening of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Lasya Loganathan was still at the Erode office, three days after the Deepavali shutdown ended and the powerlooms on the Perundurai road restarted their night shifts. On the table lay two printouts her company had produced within four days of each other. One said Lipi Weave Cloud retained 118.6 per cent of the revenue of the customers it kept. The other said that of every hundred textile units that bought the product two years ago, fewer than fifty still paid, and perhaps only thirty-three had chosen to.

At 9.30 next morning the board would meet here, Lavina Lobo joining from Mumbai. Three items: the Series B term sheet from Laghima Capital Partners, expiring 30 November; the ₹4.5 crore retention budget approved on 28 August; and the first-renewal retention target, proposed at 70 per cent before anyone finished checking what the current one was.

She had built the company for seven years on the belief that acquisition was the hard part. The printouts suggested it had never measured the other part.

2. How Lipi Weave Cloud Came to Be Built This Way

Lasya Loganathan, forty-one, grew up above her family's yarn-sizing unit in Erode and spent seven years as a product manager at Zoho in Chennai before returning in 2019. The problem was mundane and enormous: a knitting unit with fourteen machines kept its order book in a notebook, job cards on a nail and wages in a second notebook, and as GST e-invoicing reached smaller thresholds, none of it could be produced on demand.

Lipi Lite shipped in 2020: order book, job cards, wage register and GST-compliant invoicing, in Tamil, Hindi and Gujarati, built for a phone. Lipi Lipik followed for units needing costing and piece-rate wages, and Lipi Laabh for multi-unit groups and export jobwork chains needing traceability across dyeing and stitching.

The decision that shaped everything came in March 2022. Erode and Tiruppur could be sold to directly; Surat, Bhiwandi, Ludhiana and Panipat could not. Lomash Lanka argued for a self-serve funnel; Lasya chose a district-level reseller network — the Lok partners, 420 today across eleven states, usually men already selling weighing scales, ledgers or yarn on commission. To make the economics work for a partner in Malegaon, the company offered a prepaid annual plan and paid 25 per cent of the first year's value on activation, against 5 per cent on any renewal. The agreement, last signed in March 2025, runs to 31 March 2028.

The structure did what it was built to do. It also meant cash arrived twelve months before the customer's verdict, and nobody in the field earned anything worth chasing when a unit renewed.

3. The Industry

India's textile clusters are not one market. Erode and Tiruppur run on knitted garments and export jobwork; Surat on man-made fabrics; Bhiwandi on greige cloth; Ludhiana and Panipat on hosiery. A unit with twelve to sixty machines has a proprietor, a supervisor and no administrative staff, and the Income Tax Act's forty-five-day payment rule for small enterprises has made large buyers punctual and small ones anxious about documentation.

Software reaches these units from four directions: Tally in the accountant's office; Zoho and Vyapar selling invoicing cheaply; Udaan, Meesho, Flipkart and the ONDC network bringing order tooling; and exporters imposing traceability on suppliers. Lipi's ground is narrower — the jobwork chain, where an order is cut in one shed, dyed in another and stitched in a third, and an invoice means nothing without a job card.

Two regulatory facts bear on the decision. The lowering of the GST e-invoicing threshold has been Lipi's best salesman and its weakest retention lever: a unit that buys software to clear a deadline has satisfied its need on day one. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act makes the field practice awkward, since many Lok partners operate customers' accounts on a shared password and an understanding never written down.

Lamsa Textile Trading LLC, a Dubai buying house, requires 140 of its Tiruppur and Erode suppliers to keep traceability on Lipi Laabh and pays for none of it. Those 140 of the 900 Laabh units (15.6 per cent) renew because their buyer says so.

4. What Happened, and What Turned Out to Be Wrong

For three years the company grew as its board deck said. Exhibit 1 is that deck.
