5. The People

Lasya Loganathan, 41, co-founder and chief executive, Erode. She wants a decision that closes the round and fixes the leak, in that order. The term sheet values the company at eight times ARR: ₹238.56 crore pre-money on ARR of ₹29.82 crore. Untold: a Lok partner in Bhiwandi mentioned in 2024 that he renewed accounts on his customers' behalf, and she took it then for diligence rather than measurement.

Lomash Lanka, 38, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune. Onboarding belongs in the product, he argues, not in field visits: guided in-app setup would cost a tenth of a human one. His incentive is a platform rewrite he has wanted for two years. Untold: he distrusts the 14 per cent telemetry gap in Exhibit 4 and thinks it above twenty in Surat, which would make the usage curve worse than it looks.

Lohit Limaye, 45, chief revenue officer, Bhubaneswar, where he runs a 210-seat renewals floor. He wants nothing structural touched before 30 November and would sell three-year contracts hard instead: locked revenue is retained revenue. His variable pay is on new bookings. Untold: a competitor has approached two of his largest Lok partners.

Leela Lokhande, 36, vice-president of customer success, Singapore, covering the Gulf and South-East Asia. She ran the consent audit and believes the first ninety days are where all of it is lost. Her targets are set on Laabh accounts alone, 900 of 20,000 units. Untold: Lamsa's procurement head has twice asked her what alternatives exist ahead of the April 2027 review.

Labdhi Laddha, 33, head of product, Pune. None of the three programmes, she says, addresses the real fault: a product built for a sixty-machine unit is sold to a fourteen-machine one. She wants features removed, and a rebuild of her own. Untold: she has deprioritised the Lite roadmap for two quarters, which may be part of why Lite's day-90 usage is what it is.

Lokesh Lulla, 52, head of field operations, Erode, who built the Lok network and knows most partners by name. He regards the network as the only durable advantage and any change to commission as self-harm. His bonus is paid on activations. Untold: 38 of the 420 partners produced 5,084 of the 12,400 new units in FY2025-26 (41.0 per cent), so the network is far more concentrated than its headcount suggests.

Lubna Latheef, 34, head of analytics, Toronto. She wants the retention definition withdrawn before a rupee goes to programmes: the company cannot choose a lever while it cannot measure the curve. Untold: her consent audit reached 300 owners out of 1,200 attempted, and the 900 who did not answer may not resemble those who did.

Lavina Lobo, partner at Laghima Capital Partners, Mumbai, a director since the Series A. Close the round, she advises, and fix retention afterwards; her fund's position marks up on completion. Untold: her own investment committee has already queried the retention definition in the data room.

6. Voices

"I will not stand in front of an investment committee and explain that our best number was measured only on the customers who stayed. Every company's best number is measured that way. That is the point of it." — Lohit Limaye, management call, 9 September 2026

"The definition is not wrong. It answers one question: when a unit stays, does it grow? Yes, by 18.6 per cent. It does not answer whether a unit stays. We have never put that second question on a slide." — Lubna Latheef, replying on the same call

"The mistake is to think the partner is being clever. In Bhiwandi the proprietor asks him to handle everything — GST, the scale certification, the software. He renews because that is what handling everything means. Change the commission and he hands back the customer, not the money." — Lokesh Lulla, 21 October 2026

"Can we please stop calling it churn. Half of these units did not leave us. They stopped weaving. A retention programme aimed at a shed with the shutters down is a donation." — Labdhi Laddha, product channel, 3 November 2026

"Build onboarding into the app and the partner has nothing to do on day one and nothing on day 365. That is the honest version of our business. It is also the version that takes two years." — Lomash Lanka, four minutes later

7. The Options as Lasya Sees Them

By early November the choice had settled into three programmes, costed by Limaye's team on Latheef's estimates. At 31 October 2026 the company had 20,000 paying units — 15,000 Lite, 4,100 Lipik, 900 Laabh — and ARR of ₹29.82 crore, an average of ₹14,910 a unit. Of those, 18,000 fall due for renewal between 1 December 2026 and 30 November 2027, carrying ₹26.79 crore of ARR: 13,500 Lite, 3,700 Lipik, 800 Laabh.

Lagaav would give every newly activated unit a twelve-week onboarding: two visits from a specialist in its own language, ninety days of order book and wages migrated, e-invoicing configured against its GSTIN, two staff trained. It acts on the FY2026-27 intake of 14,000 units, so pays nothing until first renewal in FY2027-28.

Lachak would move Lite onto a monthly mandate at ₹900, with two pause months a year for the slack season. A unit pausing twice pays ₹9,000, exactly today's prepaid price; one that does not pays ₹10,800. It makes churn visible monthly rather than annually — and removes the partner's upfront cash.

Lambai would offer Lipik and Laabh units a three-year plan at a 12 per cent discount, with a named account manager for Laabh. It acts on the 4,500 larger units in the renewal book, where retention is already best.

It is the only option that touches what the exhibits keep pointing at, and the one the March 2025 agreement forbids before 31 March 2028 without ninety days' notice and a make-good of one quarter's average commission, ₹1.22 crore.

8. The Deadline and the Hard Constraints

The board meets at 9.30 on Monday, 16 November 2026. The retention budget is ₹450 lakh and cannot be exceeded without a fresh resolution. On the costs the board will see, Lagaav with Lachak comes to ₹405 lakh and Lachak with Lambai to ₹350 lakh. On the costs Lasya now understands, those pairs are ₹527 lakh and ₹472 lakh, leaving only Lagaav with Lambai at ₹425 lakh — the slowest option joined to the weakest.

Cash at 31 October stood at ₹18.40 crore against a burn of ₹1.35 crore a month: 13.6 months of runway without the round. The Bhubaneswar floor is frozen at 210 seats until April 2027, when the Lamsa contract also falls due for review. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act the company must show a consent trail for partner-operated accounts, and the September audit is the only document bearing on it. The term sheet expires on 30 November, priced on an ARR nobody disputes and a retention figure that is now disputed.

At a quarter past ten Lasya wrote one line in her notebook and did not finish it: we spent four years measuring whether they paid, and none measuring whether they — and the lights in the mill opposite came on for the second shift, and she sat looking at the two printouts, both correct.

9. Questions for Discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 to 3, explain how the company reported rising retention while losing more units each year. Which figure — 118.6, 67.8 or 49.2 per cent — belongs in a board pack, and what is each good for deciding?

2. Exhibit 4 shows more units renewing at day 365 than were active at day 300. List every explanation consistent with the data, including those that make the usage curve wrong rather than the billing figure. What evidence would separate them?

3. Laddha argues that a third of lapsed units stopped operating and are no retention problem at all. If she is right, what is the correct denominator for a target, and how should Lipi decide whom it is trying to keep?

4. The three programmes act at different stages. Using the usage curve, argue for the stage where the money should go; then argue the opposite from the renewal book, and say which case is weaker.

5. Every incentive — partner commission, Limaye's variable pay, Lulla's bonus, Lokhande's targets — rewards something other than a unit still working in month thirteen. Can a retention programme succeed while that holds, and what would changing it before 31 March 2028 cost?

6. It is Monday morning. Where does Lasya put the ₹450 lakh, what number replaces 118.6 per cent on the slide, and what does she tell Lavina Lobo about a term sheet expiring in fourteen days?

Retention Strategy: Bending the Curve at Every Stage of a User's Life

A Rajkot fitness-booking marketplace decides where to spend its next growth lakh — and why the answer turns on which stage of the retention curve is actually broken.

1. A cohort that would not hold

On the morning of 11 August 2026, Umang Kothari, VP of Growth at Vyayam Fitness Systems — a Rajkot app booking classes across some forty partner studios in Rajkot, Jamnagar and Bhuj — opened a dashboard he had checked every Monday for eighteen months.

A member pays ₹1,800 a month for unlimited class credits; studios are paid per class attended. August's ₹9,00,000 acquisition budget could go to widening the paid-ads campaign behind the last 5,000-member cohort, or scaling a six-week pilot — a trainer callback plus a nudge to book within seven days of signing up. The board would fund only one.

Vyayam had a clean benchmark to decide with: its January 2025 cohort of 5,000 had now been observed for nineteen months, long enough to show its full curve. Umang had to decide whether ₹9 lakh fixing month-one activation would out-earn the same ₹9 lakh spent acquiring more members at the unfixed rate — get it wrong, and he'd waste a budget on a leak that wasn't real, or pour 5,000 more members into a bucket that would lose most of them anyway.

2. The idea

Retention strategy is the deliberate set of product and lifecycle interventions — matched to the stage a user is in, newly signed up, newly habitual, or long settled — that bend a cohort's retention curve upward from whatever shape unmanaged behaviour would produce. A retention curve is a plot, for one cohort of users who started on roughly the same date, of what share are still active at each later interval.

The idea was forced into existence by an earlier failure. Early mobile and web growth teams tracked downloads, signups and total active users — numbers that could rise weekly even as the product quietly lost most people it had just acquired, because a growing front door hides a leaking back one. Analysts borrowed a fix from survival analysis, the statistics actuarial and medical research uses to track what share of a population is still "alive" at each interval after a starting event; applied to a product, "alive" became "active." Through the 2010s, tools such as Mixpanel and Amplitude built cohort tables into core reporting, and growth writers, notably Brian Balfour at Reforge, argued that acquisition, activation, retention and referral had to be managed as four separate levers, not one problem. The sentence Umang could repeat without sounding glib: "We don't manage growth, we manage a curve."

3. How it actually works

A retention curve is only useful once separated into three stages, since a lever that moves one does almost nothing to the others. The new-user stage runs from signup to an activation window — for Vyayam, roughly seven days, since class-booking is weekly, not daily, so a Day-1 metric borrowed from a social app is close to meaningless. The job is getting a member to their first real value moment, which Vyayam learned was not signing up or booking, but attending a class. A member who books but no-shows behaves afterward almost like one who never signed up.

The mid-term stage, week two to month three, converts a first class into a routine — Vyayam's benchmark for "habitual" is three classes a week. Its levers differ in kind: calendar reminders, credit-rollover so a missed week isn't punishing, and enough studio variety that boredom doesn't set in.

The long-term stage, month three onward, is where a curve that will flatten actually does, into a plateau — the loyal core a forecast is built on. The job is no longer persuasion but defence: catching a skipped week before it becomes a lapsed month.

Newcomers routinely skip three steps: grouping cohorts by the date of the value event, not an arbitrary calendar boundary, or the batches compared age inconsistently; defining the activation event behaviourally — attendance, not booking — or every downstream number is meaningless; and reading a curve for its shape, since only a flattened one says there is a durable core worth defending.

4. A worked example, line by line

Vyayam's January 2025 benchmark cohort began at 5,000 members: paid digital ads (2,600, 52 per cent), member referrals (1,500, 30 per cent) and studio walk-ins (900, 18 per cent).

Table 1 — January 2025 cohort, by acquisition channel

Tracked monthly: by month one, 3,000 of the original 5,000 — 60 per cent — were still booking classes. By month two, 2,250 of the 5,000 — 45 per cent — were active, also 2,250 of the 3,000 who remained at month one, a rate of 75.0 per cent. By month three, 1,900 of the 5,000 — 38 per cent — remained, an 84.4 per cent rate on the 2,250 base. The curve kept flattening: 1,650 — 33 per cent — by month six, and 1,500 — 30 per cent — by month twelve, where it held. That final 1,500 is Vyayam's loyal core.

Piloted (M1 = 70%)1,750₹1,800₹31.5 lakh
Difference250—₹4.5 lakh

At ₹1,800 a member, the benchmark cohort is worth ₹27.0 lakh a month by month twelve; the piloted cohort, ₹31.5 lakh — a ₹4.5-lakh gain from identical spend, purely from moving month-one activation. Against the ₹9,00,000 programme cost, that pays back in two months — provided only activation changed and the later rates truly carried over, an assumption the next section interrogates.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Shape matters more than any single point

A curve flattened by month six or twelve, however low, tells a different story than one still falling toward zero. The first has found a durable core; the second only looks stable because nobody waited long enough. Month-one alone, without asking whether the curve later bends, is half the picture.

Cohort curves versus blended aggregates

Active users can climb even as every new cohort retains worse than the last, since a blended total mixes a mature base with a poorly-retained new one and reports only the average. Vyayam's mature Rajkot base could mask a Jamnagar cohort quietly failing in the same chart.

Correlation is not the lever

Engaged members retain better, but pushing an engagement metric up — more opens, longer streaks — does not make retention follow, since the correlation is partly self-selection: people staying anyway also open the app more. Only a controlled pilot separates a lever from a symptom.

Matching the lever to the stage

A streak badge aimed at brand-new members, who haven't yet felt the product's value, does little — it's a mid-term habit tool misapplied to an activation problem; a trainer callback aimed at month-nine loyalists is wasted the other way, persuading people who need no persuading.

Retention is behaviour, loyalty is attitude

A member on an annual plan who stopped booking but hasn't cancelled looks, on a billing chart, identical to a delighted regular. This is involuntary retention — the contract, not the enthusiasm, holds them — and it resolves as a churn wave at renewal.

What the curve cannot tell you, and how small a cohort can mislead

A curve shows members leaving and roughly when; it says nothing about why — a drop needs exit surveys and support tickets, not another chart, to diagnose. And size matters: a curve built on 5,000 members can be trusted to a couple of percentage points, while one built on a 200-member pilot swings wildly from sampling noise alone.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

Vyayam is a marketplace, so the member side is only half the curve. Every studio partner has its own retention curve, and if partner density in a neighbourhood thins out, members churn regardless of how well onboarding works, because there is nothing nearby left to book — a supply-side curve a pure consumer app rarely manages in parallel.

Contrast B2B SaaS, where the unit of retention is the account, not the user, and the standard metric is Net Revenue Retention — netting expansion, contraction and cancellation across a renewal cycle that is often annual, with churn risk invisible until renewal.

Stage matters too. An early-stage, single-city Vyayam leans almost entirely on activation — cheapest, and the only lever with enough data yet. A larger, multi-city Vyayam moves to curves segmented by city, studio category and channel, plus win-back programmes for lapsing members — past a certain size, no single lever fits every segment.

7. Common mistakes

Chasing the blended number. Symptom: total active members keeps rising. Misunderstanding: front-door growth is read as retention health. Diagnostic: pull the newest two or three cohorts onto their own curve before trusting any aggregate.

Engagement features without a named stage. Symptom: an engagement score climbs while the retention point it should move stays flat. Misunderstanding: treating "engagement" as one goal instead of tying each feature to a stage's job. Diagnostic: name the exact curve point a feature should move, then check that point.

Reading contract lock-in as loyalty. Symptom: billing-based renewal looks strong, around 92 per cent, while attendance among those renewing is quietly falling. Misunderstanding: "still paying" is treated as "still getting value." Diagnostic: cut retention by classes attended in the trailing thirty days, not billing status.

Borrowing the wrong interval. Symptom: Day-1 retention looks alarmingly low, triggering a panic fix. Misunderstanding: a daily-use interval applied to a weekly-use product. Diagnostic: check the product's own usage-frequency distribution first.

8. What good looks like

When Vyayam's Jamnagar pilot launched with a 200-member cohort, city lead Omkar Trivedi saw month-one retention land at 90 of 200 — 45 per cent, well under benchmark. He didn't reach for a discount or copy the Rajkot script — he noted 200 was small enough for a wide margin of error, and waited rather than reacting to one point. Exit interviews surfaced the real constraint: Jamnagar had only four partner studios against Rajkot's forty, so members couldn't find a class nearby. Omkar's team signed three more studios instead of spending on nudges. The next cohort's month-one retention rose to 130 of 200 — 65 per cent: diagnose the constraint before prescribing the fix.

9. What Umang decided

Umang approved the ₹9,00,000 onboarding programme for August and left the paid-ads budget alone. The pilot showed a causal lift on the number that mattered most at this stage, month-one activation, not a correlation borrowed from a dashboard, and the arithmetic showed a two-month payback well inside what the board already accepted elsewhere. He also asked his team to build a supply-side view — studio density by neighbourhood — before the next launch, a direct lesson from watching Omkar diagnose Jamnagar correctly rather than copying Rajkot's playbook.

What to learn next: clean experiment design for cohort pilots, so a test like this doesn't contaminate the cohorts compared; and segmentation by channel and city, since a blended curve turns misleading once no one lever fits every part. Two questions worth sitting with. First: if the lift had come from discounting the fee rather than a trainer callback, would the same arithmetic still justify calling this a win — or manufacture a price-driven version of the involuntary retention this page warned against? Second: for a curve still falling at month twelve, what is the cheapest test to tell whether it will flatten, or keep falling regardless?

Haveli Thali Club: Bending the Curve

A decision case in retention strategy

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Hitesh Anand sat in the glass-walled meeting room above the central kitchen in Jalandhar, watching a cohort chart that refused to improve. Anand was co-founder and chief executive of Haveli Thali Club, a subscription service that delivered home-style lunch thalis to office workers and paying-guest residents across Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh. His board would meet on Monday, 12 October. Before then he had to commit the company's entire retention budget for the coming quarter, ₹20 lakh per monthly cohort, to one of three programmes. Diwali fell on 8 November, always a weak time for renewals.

The problem was not acquisition. Every month roughly 40,000 new people paid for their first Haveli Thali Pass. By the end of a year, only a quarter of them were still eating with the company. He had to decide where to stop the leak.

2. Company Background

Haveli Thali Club was founded in 2019 by Anand, a former hotel-management graduate, and his cousin. The idea was plain: a rotating weekly menu of dal, sabzi, roti and a sweet, cooked by about 1,800 home-cooks and small cloud kitchens who were trained, audited and licensed under FSSAI rules, and delivered in steel-lined boxes between 12:00 and 1:30 in the afternoon. The Haveli Thali Pass was a monthly subscription priced at an average of ₹2,400, the equivalent of 24 lunches at ₹100 each.

The competition was formidable. Zomato and Swiggy offered on-demand lunch with vast choice, and Zepto was testing cooked meals. None of them offered a predictable, home-tasting plate at a fixed monthly price, which was Haveli's ground. Renewals ran on UPI mandates. The company operated in 14 cities, and it was profitable at the kitchen level: after food, packaging and delivery, contribution came to 30 per cent of revenue, or ₹720 per subscriber per month.

3. The Situation

In August, Hiral Mistry, the head of growth, working from Ahmedabad, rebuilt the cohort dashboard so that every monthly cohort could be followed by day. She took a typical cohort of 40,000 new subscribers and traced them (Exhibit 1). After 30 days, 24,800 were still paying. After 90 days, 15,200. After 180, 11,600. After a full year, 10,000.

Of the 30,000 subscribers lost over the year, 15,200 left in the first month, just over half. A further 9,600 left between day 30 and day 90, and only 5,200 in the remaining nine months combined. The curve flattened. Those who survived the first quarter tended to stay. The curve had a floor, a good sign of product-market fit, but the company was losing most of its customers before they discovered why the product was good.

Anand asked why people left in the first month. The customer-success team, led from Kochi by Hridaya Nair, had for a year sent an exit survey to every subscriber who cancelled. Nair tabulated the 15,200 first-month leavers (Exhibit 2). The largest reason, at 4,560 people or 30 per cent, was delivery timing: the box arrived at 1:20 when the customer needed to eat at 12:45. Menu monotony and taste accounted for 3,800, or 25 per cent. Price was cited by 2,280, or 15 per cent, and travel or a wish to pause by 2,432, or 16 per cent. Nair noted that most first-month leavers had never called a single agent, never changed a delivery slot, and never told the kitchen what they disliked. "They did not quit the thali," she said. "They quit a default setting that nobody ever asked them to change." In Ahmedabad, Mistry added that the sign-up flow assigned a slot and a menu automatically, so the first real conversation happened only when the customer complained.

4. The People

Hitesh Anand, Jalandhar, chief executive, needed a decision the board would trust. He feared spreading the budget thinly.

Hiral Mistry, Ahmedabad, head of growth, owned the dashboard and the engineering squad of nine. She favoured fixing the beginning of the journey, but was candid that her squad could build only one large programme before the Diwali rush.

Hridaya Nair, Kochi, head of customer success, ran a team of 60 agents fluent in Hindi and Punjabi. She wanted her agents on calls that changed outcomes.

Himmat Sodhi, Jalandhar, head of kitchen operations, was answerable for the 1,800 kitchen partners. He feared any programme that promised customers freedom in slots and menus, since every extra choice complicated routing and food safety.

5. Exhibits and the Three Options

Mistry and Nair together costed three programmes. Each was estimated to add a number of subscribers still active at day 180 from a single monthly cohort of 40,000, and each survivor was valued at six further months of contribution, that is 6 × ₹720 = ₹4,320. Exhibit 3 sets out the results. The survivor counts were estimates from small pilots, not measurements.

Exhibit 3. Estimated economics of each option, per monthly cohort of 40,000

Option A: Hamari Pehli Thali. Every new subscriber would receive a call from Nair's team within 48 hours, a choice of three delivery windows, a one-minute taste questionnaire, and an app checklist for the first seven meals. It would cost ₹18 lakh per cohort, most of it agent time. It attacked the stage where 50.7 per cent of losses occurred, and the two largest exit reasons, timing and taste, which together explained 55 per cent of first-month leavers (30 plus 25). Its risk was that kitchens would have to honour three slots.

Option B: Hifazat Skip. Subscribers could pause any week, skip single days with a credit, and swap dishes. It would cost ₹14 lakh per cohort and mainly addressed the 16 per cent who cited travel or pausing, plus the mid-term dip between days 30 and 90. It was cheaper, but it did nothing for someone who had never settled into the service.

Option C: Haqdaar Annual. A prepaid annual pass at a 10 per cent discount, with points redeemable against festival sweets. It would cost ₹15 lakh per cohort, including the discount. It reached only those already loyal, who needed the least help.

6. Questions for Discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, at which stage of the customer's life does Haveli lose most of its subscribers, and what does the flattening of the curve after day 90 tell you about the product itself?

2. Using Exhibit 2, which of the stated reasons for leaving can the company fix directly, and which can it only soften? What would you want to know before trusting self-reported reasons?

3. In Exhibit 3, each option is ranked by value per rupee, by net value and by what it addresses. Do the rankings agree, and how sensitive is the choice to the survivor estimates?

4. If you were Anand, what would you tell the board on 12 October, and what would you ask Sodhi and Mistry to do before Diwali?

7. A Note for the Learner

How the topic frames the decision. Retention strategy asks where on the curve a company should intervene. The lesson of the lens is that different stages have different causes. New-user retention is about reaching the first moment of value. Mid-term retention is about habit and flexibility. Long-term retention is about switching costs and reward. A programme aimed at the wrong stage can be well designed and still change nothing.

One defensible path. Choose Option A. It targets the stage that holds 15,200 of the 30,000 lost subscribers (50.7 per cent), it answers 55 per cent of the exit reasons, and it has the highest net value at ₹33.84 lakh per cohort and the highest return per rupee at 2.88. It also fits inside the ₹20 lakh budget with ₹2 lakh to spare. The economics survive a harsh test: at ₹18 lakh cost and ₹4,320 per survivor, the programme breaks even at about 417 extra survivors, roughly 35 per cent of the pilot estimate of 1,200.

The reasoning should be staged. Anand should have Sodhi confirm that kitchens can support three windows in two pilot cities, and run Option A on the October and November cohorts with a holdout group, so the board sees measured rather than estimated survivors. Option B is the natural second step once the first month is fixed, since customers who stay past day 30 are the ones who need flexibility. Option C should wait: an annual prepayment offered to a leaky base merely locks in customers who have not yet been served well. A strong answer names the trade-off: fixing the front of the curve delays annual-plan cash.

Dhwani Katha Networks: The Streak Question

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 29 September 2026, Divya Rathore sat in a quiet corner of the Indore office of Dhwani Katha Networks with two dashboards open and a deadline in front of her. The company's board would meet on Friday, 9 October, and the growth team wanted its Diwali plan approved by then. Diwali fell on 8 November, and the festival fortnight was historically the busiest listening period of the year. Any change had to reach the stores by the last week of October.

Rathore, a co-founder and the chief product officer, had to choose how the company would make users come back. One dashboard showed that a "streak" mechanic had lifted early activity sharply. The other showed that it was costing the app its goodwill.

2. Company background

Dhwani Katha Networks was founded in 2019 by Rathore and Dhruv Joshi, a former telecom engineer, to serve people who wanted stories and short learning audio in their own language. The app offered folk tales, serialised fiction and ten-minute lessons in Hindi, Marathi, Malayalam, Telugu and Tamil, to commuters and homemakers in smaller cities and to Malayali and Telugu families in the Gulf.

By September 2026 the app had 12,00,000 monthly active users (MAU) and about 3,00,000 daily active users, a DAU/MAU ratio of 25 per cent. A monthly plan cost ₹99, and roughly 3 per cent of new users converted to paid. It competed with Pocket FM and Kuku FM in vernacular audio, JioSaavn and Spotify for commute listening, and YouTube for idle minutes.

Dhwani's users had no natural daily need: a story is finished, and the next one is a want, not a task. Unlike PhonePe or Zerodha, whose triggers are bills and market hours, Dhwani had to create its own reasons to be opened.

3. The situation

In June, Hemant Kulkarni, head of growth, proposed a streak: a counter of consecutive days on which a user listened for at least five minutes, with a flame icon, a badge at seven days and a push notification at 9 p.m. warning that a streak "will be lost tonight". Hannes Vogel, the designer in Berlin, proposed a weekly "recap" of what a listener had finished, with a next-story suggestion and at most three notifications a week, timed to the user's own habits.

Rathore let both run. From 3 August to 27 September, 1,80,000 randomly chosen users were split into a control, a streak arm and a recap arm of 60,000 each. Exhibit 1 gives the results.

Exhibit 2 charts the same results as percentages. The first row favoured the streak. In week 4, 34.0 per cent of the streak arm was active against 26.0 per cent of the control and 30.0 per cent of the recap arm. Kulkarni read this as proof that loss-framed reminders worked. Deepika Iyer, the data scientist in Toronto, pointed to the later rows. By week 8 the streak arm's active share had fallen to 23.0 per cent, only two points above the control's 21.0 per cent, while the recap arm held 25.0 per cent. Of those active in week 4, the streak arm kept 67.6 per cent, the control 80.8 per cent and the recap arm 83.3 per cent. The streak had pulled activity forward from people who then left.

The opt-out and uninstall figures pointed the same way. Some 29.0 per cent of the streak arm turned notifications off, nearly double the control's 15.0 per cent, and 18.0 per cent uninstalled the app, against 10.0 per cent in the control and 11.0 per cent in the recap arm. Conversion to paid rose from 3.0 per cent in the control to 3.5 per cent in the streak arm and 4.5 per cent in the recap arm.

Harpreet Sandhu, running customer success from Singapore, reported a surge in tickets and Play Store reviews mentioning "spam" or "guilt". Gulf users wrote that a 9 p.m. India-time alert reached them at 7.30 p.m., in Dubai traffic. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, targeting also needed consent, and Sandhu worried that dark-pattern complaints could attract regulators.

4. The people

Divya Rathore (Indore) owned the decision and wanted a loop she could describe to a listener without embarrassment.

Hemant Kulkarni (Pune), head of growth, was measured on quarterly activity and argued that rivals already used streaks.

Hannes Vogel (Berlin), designer, wanted to reward listening rather than punish absence.

Deepika Iyer (Toronto), data scientist, wanted eight-week retention, not four-week activity, and warned of novelty effects.

Harpreet Sandhu (Singapore) spoke for users writing in and for the Gulf audience.

5. What the numbers imply in rupees

Iyer scaled the results to the 12,00,000 base, twenty times each arm. A subscriber was assumed worth ₹594 in the first year (six months of ₹99), and each extra uninstall ₹60 to replace through paid acquisition. Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune priced the build at ₹6 lakh for the streak and ₹28 lakh for the recap loop. Exhibit 3 shows the outcome.

The streak's revenue gain was small because its conversion gain was half a point, while its cost in lost users was large. Kulkarni objected that brand harm exceeded replacement cost, and that the test ran in a quiet season, missing the festival fortnight. Iyer agreed on the second point.

6. The options

Option A: ship the streak to all users before Diwali. It is cheap at ₹6 lakh, quick, familiar, and gives the strongest week-4 activity. The cost, visible in Exhibits 1 to 3, is faster decay, high opt-out, and a loop that works by making users anxious.

Option B: build the recap loop and cap notifications. Users would get a weekly summary, next-episode suggestions and at most three notifications a week in local time, with an easy opt-out. It costs ₹28 lakh and about six weeks, so the festival launch would be tight. It grows slower at first but held 25.0 per cent at week 8 and converted best.

Option C: change nothing and extend the test. Run both mechanics through Diwali and decide in January. This settles the novelty question but wastes the busiest season and leaves the board without a plan.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What is the trigger, action, reward and investment in each of the two loops? Which of them gives the user something they would value even if no notification arrived?
  2. Why did the streak arm lead in week 4 and fall behind by week 8? What does that pattern say about the metric the growth team was rewarded for?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, which assumptions would have to change for the streak to beat the recap loop, and how plausible are they?
  4. What would you tell the board on 9 October, and what protections (consent, time zones, opt-outs) would you build into whichever loop you choose?

8. A note for the learner

An engagement loop is a cycle in which a trigger prompts an action, the action delivers a reward, and the user invests something that makes the next trigger stronger. The question is whether the reward is real. A streak's reward is the avoidance of a loss the product invented; a recap's reward is a deeper tie to stories the user chose. Both raise activity for a time, but the first spends goodwill and the second builds it.

A good answer starts from evidence. Exhibit 1 shows the streak's week-4 lead reversing by week 8, with double the opt-outs and uninstalls, and Exhibit 3 shows the recap loop as the only positive net effect. A weak answer cites week-4 activity alone, or bans reminders on principle.

One defensible path is Option B with a hedge. Build the recap loop and the three-a-week cap, respect time zones from the first release, and store notification consent separately. Keep the streak out of the general release, but let Iyer run a 5 per cent festival holdout with an opt-in counter and no loss warnings, which answers the novelty concern without staking the season on it. Give the board week-8 retention and paid conversion as the success metrics. Dhwani has no natural daily trigger, so it must earn its returns, and the honest loop is also the one the numbers favour.

Option C is a fair second choice if the build cannot be staffed. Option A is defensible only as a labelled experiment.

Engagement Loops and Habit

Why users come back — and whether the loop bringing them back would survive being described to the people it acts on.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On 15 September 2026 Suhasini Mallya, vice-president of product at Dastoor Field Cloud in Nagpur, was handed a memo by her chief revenue officer. Dastoor sells the order-capture app that FMCG distributors’ sales reps use to walk a beat and log orders at each kirana counter. It had 640 paying accounts and 19,200 licensed seats at ₹180 per seat per month — ₹34.56 lakh of monthly recurring revenue, ₹4.15 crore annualised. Of those seats, 13,440 were active in a typical month and 6,048 on an average day: a stickiness ratio of exactly 45.0 per cent. The memo proposed a rep leaderboard with daily streaks and points. Her renewal review with the board was on 12 October.

Eighteen days earlier Nilanjan Bose, co-founder and head of product at Dincharya Money Works in Lucknow, faced the mirror image. Dincharya is a daily-savings app — a digital gullak — sweeping small sums into a liquid fund and gold. It had 38,00,000 registered users, 9,60,000 monthly actives, 1,92,000 daily actives (stickiness 20.0 per cent) and 2,88,000 on a live daily-deposit mandate, 30.0 per cent of monthly actives. Assets under management were ₹600 crore, ₹20,833 per mandate holder, earning a 0.90 per cent annual trail; a ₹99-a-month premium tier had 38,400 subscribers, 4.0 per cent of monthly actives. His lead investor, before a 20 October term sheet, wanted a streak.

Exhibit 1 — Dincharya Money Works, annual revenue at 31 August 2026
Revenue lineBasis₹ crore a year

Premium subscription38,400 users × ₹99 × 124.56
Total annual revenue—9.96

Both were asked to approve a mechanic before answering the prior question: what loop exists, how much of the returning behaviour it causes, and which parameter of the retention curve a mechanic could move.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

An engagement loop is a closed sequence — trigger, action, reward, and an investment by the user that makes the next trigger land better — through which a product earns a further use without paying again for attention. A habit is the state in which the trigger has migrated from outside the user to inside: the cue is a feeling, not a notification. The loop is the machine; the habit is what it manufactures.

The lineage runs from B. J. Fogg’s behaviour-design work at Stanford — behaviour occurs when motivation, ability and a prompt coincide — through Nir Eyal’s 2014 Hook model to the growth-systems literature of the late 2010s. It was invented for a commercial problem: software of that era bought a first use cheaply and had no apparatus for producing a second, so retention curves collapsed and paid acquisition leaked.

Four positions have since hardened. The behaviour-design camp signs: a product that does not design its return trip loses to one that does. It will not sign that engagement is evidence of value. The natural-demand camp, which reads a cohort curve’s flat part as a verdict on product-market fit, signs: the asymptote is a property of fit with a recurring need; mechanics redistribute users along the curve rather than raising its floor. It will not sign that a streak lifts a floor. The growth-systems camp signs: a loop is worth what it contributes to a compounding growth model, so measure its output into acquisition and monetisation, not its daily-active count. It will not sign that engagement is an end in itself. The attention-ethics camp, including Eyal’s later work, signs: a loop whose users wish they used the product less is defective however strong its numbers. It will not sign that revealed preference settles the question.

The first two disagree empirically, and ordinary internal data cannot settle it.

3. Mechanics in depth: the floor, the slope and the provenance of the trigger

A cohort retention curve of the kind Dincharya’s analyst Aparajita Sen produces monthly is well described by a decay towards a non-zero asymptote:

R(t) = a + c · bt, where a is the retention floor, b the monthly survival of the above-floor excess, and c that excess at t = 0.

The floor a is the share of a cohort for whom the product has joined a recurring routine, and it is what acquisition spend buys; b governs how fast the merely curious leave, and onboarding polish mostly moves b and c. That a loop is strategic rather than cosmetic is exactly the claim that it raises a — and Day-7 and Day-30 retention cannot tell a floor effect from a steeper early curve.

Aparajita fitted the model to the March 2026 cohort’s mandate-holders. With a floor of 46 per cent, a decay of 0.61 and an excess of 39 points at signup, it reproduces every month from M1 to M6 to within 0.7 of a percentage point. That is Nilanjan’s objection in one line: the mandate-holder floor already sits at 46 per cent, the non-mandate group has shown no floor after six months, and a streak that lifts Day-7 numbers is a proposal about c.

Exhibit 2 — Dincharya March 2026 cohort: monthly deposit activity, split by loop participation
MonthMandate group retainedRateNo-mandate retainedRateBlended retainedBlended rateMoM churn (blended)

The second implicit mechanic is the provenance of the trigger. A vendor push spends attention that depletes; a trigger from another human inside the customer’s own organisation costs the vendor nothing; an internal cue costs nothing and is the only kind that survives a marketing freeze.

The third is the character of the investment. The literature rarely separates an asset, which makes the product better for the user, from a hostage, which makes leaving expensive without making staying better. A rep’s beat notebook is an asset; a 43-day streak that resets to zero is a hostage. Both raise measured retention; only one survives a competitor with a migration tool.

4. Conditions, stated as testable claims

One: the underlying need recurs at least as often as the trigger. Dastoor passes — a rep walks a beat six days a week. Dincharya fails: salaries arrive monthly, so the “daily” in daily savings is a designed frequency over a monthly need, and the mandate is what makes it hold — it automates the deposit and leaves the visit optional.

Two: the core action delivers value independent of the reward. If the action is worth doing only for the reward, the reward is the product. Logging an order is how a Dastoor rep gets paid; a Dincharya deposit earns a real return. A leaderboard fails this test the moment points become the reason to open the app.

Three: the investment is an asset to the user. Dastoor passes with beat notes and fails with a streak count; for Dincharya a mandate, a balance and a goal are assets in the ordinary sense.

Four: the same person invests and benefits. This is where business software quietly breaks. At Dastoor the investor is the representative and the renewer is the distributor’s owner, so a loop built on the rep’s habit never reaches the buyer — and the memo did not mention the owner once.

The framework actively misleads twice over: for products whose value is delivered by not being used — backup, insurance, monitoring — where engagement is a cost to the user; and for episodic purchases such as a tax filing, where loop language manufactures daily reasons to visit and earns uninstalls. The right instrument there is resurrection.

5. Hard edges: multi-product, two-sided, regulated, hardware and AI-native

In multi-product companies the loops interfere. Dastoor’s owner dashboard has a weekly rhythm and its rep app a daily one; with a pooled notification budget the daily product consumes the owner’s tolerance and the weekly product’s open rates fall for reasons invisible in its own data. Mature firms allocate one contact budget per human recipient.

In two-sided businesses the loop is designed twice and the rewards conflict. Dopahar Meals Network, a lunch-subscription service in Surat with 18,000 subscribers on a ₹2,400 monthly plan, rewarded a streak with a free meal; the cost landed on its kitchens’ capacity exactly when demand spiked.

In regulated categories variable reward is often unavailable by law rather than taste. Dincharya cannot dangle randomised monetary bonuses on deposits without colliding with how investment products may be marketed in India, and the suitability question — is it right to nudge this user to deposit today — has no analogue in a games studio. Such loops run on information and progress instead.

In hardware-plus-software the object is the trigger and the app optional. Dhaatri Home Devices, a connected water-purifier maker in Raipur, has 1,40,000 installed units and 22,400 monthly active app users, 16.0 per cent of units. As an engagement number that is a disaster; correctly read it is irrelevant, because the device runs daily regardless and revenue turns on the nine-month filter cycle — yet the app team is measured on engagement and the business on consumables.

In AI-native products corrections and context make the model measurably better for that user — the strongest asset investment available. But a capable agent reduces the visits needed for the same work, so engagement falls as the product improves and teams carrying consumer instrumentation here read success as churn. Measure work completed per user, not sessions.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. The floor and the slope are different businesses. A competent practitioner reports that retention improved; an expert asks which parameter moved. The tell is a deck showing Day-7 up and Day-30 flat: that is a change in c — more people looked twice, the same number formed a habit. The obvious reading fails because curiosity and fit are different causes.

2. A ratio without its denominator’s calendar is noise. Dastoor’s 45.0 per cent stickiness invites benchmarking against consumer apps. An expert notes that a representative works about 26 days a month, not 30, so the real question is what share of working days a rep opens the app.

3. Loop participation is almost always selection. Dincharya’s mandate-holders retain at 48.0 per cent at M6 against 3.7 per cent for the rest — a 44.3-point gap that reads as the case for pushing everyone onto a mandate. The expert’s tell is the size of the gap: effects that large in observational data are dominated by who chose the feature. A September holdout of 12,000 new depositors, split evenly, found day-60 retention of 24.0 per cent against 16.5 per cent — 1,440 users against 990 — a causal lift of 7.5 points.

4. A reward with a marginal cost is a liability that scales with success. Points cost nothing per unit; free meals and cashback do. The tell is a reward budget growing with the metric it improves, so the mechanic costs most exactly when it works. The obvious reading — that the reward pays for itself — needs the retained user’s contribution to exceed the reward’s cost, an inequality nobody writes down before launch.

5. Trigger provenance is the honest maturity metric. The tell is push volume rising quarter on quarter while sessions per active user stay flat. An expert tracks the share of sessions with no message in the preceding day, as in Figure 2, and treats a rising push share as a warning.

6. Asset and hostage investment look identical in the data. Both raise retention and switching cost. They diverge under two conditions only: a competitor with a migration path, and a user asked plainly whether the product serves them. The tell is in churn interviews — leavers from an asset-based product describe what they lost, leavers from a hostage-based one describe relief.

7. Engagement that does not touch the revenue equation is a vanity loop. The tell is an engagement win presented without a contribution line. Dopahar’s weekday order rate rose 14.5 per cent while monthly contribution fell 73.3 per cent. In business software the same question applies to people: the loop is built in a rep’s hands, the contract is signed by an owner, and Dastoor’s high field-sales attrition means many habituated seats change occupant yearly. The tell there is seat-level engagement beside account-level churn.

8. The cheapest decisive experiment is a blackout, and teams refuse to run it. Switching off vendor triggers for two weeks against a holdout reveals the internalised share directly. The tell is the reason for refusing — that the quarter cannot absorb it — which concedes that the engagement is borrowed rather than built.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

The anatomy does not change across contexts; three things do. Who owns the trigger: the vendor in consumer, a colleague or scheduled event in B2B, the other side of the market in a platform, the object in hardware. What the investment is: personal history in consumer, configuration and integrations in enterprise, reputation in marketplaces, context in AI products.

Enterprise habit forms more slowly and breaks less easily, because the investment is organisational and a manager’s mandate substitutes for motivation; it fails differently, dying when the sponsor leaves. In platforms engagement on one side is the reward on the other, so a loop raising buyer visits without raising seller earnings merely moves cost around. Hardware businesses should adopt consumption-cycle targets.

Stage changes emphasis more than method. A pre-fit company should not build mechanics at all: its floor measures whether the product is needed, and mechanics contaminate the reading. Scaling is where designed loops pay, because the floor exists and the task is moving more of each cohort onto it. At maturity the loop is optimised so well that nobody asks whether it should exist.

8. Three worked examples

Dastoor Field Cloud: the loop as a renewal instrument

Tejeshwar Bhatia, Suhasini’s analyst, segmented the 500 accounts that came up for renewal in the twelve months to 31 August 2026 by the average stickiness of their seats.

The 7:30 a.m. vendor push gave way to the supervisor’s beat assignment appearing in the app, and reps got a private beat notebook whose notes and photographs persisted into the next visit.

Dincharya Money Works: the floor that has to move, and by how much

Dincharya’s March 2026 cohort cost ₹96 per first-time depositor, ₹230.40 lakh for 2,40,000 depositors. Six months on, the surviving 40,800 users generate two streams: 3,264 of them, 8.0 per cent, pay for the premium tier at ₹99, which is ₹3,23,136 a month; and cohort assets of ₹32.04 crore — 34,560 mandate-holders averaging ₹9,000 and 6,240 others averaging ₹1,500 — yield a 0.90 per cent trail worth ₹2,40,300 a month. Monthly revenue from the cohort is therefore ₹5,63,436 and acquisition cost is recovered in 40.9 months, against the 24 the investor’s model assumed. Reaching 24 months needs ₹9.60 lakh a month, 1.70 times today; from retention alone the M6 floor would have to rise from 17.0 per cent to roughly 29.0 per cent.

Dopahar Meals Network: the mechanic that worked and nearly killed the company

Dopahar launched a streak on 1 February 2026: twenty consecutive weekday lunches earned a free meal. It worked as designed: the weekday order rate per subscriber rose from 0.62 to 0.71 within six weeks, up 14.5 per cent. On a 22-weekday month at a food cost of ₹142 a meal, the arithmetic of a fixed-price plan turned against them. A subscriber on the ₹2,400 plan eating 13.64 meals cost ₹1,936.88 and contributed ₹463.12; at 15.62 meals the cost was ₹2,218.04 and the contribution ₹181.96. In March, 7,380 subscribers — 41.0 per cent of 18,000 — completed at least one streak, a free-meal cost of ₹10,47,960, or ₹58.22 per subscriber, taking contribution to ₹123.74. Monthly contribution fell from ₹83.36 lakh to ₹22.27 lakh, a loss of ₹61.09 lakh, while every engagement metric improved.

The recovery, led by product lead Hemant Zope, had three parts. The guaranteed free meal became a variable reward with a bounded expected cost: a one-in-six chance of a ₹38 dessert, an expected ₹6.33 per meal served. Utilisation settled at 0.67, giving 14.74 meals at ₹148.33 including the reward, ₹2,186.38 of cost and ₹213.62 of contribution. Third, the plan was repriced from ₹2,400 to ₹2,760, up 15.0 per cent, which cost 11.0 per cent of subscribers and left 16,020. Contribution per subscriber became ₹573.62 and monthly contribution ₹91.89 lakh, 10.2 per cent above the pre-streak baseline. The lesson was not that streaks are bad but that a loop raising consumption of a fixed-price service is a pricing decision in disguise.

9. Failure modes, their early signs and the cost of late detection

Pumping the loop instead of building it. Early sign: push volume per active user rising while sessions stay flat. Diagnostic: what share of sessions began with no message in the previous 24 hours, and is it rising? Caught late, the base has learned to ignore the channel.

Rewarding the metric rather than the behaviour. Early sign: engagement improves while contribution does not. Diagnostic: which term of unit economics does this mechanic change?

Designing above natural frequency. Early sign: uninstalls concentrated days after a notification-heavy onboarding. Diagnostic: how often does the need actually recur for this segment? Caught late, the brand acquires a reputation for nagging and acquisition cost rises permanently.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live dispute is whether mechanics can move the floor. The natural-demand position, steelmanned: the floor measures how many people have a recurring need this product serves better than the alternatives, and the evidence is the stability of floors across redesigns: the early curve moves, the asymptote does not. For it to be wrong there would have to be identified cases where a mechanic changed the asymptote rather than the approach to it; those are scarce because almost nobody runs a holdout long enough.

The behaviour-design position, steelmanned: the floor is not a constant but the share of users who got far enough in to discover the recurring value, so mechanics carrying more users past that threshold do raise it. Dincharya’s holdout supports this — a mandate prompt produced 7.5 points of causal day-60 retention. For it to be wrong, that lift must decay to zero by M6, the measurement Dincharya has now committed to.

A second disagreement is normative. One camp holds that a loop the user would not endorse is a defect and that a regret question belongs beside stickiness; the other holds that stated preferences about one’s own behaviour are unreliable and that a regret metric imports one group’s aesthetics. The middle ground in Figure 5 is a compromise neither camp fully accepts.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in three visible ways. They describe the existing loop before proposing a new one, including the weak steps. They state which parameter of the retention curve a proposal should move before the experiment runs. And they put the mechanic’s cost, in rupees and in attention, in the same table as its benefit, so the decision reads as a trade rather than an improvement.

12. What each protagonist decided

Suhasini took neither the leaderboard nor a refusal to the 12 October review. She took the pilot: trigger ownership moved to the customer’s own supervisor, daily actives up 71.4 per cent on 1,500 seats, notification-free sessions up from 32 to 67 per cent, and a conditional benefit of ₹13.50 lakh across the Low band if its renewal rate reaches the Medium band’s 80.0 per cent. She asked for a renewal cycle with a holdout of 25 Low-band accounts first, and told the board the figure was an assumption with a test attached.

Nilanjan declined the streak on 20 October. A 40.9-month payback cannot be closed by a mechanic, because closing it from retention alone needs the M6 floor to move from 17.0 per cent to about 29.0 per cent. He committed to raising first-fortnight mandate adoption, causally worth 7.5 points of day-60 retention, and to a pricing review of the ₹99 tier, whose 4.0 per cent penetration of monthly actives he considered the real constraint.

One: Dincharya’s mandate-holders retain at 48.0 per cent and its other users at 3.7 per cent, but the randomised lift is 7.5 points at day 60. Which number belongs in an investor deck, and how would you present the other two?

Two: Dastoor’s most effective change handed the trigger to the customer’s own supervisor. What does a vendor lose by not owning the trigger, and when is that loss worth accepting?

Three: Dopahar’s streak improved every engagement metric and cut monthly contribution by 73.3 per cent. What single artefact, required before launch, would have caught it, and who should own it?

13. Going deeper

  2. The Hook model — the four-step formulation and its critiques.
  3. Notifications, email and lifecycle messaging — the machinery of external triggers.
  4. Engagement and retention in consumer apps — where the ethics are sharpest.

  6. Building a growth model — turns a 40.9-month payback into a decision.
  7. Acquisition channels and economics — an immovable floor may still be affordable.
  8. Activation and onboarding optimisation — governs the excess term c.
  9. Retention strategy — floor, slope and resurrection as a portfolio.
  10. Resurrection and win-back — for the episodic products this framework misleads.

Engagement Loops and Habit

Why users come back, and whether the loop bringing them back is one you would explain to their face.

1. A Tuesday in Jaipur

On the morning of 11 August 2026, Ritvik Choudhury, head of growth at Laya Wellness, a home-workout app headquartered in Jaipur, opened a dashboard he had stared at for three weeks and saw the same flat line. Laya Wellness let users book seven-minute guided movement sessions, and its board — meeting on 2 September — had asked for a credible path from the app's current monthly recurring revenue of roughly ₹8.38 lakh to something closer to ₹10.5 lakh, without raising acquisition spend. Acquisition was not the problem; installs converted into first sessions at a respectable clip. The problem sat downstream — users tried the app, liked it well enough, and quietly stopped opening it. Ritvik's designer, Meher Anand, had a redesign ready, built around notifications, streaks and a points system. His job before 2 September was not to approve or reject it on instinct, but to work out, with numbers his analyst Naveen Iyer could defend line by line, whether the loop would actually bring people back — and whether he could describe it honestly to the board.

2. The idea

An engagement loop is a repeatable sequence — a cue that prompts a user to act, an action, a reward that follows, and something the user invests that makes the next cue land better — engineered so a product gets used again without the company winning the user back from scratch each time. The term entered product vocabulary from B. J. Fogg's behaviour work at Stanford in the early 2010s and was popularised by Nir Eyal, whose 2014 book Hooked packaged it into the four-step "Hook model": Trigger, Action, Variable Reward, Investment. Eyal was solving a specific problem — venture-backed consumer apps of that era acquired users cheaply but had no reliable mechanism for turning a first use into a habit, so retention curves collapsed and paid acquisition became a leaking bucket. The engagement loop was his answer: design the return trip, not just the first visit.

The sentence Ritvik could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: an engagement loop only counts as designed, rather than accidental, if you can name what triggers the next visit, what the user gets for it, and what they leave behind that makes the next trigger land better. A founder who cannot answer those three questions does not have a loop — only a funnel that happens to repeat, and repetition without design decays the moment a competitor offers a shinier reward.

Figure 1 — The loop, walked through Laya Wellness

3. How it actually works

The mechanics practitioners state out loud are the four boxes in Figure 1. The ones they usually leave implicit are the conditions under which the arrows hold. The trigger can be external — a push notification, an email — or internal, a cue in the user's own head, such as boredom at 7pm or the itch of an unbroken streak. Early in a product's life almost every trigger is external, because the user has not yet built an association between the product and a feeling; Laya Wellness's push notification is doing that work for now.

The action has to be the smallest behaviour that plausibly delivers value — Fogg's own work argued that action happens only when motivation, ability and a trigger arrive together, which is why Laya Wellness's core action is a seven-minute session, not a forty-five-minute class: it lowers the ability bar so a modestly motivated user still clears it. The reward has to be variable — unpredictable enough that the user cannot fully anticipate it, since a fixed, expected reward habituates far faster than one that varies. The step most founders skip is investment: something the user puts in — data, a public streak, a friend invited — that improves the next round and honestly raises their switching cost. Ritvik's read was that trigger and action were fine at Laya Wellness; reward and investment were thin, so users completed one or two sessions and had nothing pulling them back but a notification they had started to ignore.

4. A worked cohort, and what changes when one input moves

Naveen Iyer pulled the June 2026 cohort for a clean baseline. Of 80,000 installs, 34,000 opened the app within 24 hours — 42.5 per cent. Of those, 20,400 completed a first session, the activation event — 60.0 per cent of openers, 25.5 per cent of all installs. That 20,400 is the base every later step has to work from.

Exhibit 1 — June 2026 install cohort, Laya Wellness (n = 80,000 installs)

Every later figure had to build from the 20,400 activated users, not the 80,000 installs — a mistake Naveen had already flagged, where a colleague quoted a "retention rate" against the wrong base. From all recent cohorts combined, Laya Wellness's steady-state base by August 2026 stood at 42,000 monthly active users (MAU) with an average 8,820 daily active users (DAU) — a stickiness ratio of exactly 21.0 per cent. At a 4 per cent paid-conversion rate, that MAU produced 1,680 paying subscribers at ₹499 a month, or ₹8,38,320 (₹8.38 lakh) in monthly recurring revenue — the flat line Ritvik had been staring at.

Meher's redesign targeted the step Ritvik suspected was weak: reward and investment between Day 1 and Day 7. It left the funnel's front untouched — 80,000 installs, 34,000 openers, 20,400 activated users — and modelled Day-7 return rising from 35.0 to 45.0 per cent, on the logic that a better variable reward and a visible streak would pull more first-time users back a second time. That lifts Day-7 returners from 7,140 to 9,180. Holding Day-30 conversion at 60.0 per cent of Day-7 returners, Day-30 habitual users rise from 4,284 to 5,508 — a 28.6 per cent increase, carried through the chain from the one input Meher's team controlled.

5. What a learner has to become sharp about

Loop versus funnel. A funnel is something a user passes through once; a loop is a funnel that feeds itself, where the last step becomes input to a future first step. Many "retention initiatives" are funnel optimisations wearing loop language, and plateau where a real loop would keep compounding.

Habit versus dependency. The honest test is whether the user, asked directly, would say the returning behaviour serves them. A loop that survives only because leaving is more painful than staying — a lost streak, sunk social capital — is not a habit in the healthy sense; it is a toll booth, and invites reputational risk once users notice.

Variability is not manipulation by itself, and it is not gamification either. Slot machines and a language app's streak both use variable reward; the difference is whether the action delivers value independent of the reward. A seven-minute session is worth doing even without the bonus points — the reward accelerates habit around something already worth doing. Points bolted onto a weak core action produce only a brief novelty bump that decays within weeks.

Internal triggers are the real milestone. A loop that still needs an external push after a year has not matured. The metric to watch is not notification open rate but the share of sessions with no notification at all.

Natural frequency sets a ceiling. No loop can make a user return more often than the underlying need recurs — this topic sits downstream of stickiness for that reason. Forcing daily triggers onto a weekly-rhythm need manufactures irritation, not habit.

What it cannot tell you, and what to ask before relying on it. A well-designed loop explains why a user who tried the product keeps returning; it says nothing about why they tried it first, and cannot manufacture product-market fit where none exists, nor prove causation until tested against a cohort that did not get the new mechanic. Ask what exactly the user invests, whether that makes their next visit better for them and not just more likely, and what happens if the external trigger is switched off for two weeks.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

ContextTypical triggerTypical investment
Consumer app (Laya Wellness)Push notification, social proofStreak, logged history, invited friends
B2B / workplace softwareTeammate's action, scheduled reportConfigured workflow, stored data, integrations
Marketplace (two-sided)New listing, price drop, message receivedSaved searches, seller reputation, reviews left

In consumer products the loop competes hard for attention, so the variable reward carries real weight. In B2B software the trigger is often a colleague or scheduled event rather than the vendor, and the investment is organisational — a configured dashboard, an integration another team depends on — so B2B habits form slower but stick harder. In a marketplace the loop must be designed twice: a reward that pulls buyers back can irritate sellers, whose loop runs on demand signals instead. An early-stage team like Laya Wellness's leans on manual external triggers because it has not earned internal ones; a scaled company can afford richer loops, but risks optimising one so hard it never asks whether the loop should exist.

7. Common mistakes

Mistaking a busy notification calendar for a designed loop. Symptom: push open rates quietly decline quarter over quarter. Error: treating "send more triggers" as the fix rather than building a reward or investment step that needs fewer nudges. Diagnostic: plot the share of sessions with no notification in the prior 24 hours — if it is not rising, the loop has not internalised.

Measuring retention against the wrong denominator. Symptom: a retention number that looks strong in a deck and weak in the ledger. Error: dividing returners by total installs instead of the activated base that ever had a chance to form the habit — exactly what Naveen caught in an earlier draft. Diagnostic: ask what population the percentage is out of, before trusting it.

Optimising the loop past the point users want it. Symptom: engagement rises while reviews mention feeling "hooked." Error: treating every extra nudge as pure upside with no cost to trust. Diagnostic: halve trigger frequency for two weeks — if notification-free sessions hold steady, the extra triggers were only borrowing habit, not building it.

8. What good looks like

A team handling this well starts, as Meher's group did after Ritvik pushed back on the first draft, by naming the existing loop in full before touching it — trigger, action, reward and investment, one sentence each, including the weak parts. They isolate one step to change, hold the rest of the funnel fixed so the effect is legible, and state in advance what they expect the specific metric that step governs to do — here, Day-7 return — rather than promise to "improve engagement." They also build in a check for the unhealthy version of the win: if Day-7 return rises but notification-free sessions do not, that signals borrowed behaviour, and they say so in the same deck rather than a later post-mortem.

9. What Ritvik decided

Ritvik took Meher's redesign to the board as a monetisation case built on one named assumption: Day-7 return rising from 35.0 to 45.0 per cent among already-activated users, worth ₹2.40 lakh a month if it held, and nothing if the lift came only from users who would have returned anyway. He asked for a four-week holdout test first, 20 per cent of the activated cohort kept on the old mechanic, so Naveen could isolate the real effect before engineering scaled it. The board approved the test, not the rollout — the honest version of the ask. From here, the natural next reading is how the trigger itself gets designed — notifications, email and lifecycle messaging — since a loop is only as good as the cue that starts it. Two questions worth sitting with: if your product's notifications were switched off for two weeks, which users would come back anyway — and would you be comfortable telling them exactly what you are inviting them to invest, and why?
