Jatan Vidya Cloud: The Two Thousand Six Hundredth School

1. The night before

On the evening of Tuesday, 13 October 2026, rain came down the Sevoke Road in Siliguri in the flat, unhurried way of a Dooars monsoon that has not finished. Jharna Jalota, co-founder and chief executive of Jatan Vidya Cloud, sat alone above a tyre showroom with two printouts and a board meeting at eleven the next morning.

The first was the figure her chief financial officer, Jiten Jetley, had put on the agenda: annual recurring revenue at 30 September 2026 of ₹38.04 crore. The second was the same figure a quarter earlier, ₹38.21 crore. For the first time in seven years the number had gone down — in a quarter when the company added eighty-five schools net, opened two districts in Odisha and spent more on sales than ever before.

Page four of the board pack said "temporary seasonality", a sentence she had written on Sunday and stopped believing on Monday, when Joyeeta Jash sent her cohort file from Toronto under the subject line "read the students column, not the schools column". Jarnail Jassal of Jarul Growth Partners would fly in from Mumbai at dawn. The Series B carried a second tranche of ₹30 crore, released on annual recurring revenue of ₹48 crore at 31 March 2027. The gap was ₹9.96 crore, and the last two quarters had produced ₹0.59 crore between them.

2. How Jatan got here

The company began in 2019 as Jatan Rasid, a fee-receipt tool Jharna wrote with Jishnu Jhingran while auditing schools around Siliguri. Reconciliation that took a clerk eleven days a month took an afternoon; at ₹9,000 a year per school, it had a hundred schools by March 2021.

The move that made the company, and now constrains it, was the shift in 2022 to a price per student per year. Jatan Patrika, the administrative core, went out at ₹300 per student, later ₹380; Jatan Shulk followed in August 2022 for fee collection over UPI mandates, priced the same way. Every large school became worth ten small ones.

Two decisions from that period still bind. In March 2023 Jatan signed Jasim Education Holdings, a Dubai group of thirty-one Indian-curriculum schools in the UAE and Oman, at ₹700 per student to 31 March 2028, price frozen, with a client exit window at 31 March 2027. In February 2024, chasing scale before the Series B, it signed the Janhit Schools' Consortium — budget schools across North Bengal, Sikkim and western Assam — for 612 members at ₹165 per student to 31 March 2027, under a most-favoured-pricing clause barring any member being charged more than a comparable school nearby. It bought 612 logos in one quarter and fixed the ceiling on home-market pricing for three years.

The Series B, ₹62 crore, closed in September 2024 on a plan assuming 1,100 new schools a year and revenue per student holding at ₹290. Headcount is 428: 196 in Siliguri, 114 in Pune, 92 in Guwahati, the rest distributed, including Joyeeta Jash in Toronto and Jeet Jhaveri in Singapore.

3. The industry

India has more recognised private unaided schools than most countries have schools, and very few buy software. The decision sits with a trustee, is made once a year before the new session, and is judged against a clerk's salary. Teachmint, Classplus, LEAD Group and Extramarks reach the same tier-two towns, several giving an administrative module away to sell content or financing, while Zoho and Tally hold the back office.

Three outside forces bear on the arithmetic. Fee-regulation law in West Bengal and Odisha limits what a school may add to its fee, and so what a principal believes he can pass on to parents. NPCI's mandate framework and the aggregators — Razorpay, PayU, the bank-sponsored players — have driven collection pricing towards commodity levels, thinning the rebate Jatan earns on flow through Jatan Shulk. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with its rules on verifiable parental consent, applies squarely to a platform holding attendance and bus locations for fourteen lakh minors.

Exposure outside India is small in logos and large in margin: forty-eight Gulf schools, 1.8 per cent of the live base, produce ₹4.20 crore of the ₹38.04 crore of annual recurring revenue, at ₹700 per student against a domestic realised average of ₹247.

From Joyeeta Jash to Jharna Jalota, 12 October 2026, 02:14 IST:

"Every chart we show the board counts schools. Our price is per student. Last quarter schools grew 3.4 per cent and students 1.4 per cent, and realised price fell from ₹271 to ₹266. Two of those lines are about size and price, not about how many logos Jishnu can close."

From the internal chat, 9 October 2026:

Juhi Jariwala: "₹12,500 a school on self-serve. ₹2.28 lakh in the field. Can somebody explain why we are hiring executive number 95?"

Jiten Jetley: "Because your schools are 168 students each, ₹0.64 lakh a year at list, and 26 have gone. Show me a hundred self-serve schools above 400 students and I will fund you tomorrow."

"Forty-eight schools out here pay ₹700 and two and a half thousand at home pay ₹247. When I ask Pune for Arabic report cards I am told consent work comes first. But Jasim can leave in March, and the day they ask for an export file is not the day to start that conversation."

8. The options as Jharna sees them

A — fund the frontier. Forty executives and ₹4.2 crore over two quarters, aimed at Odisha and Jharkhand. At the latest ₹2.28 lakh a school that buys about 184 schools; at the trailing blended ₹1.41 lakh, about 298. At ₹0.86 lakh of first-year ARR each, neither approaches the ₹9.96 crore the covenant needs, which would take roughly 1,158 new schools in two quarters against the 397 signed in the last two.

B — stop selling and start collecting. Freeze new logos for two quarters, point the roadmap at usage and billing coverage, raise realised price at renewal. Moving coverage from 76.9 per cent to 90 per cent at ₹266 per student would add roughly 2,44,000 billed students and about ₹6.49 crore, the largest single number available. It needs implementation capacity the company does not have, and a pricing move the Janhit clause may forbid until April 2027.

C — change the channel. Cut forty field executives, move schools under 400 students to self-serve and partner onboarding, redeploy the saving. It lowers cost per school by an order of magnitude and revenue per school with it, on a test of 112 schools of which 26 have gone.

D — follow the price. Fund the Gulf roadmap, defend the Jasim renewal, sell into the region's 520 Indian-curriculum schools at ₹700. ARR per school is about six and a half times better than at home, ₹8.75 lakh against ₹1.32 lakh; the whole market is 520 schools.

Every option is a claim about where to sell, to whom, or through which channel. None is a claim about what the company sells, or about the unit it charges for — and the consortium agreement, the frozen Dubai price and the per-student model were all decisions about that unit. Jharna noticed this on Sunday and cannot decide whether it is an insight or an evasion.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at eleven on Wednesday, 14 October 2026. The second tranche of ₹30 crore releases on annual recurring revenue of ₹48 crore at 31 March 2027; the gap is ₹9.96 crore. Cash is ₹21.4 crore against ₹1.35 crore of net burn a month, and sales and marketing has run at ₹11.60 crore over four quarters.

The Janhit clause runs to 31 March 2027 and covers 612 live schools, 3,64,000 billed students and ₹6.01 crore of ARR at ₹165 per student. The Jasim contract holds ₹700 to 31 March 2028, its exit window a year earlier. Fourteen of the eighty-six engineers in Pune are committed to consent work under the DPDP Act until March, and it cannot slip. Renewals for the North Bengal base, about 1,600 schools, fall between February and April — the window in which new schools also decide and implementation capacity is exhausted.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2 only, argue that this is market saturation, then argue against it. What must each side ignore?
  2. Exhibit 3 shows blended net revenue retention of 110.4 per cent while Exhibit 1 shows revenue falling. Reconcile them. What would let you decide which exhibit to believe?
  3. Exhibit 5 shows cost per school rising from ₹1.08 lakh to ₹2.28 lakh in four quarters. How much is mix and how much the sales organisation? What further table would settle it?
  4. Exhibit 6 puts Jatan at 52.0 per cent of its own addressable list and 5.1 per cent of all recognised private schools in those states. Which number should the board use, and what does choosing it commit them to?
  5. Joyeeta argues that the company counts schools and prices students. If she is right, which option survives, and what would a fifth look like?
  6. It is eleven on Wednesday. What does Jharna put in front of the board, what does she ask them to approve, and what does she say about the ₹48 crore milestone, when the Janhit clause, the Jasim window and the consent build all resolve within six months?

11. Wednesday, 11 a.m.

At a quarter past midnight Jharna laid the two pages side by side: 2,606 schools, and 14,30,000 students in schools that hold 18,60,000. Somewhere between those numbers was the sentence she had to say at eleven, and she could construct four defensible versions. Jishnu's would be the easiest to fund and the hardest to deliver. Jahnavi's would be the most honest and would show as a flat January, three months before the covenant was measured. Juhi's was cheap and untested. Jeet's was the most profitable per school and the smallest.

The rain had not stopped. Jharna turned to page four, read her own sentence about seasonality once more, and deleted it, which left the page blank and the meeting ten hours away.

Growth Plateaus and Saturation

Two school-ERP companies in coastal Andhra Pradesh watch their growth lines flatten in the same quarter of 2026. The arithmetic that tells the cases apart also shows the flattening was visible five months earlier, to anyone computing the one ratio that leads the top line.

1. Two flat lines, two different diseases

On 30 September 2026, Deepthi Kolluru, vice-president of growth at Yojana Campus Systems, closed the month with 1,997 schools under licence — six fewer than she had opened it with. Yojana, founded in Vijayawada in 2019, sells fee-collection and administration software to private K-12 trusts across coastal Andhra Pradesh and Telangana at ₹180 per student per year, and had added schools every month for four years. Annual recurring revenue had just crossed ₹3,963 lakh, up from ₹3,378 lakh on 1 April: one line falling, the other climbing. Her board wanted to know which to believe.

Ninety kilometres away in Rajahmundry, Nagaraj Bhagavatula faced the same question with opposite symptoms. Jatan School Systems, which he co-founded in 2021, sells to single-school proprietors with no salesperson: the head clerk signs up on the web, uploads a roster and pays ₹1,450 a month. In April 2026 Jatan took 3,000 signups and converted 378; in September it took 4,500 — half again as many — and converted 360. Its paid base moved from 9,832 schools to 9,840, marketing spend from ₹15.12 lakh to ₹27.00 lakh a month.

The cases share a surface and nothing else. Yojana's channel was still producing, but qualified schools had stopped converting and customers had stopped staying; Jatan's was producing more than ever, and the extra volume was worth less. Both boards were offered the same word — saturation — and in neither case was it doing analytical work.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

A growth plateau is a period in which net additions to the quantity a business grows — users, accounts, revenue — fall to near zero while the business keeps doing what produced growth before. Saturation is one candidate explanation: that the pool available to grow into has been substantially consumed. A plateau is a measurement; saturation is a diagnosis, and conflating them is the most expensive category error in growth work, because the two license opposite investments.

The lineage has two strands never properly joined. The first is diffusion theory: Everett Rogers's 1962 account of adoption, formalised by Frank Bass in 1969, in which cumulative adoption traces an S-curve whose flattening is arithmetic rather than failure — each period's adopters come from a pool the previous period shrank. The second is growth accounting, which took shape in consumer internet companies in the early 2010s on Dave McClure's 2007 funnel scheme and, more directly, on the flow identity Facebook's analytics group popularised: closing base equals opening base, plus new, plus resurrected, minus churned, with revenue further split by expansion and contraction. Diffusion explains why plateaus are inevitable, growth accounting where one is happening. Neither explains why.

Three schools disagree, and what each refuses to sign is the more informative half. The market-ceiling school reads the S-curve literally: the only durable escape is a new segment, geography or product. It signs the claim that onboarding never materially moves a ceiling, and refuses the claim that a plateau proves the pool exhausted, since a pool's boundary is a choice. The growth-accounting school holds that most plateaus presented as saturation are decomposable flow problems. It signs that the identity localises the change, and refuses both that it explains causation and that a healthy blended funnel means no lever broke. The retention-primacy school, running from Frederick Reichheld's customer economics to practitioners such as Casey Winters, makes a formal claim: in flow equilibrium the sustainable base is gross adds divided by churn rate. It signs that most plateaus are retention plateaus in an acquisition costume, and refuses only that channel saturation is rare.

3. The mechanics, worked rather than named

Expert practice starts with the flow identity at the grain the business transacts — for Yojana, the school account. Exhibit 1 carries a column most dashboards omit.

That last column is why the exhibit exists. If a month's gross adds and churn rate held indefinitely, the base would converge on gross adds divided by churn rate. In April, Yojana added 103 schools a month and lost 2.23 per cent of its base, implying equilibrium near 4,622 schools — two and a half times the base it held, which is what healthy growth looks like from inside. By September, gross adds of 65 against 3.54 per cent implied 1,834 against a base of 1,997: the ceiling had dropped below the base in the same month net adds turned negative, having more than halved over the five months before.

The identity localises; it does not explain. The next step decomposes gross adds into the chain producing them. Yojana's median sales cycle is 34 days, short enough to book opportunities and wins in the same month; a longer cycle would force opportunities to be cohorted by creation month, and neglecting that is a common misreading.

This is the evidence that acquitted the channel. Opportunity volume fell by 60 out of 640, 9.4 per cent — unpleasant, not collapse. Conversion fell ten points at the demonstration step and ten at the pilot step, while pilot-to-paid held exactly. Yojana was still reaching schools, still getting the meeting, still winning those that piloted; it lost them in between. That is neither a channel nor a retention story: asking which schools stopped piloting separates product fit from market mix.

Exhibit 3 is the answer, and the reason blended penetration is nearly useless. Yojana holds 1,610 of the 2,750 schools in Segment A — 58.5 per cent. Blended, the figure is 17.2 per cent, reading as five-sixths of the runway intact. Segment A supplied the growth, the references, the product design and the revenue; it is more than half consumed, and every one of September's net losses sits there, at minus nineteen schools. Segments B to D are barely touched and together netted plus thirteen, but they have thinner clerical staff and, in Segment D, fee volumes that do not justify ₹180 per student.

The revenue layer is a separate identity, and where Yojana's two lines part company.

Three ratios follow. Gross revenue retention for the half-year is (3,378.2 − 359.0 − 87.5) ÷ 3,378.2, or 86.8 per cent; net revenue retention, adding back 255.8 of expansion, is 94.4 per cent; the quick ratio — gross revenue added over gross revenue lost, as Mamoon Hamid proposed in 2015 — is (722.3 + 53.4 + 255.8) ÷ (359.0 + 87.5), or 2.31. None alarms alone. Beside a falling school count they describe a precise condition: Yojana is losing small schools and growing inside large ones. That is survivable for perhaps three quarters, because expansion draws on unlicensed students inside licensed schools, a pool bounded by the same penetration arithmetic.

4. When the framework applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions. First, the loop must be stable enough for month-over-month comparison to mean anything; Yojana passes, its pricing, channel mix and implementation unchanged since April, while Jatan does not, having doubled paid search in June, which is why its blended rates moved. Second, the identity's grain must match the money's: Yojana's money is per student, so the school-account identity alone shows a plateau the revenue identity denies. Third, the pool must be definable by segment; for a horizontal product, penetration arithmetic is theatre.

It misleads in three situations. Before product-market fit the flows are too noisy, and the identity invites optimising a funnel that should be replaced. Where price or regulation causes the plateau, the flows report contraction faithfully while saying nothing of cause. And where the period spans a structural break, such as the June academic-year transition, comparison produces artefacts indistinguishable from saturation.

5. Hard edges: multi-product, two-sided, regulated, hardware, AI-native

Yojana sells three modules — fee collection, attendance and transport, and a parent app. Run the identity on the company and the fee-collection plateau vanishes inside transport growth; run it per module and it is plain. Multi-product companies report the blend, because that is what the board asked for. The organisational tell: growth owns gross adds, customer success churn, finance ARR, and the ratio combining all three has no owner.

The two-sided edge is sharper. Yojana's parent-payments side has its own adoption curve: of 22,01,800 students under licence, only 6,82,600 had an active UPI autopay mandate, 31.0 per cent. A school can be fully onboarded while its parents stay on cash, so payments revenue plateaus well before licence revenue. Hardware adds a service constraint: Yojana's crews cap additions near seventy schools a month in the monsoon quarter, a capacity ceiling indistinguishable in flow data from a demand one. AI-native products fail more subtly: where revenue is consumption-based, as with Jatan's reconciliation assistant, an account can decay to near-zero usage without churning, so the churned line stays clean while revenue rots and the identity must run on consumption, not seats.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A plateau is observationally under-determined. Figure 3 fits two models to Yojana's six months: a logistic curve asymptoting near 2,050 schools, and a constant-channel model with rising churn. They agree on history and disagree about next quarter. The tell is two competent analysts reading one table differently; the expert asks what each predicts for October, then waits.

The steady-state ratio leads the net-add line. It collapsed from 4,622 to 2,120 between April and August while net adds stayed positive. Any month in which that ratio falls faster than the base grows is a month when the plateau is already determined. The tell is a board pack reporting net adds and churn rate on separate pages, nobody dividing them.

Logo churn and revenue churn plateau at different times. Yojana's school count fell while ARR grew 17.3 per cent, because departures averaged 590 students against 880 for arrivals. The naive reading — revenue is fine, the count is vanity — fails because references and expansion capacity scale with logos. The tell is net revenue retention above 90 per cent beside a falling account count.

Blended penetration averages away the binding constraint. A company at 17.2 per cent overall and 58.5 per cent in the segment generating its growth is saturated for practical purposes; the obvious reading, abundant runway, fails because untouched segments carry different price tolerance and support cost. The tell is a lengthening sales cycle in the core segment while pipeline volume holds.

Expansion revenue buys quarters, not a cure. Yojana's ₹255.8 lakh of expansion covered its contraction and most of its churn, but is drawn from a bounded pool. The tell is expansion's share of gross revenue added rising while new-logo share falls — a ratio that reads as efficiency and is depletion.

Mix shift makes every blended rate lie. Jatan's activation rate fell from 45.0 to 32.0 per cent while no channel's own rate fell: paid search grew from a fifth of signups to 72 per cent, and had always activated at 25 per cent against word of mouth's 50. This is Simpson's paradox in a funnel; the tell is a blended rate moving while every decomposed rate holds.

Churn denominators must match contract mechanics. Yojana's contracts are annual and anniversary-dated, clustered in July–September because that is when most schools first went live. Of 614 schools whose contracts fell due that quarter, 198 did not renew — 32.2 per cent — against a 3.3 per cent average monthly rate on the whole base for those months. Both are correct; one is decision-relevant.

A plateau can be a pricing artefact with no behavioural content. Where a state fee-regulation order caps a school's fee increase, Yojana's per-student revenue is capped with it, and contraction appears without any customer changing their mind. The tell is contraction concentrated in one state in one quarter; reading it as product failure buys a roadmap response to a regulatory event.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer subscriptions the pool is measured in households and retention usually breaks first, substitutes being free and switching costless. In B2B and enterprise the pool is a countable list, so saturation is more literal and arrives faster, while churn in small numbers of logos is noisy — Yojana's Segment A, at 2,750 members, is a list a sales team can enumerate. Platforms need the identity per side; the plateau appears on the constrained side first.

Stage matters more than product type. An early company on one or two channels sees channel saturation unmistakably; a multi-channel incumbent rarely sees it in blended numbers, since many small channels smooth any one's decline, so its plateaus are disproportionately retention-driven. What does not differ, though it is often claimed to, is the arithmetic: the identity and the ratio hold for a two-person company and a listed one alike.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Yojana, correctly diagnosed. Exhibits 1 to 4 are the working: channel volume down 9.4 per cent, the overall opportunity-to-paid rate down a third, churn up to 3.54 per cent a month, losses inside the segment that is 58.5 per cent penetrated. A segment-exhaustion plateau with a retention accelerant.

Jatan, the opposite shape. Exhibit 5 shows a channel working harder for less.

Jatan's plateau was purchased. Half again as many signups produced eighteen fewer customers, because the marginal signup came from paid search and behaved worse at every step. The unit economics still clear a 3-to-1 bar, which is why nobody noticed: the ratio was healthy, the direction was not, and on the observed decay it crosses 3.0 within two quarters.

Yantrik Campus Software, where the diagnosis failed. In Eluru, Nithya Hiremath read a 2024-25 plateau as a channel problem and tripled her field sales force from 18 representatives to 54.

Tripling sales cost lifted new wins by 59 schools, from 372 to 431, and raised cost per win by a factor of 2.59. Churn, untouched, rose from 296 to 452 and net change fell to three schools. The recovery was unglamorous: Yantrik cut back to 30 representatives, moved the ₹288 lakh of released annual cost into implementation staffing and a rebuild of its fee-reconciliation module, and accepted fewer wins. New schools fell 17.4 per cent to 356 while churn fell 33.2 per cent to 302, and net change went from 3 to 76. Nithya's account is that she had the right identity and read one side.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Spending into a saturated channel. Warning: cost per acquisition rising faster than volume. Question: what is cost per win by channel now against last quarter? The late catch cost Yantrik ₹432 lakh for 59 extra schools.

Treating revenue growth as proof the base is healthy. Warning: strong net revenue retention beside a falling account count. Question: what would revenue do if expansion went to zero? Late catch costs two quarters of erosion in the logo base that feeds referrals.

Acting on one flat month. Warning: a reset triggered by one period beside a seasonal boundary — Indian school administration runs on a June academic year, with the fee cycle in the quarter after. Question: what did the same month look like a year ago?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether the steady-state ratio should drive decisions. Defenders note it is the only forward-looking number in the identity, and that it more than halved before net adds moved. Critics note that it assumes both inputs stationary, which they are not — Yojana's churn rose every month — so the equilibrium is the fixed point of a system that never sits still. They are wrong only if the ratio out-forecasts a naive trend, and the evidence is thin.

The second is whether saturation is ever the right first diagnosis. Retention-primacy at its strongest observes that 1,997 schools against a serviceable market of 11,600 cannot be arithmetically saturated, that a doubling of churn explains everything in Exhibit 1, and that teams reach for saturation because it blames nobody. Market-ceiling at its strongest observes that the segment which produced the growth is 58.5 per cent penetrated, that the rest have worse unit economics, and that perfect retention inside a consumed segment raises the ceiling by a few hundred schools. Both are defensible on the same data; the tie breaks on whether Segments B to D convert at a price Yojana can charge.

The third concerns aggregation: money grain or customer grain. Those who choose money argue revenue is what a business is for and that logo counts flatter small-account churn; those who choose customers argue logos lead everything downstream, and that Yojana's 2026 revenue growth was borrowed from its 2027 logo base. No general rule exists: a company needs both, and a view of which governs when they conflict.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs the identity when the top line flattens. Someone who has internalised it computes the steady-state ratio monthly whether or not anything looks wrong, keeps penetration at segment grain, refuses a blended rate without the mix behind it, and states in advance what each model predicts, so next month's data adjudicates rather than next quarter's argument. The signature is temperamental as much as technical: slower to name a cause, faster to design the test separating two, and able to tell a board that the plateau is real, the mechanism unproven, and here is the number that settles it.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Deepthi Kolluru held acquisition spend flat, moved four of her eleven growth engineers onto the demonstration-to-pilot step where ten points of conversion had gone, and commissioned a priced pilot in Segment B to test whether trusts with 400 to 799 students per school would accept a stripped implementation at a lower price. Exhibit 3, she argued, made segment exhaustion the leading hypothesis without establishing it; the test would separate exhaustion from product fit within a quarter, for less than a sales territory costs.

Nagaraj Bhagavatula did the harder thing and cut. He returned Jatan's paid-search budget to its April level, accepting fewer signups, and moved the released spend to assisted onboarding for the first roster upload, where activation had lost thirteen points. A value-to-cost ratio falling from 7.44 to 3.97 in six months, he argued, is a trend, not a level, and buying volume he could not activate was converting cash into a plateau.

Three questions. First: shown only Exhibit 4, with ARR up 17.3 per cent, what is the most expensive decision Yojana's board might have approved? Second: Deepthi's pilot tests price and implementation together — is that confound worth tolerating? Third: Yantrik traded 75 new schools for 150 retained ones; when is that the wrong trade?

13. Going deeper

  • Building a growth model. The model this diagnosis interrogates; without it, no baseline.
  • Growth loops vs funnels. Why a falling logo count threatens growth while revenue rises.
  • Acquisition channels and economics. Turns "the channel saturated" into a cost curve.
  • Activation and onboarding optimisation. The lever both chose; Jatan lost thirteen points here, Yojana ten.
  • Engagement loops and habit. The mechanism behind silent usage decay.
  • Retention strategy. Turns "churn rose to 3.54 per cent" into hypotheses about who leaves.
  • Resurrection and win-back. The smallest flow in Exhibit 1, and the best economics once a segment is used up.

Boond Krishi Cloud: When the Curve Flattens

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 5 October 2026, Bharat Birajdar sat in a glass-walled meeting room above a tractor-parts showroom in Kolhapur, with a printed dashboard in front of him and a board meeting four days away. The chart on the first page had been steadily climbing for eighteen months. In the last two quarters it had bent sideways.

Birajdar was the co-founder and chief executive of Boond Krishi Cloud, a farm-inputs and advisory app built for growers in western Maharashtra and northern Karnataka. On Friday, 9 October, he had to present the acquisition budget for October to December 2026, the rabi sowing quarter and the run-up to Diwali on 8 November. Bageshri Bapat, his head of growth, wanted the usual ₹60 lakh spent the usual way. Bindu Bellad, his data lead, had sent a note the night before with a single sentence in its subject line: "We may be measuring the wrong stall." Birajdar had four days to decide where the ₹60 lakh would go, and, more importantly, what he believed had gone wrong.

2. Company background

Boond Krishi Cloud was founded in 2023 and launched its app, Boond Khet, in April 2025. The product does three things: it lets a farmer order seed, fertiliser and drip-irrigation fittings for doorstep delivery, it sends irrigation and pest advisories in Marathi and English, and it lets him pay by UPI or against a cooperative credit limit. Its customers are small and mid-sized growers, mostly of sugarcane, soybean, grapes and vegetables. The company raised ₹24 crore in a Series A round in February 2025 and employs 118 people, most of them in Kolhapur, with product and engineering in Pune and the data team in Bengaluru.

The market around it is crowded from the top and the bottom. AgroStar and DeHaat are national players with large field networks. Mahindra's farm-services business and the cooperative sugar mills bring their own relationships. Ordinary agri-input dealers, who extend credit on a handshake, remain the default for most farmers. PM-Kisan and NABARD-backed credit shape what farmers can afford. Boond's advantage was that it had grown up among the sugarcane farmers of the Kolhapur-Sangli-Satara belt; it added 40,000 registered farmers in its first quarter.

3. The situation

Since launch, 3,07,000 farmers have registered on Boond Khet. The number that matters to the company, however, is the share who place an order within 90 days of registering, because only ordering farmers generate revenue. Exhibit 1 shows the six quarters to September 2026. Registrations peaked at 66,000 in October to December 2025, when Diwali offers and the sugar-crushing season pulled farmers in, and fell to 41,000 in the latest quarter. Over the same period quarterly acquisition spend more than doubled, from ₹20 lakh to ₹46 lakh.

Bapat, who runs the acquisition channels from the company's Pune office, reads Exhibit 1 as a channel problem. Her paid campaigns on YouTube and Meta have grown expensive as competitors bid for the same farmers, and she wants WhatsApp referral incentives and the full ₹60 lakh. The cost of an ordering farmer has risen from ₹167 to ₹660, almost four times, and she attributes it to tired ads.

Bellad, in Bengaluru, cut the same data by geography and by cohort. Exhibit 2 shows where the registered base sits. North Karnataka and the Solapur-Pune-Nashik arc hold 14,00,000 addressable households between them, with penetration of 12.0 and 6.9 per cent. The latest quarter's mix is telling: only 9,000 of the 41,000 new registrations came from the core belt, and those converted at 12 per cent. 4. The people

Bharat Birajdar, chief executive, Kolhapur. He wants a story the board can fund: a credible re-acceleration or an honest reset.

Bageshri Bapat, head of growth, Pune. She wants the budget kept whole, because a smaller budget would confirm the decline in public.

Bindu Bellad, data lead, Bengaluru. She wants the company to decide from the diagnosis, and asks for stage gates so that money follows evidence.

Balwant Bagal, field operations head, Belagavi. He wants Kannada content and local agents in cooperative societies.

5. The options

Option A: Stay the course. Spend ₹60 lakh in the existing channels, mostly aimed at the core belt, with new creatives and WhatsApp referrals. At the latest cost of ₹660 per ordering farmer, ₹60 lakh buys about 9,100 ordering farmers, more than in the last quarter. Upside: no disruption. Cost: the money goes mostly to a region where 40 per cent of households have already registered, and the marginal cost will probably keep rising.

Option B: Shift the money to the two under-penetrated regions. Allocate ₹15 lakh to the core belt, ₹25 lakh to North Karnataka and ₹20 lakh to Solapur-Pune-Nashik, and use part of it to build Kannada content and recruit local agents through cooperative societies. Upside: the 14,00,000 households outside the core convert at 18 to 19 per cent already, before localisation. Cost: two quarters before the agent network matures, and no cohort data yet on whether outer-region farmers reorder as well as those in the core.

Option C: Stop acquiring and monetise the base. Cut acquisition to ₹15 lakh and spend the rest on new products for the 1,80,000 core farmers, such as drip-irrigation financing and crop insurance. Upside: revenue per farmer rises. Cost: repeat ordering is already steady at 54 to 55 per cent, so the evidence does not show the base is neglected, and growth would lose its engine.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 to 3, which of the four suspects (channel, market, product, retention) can you rule out, and which single exhibit does most of the work?
  2. Bapat reads the rise from ₹167 to ₹660 as ad fatigue. What in Exhibit 2 offers a different explanation for the same number?
  3. What would you need to know about outer-region farmers before committing the majority of the budget to them?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 9 October, and what measures would tell you by January that you were wrong?

7. A note for the learner

A stalled curve invites a tactical reply; the first discipline is to decompose it. The four suspects each leave a distinct fingerprint. A channel problem shows as rising cost with unchanged conversion. A market problem shows as high penetration in the segment being bought. A product problem shows as low conversion in a specific group. A retention problem shows as falling repeat rates. Boond's data shows a stable repeat rate of about 55 per cent, so retention is cleared. Cost per registration rose because the company kept buying from a base that is 40 per cent penetrated. The core belt is a saturation problem, and the outer regions show a product-fit gap in language.

One defensible path is Option B, staged. Release the ₹15 lakh, ₹25 lakh and ₹20 lakh split, but tie the last half of the outer-region money to two gates: repeat rate in the first outer-region cohort at or above 50 per cent, and spend per ordering farmer below ₹350 by the January to March quarter. If either gate fails, the money returns to product work rather than to more advertising. Option A misdiagnoses the cause; Option C solves a retention problem the company does not have. Option B fits the diagnosis, and its main risk can be measured within one season.

Notifications, Email and Lifecycle Messaging

A triggered message is a withdrawal from a finite account. How experts price it, why competent teams under-price it, and where practitioners still disagree about the exchange rate.

1. Two desks, two Augusts

On 4 August 2026 Sharvari Deodhar, Vice-President for Growth and Lifecycle at Palash Invest Networks, a retail investing app in Jaipur, read a one-slide proposal: a market-open digest pushed at 9.05 a.m. daily to the whole reachable base, projected to add four percentage points of daily actives in a quarter. Palash had 41,00,000 registered users and 11,50,000 monthly actives, of whom 7,13,000 — 62 per cent — had push enabled. Sending cost nothing, and the board wanted actives.

What made her hesitate was on no slide. Palash was losing push permission at 2.6 per cent of the reachable base a month, which the deck annualised by multiplying: 31.2 per cent, 2,22,500 people. Compounded, twelve survivals of 97.4 per cent leave 72.89 per cent — 5,19,700 of the 7,13,000, or 72.9 per cent — so the annual loss is 1,93,300 users, 27.1 per cent of the base. The deck overstated the bleed by 29,200 while proposing to accelerate it.

Her data scientist, Hemant Kalyanpur, had spent July capping non-transactional push at one through six a week across a randomised slice, against a never-messaged holdout. The uncapped policy averaged 5.2 pushes per user per week.

Eight days earlier, Aniruddh Vaze, Vice-President for Product at Pratidhwani Ops Cloud in Lucknow, faced the same problem. Pratidhwani sells warehouse exception management to 340 accounts, 8,400 named seats. Alerts per seat per day had risen from 6.1 in January to 17.4 in June, and acknowledgement within ten minutes had fallen from 78 per cent to 41. On 2 July a chiller failure at a customer's Rajkot cold store raised a severity-one alert that sat unacknowledged for 94 minutes, and roughly ₹38 lakh of stock was written off. Nupur Samant in customer success reported that three of the ten largest accounts had muted an alert class at the operating-system level: Pratidhwani no longer knew what its customers could hear.

Neither is a copywriting decision. Both are one problem: a channel of finite capacity, depleting at a rate that appears in no campaign report, spent by teams paid for what it produces.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

Define the terms; looseness hides the argument. A triggered message is sent because a user entered a state — an event (a mandate failed), a time (day three, no first investment), a threshold (a watchlist stock crossed a price). Lifecycle messaging is the state machine above them: the ordered states from signup through activation, habit, decay and dormancy, each with its own suppression rules and success measure. Reachability is the share of the base a channel can still address. And the idea separating expert from competent practice is permission stock: the reachable base treated as an asset with a value, a depletion rate and a replacement cost.

Three inheritances built the field. Catalogue direct mail codified recency-frequency-monetary segmentation in the 1970s. Permission marketing, named by Seth Godin in 1999, was given machinery by Eloqua, Responsys, Marketo and HubSpot, which made the trigger a behavioural event rather than a mailing date. Then mobile: Apple's push service in 2009 and Google's cloud messaging in 2010 handed every product a free, interrupting, permissioned channel, which teams soon learned is a dangerous pair. The reaction, in practitioner writing associated with Reforge from about 2015, gives the proposition this topic rests on: a notification is healthy when it surfaces value the user already created or requested, and a tax when it manufactures urgency the product did not earn.

Four schools disagree. The permission-stock school signs: never send a message whose expected incremental margin is below its expected permission damage; it will not sign that frequency is bad in itself. The demand-shaping school signs: at scale a message not sent is a sale certainly not made, and reachability is renewable; it will not sign that opt-out is irreversible. The attention-rights school signs: no metric measured inside your own app can price the harm your notification does; it will not sign that the right cadence is discoverable by experiment. The incrementality sceptics sign: most reported lift is timing displacement; they will not sign that holdouts are useless, only that short ones are.

Sharvari's opening line in the August memo: “Our reachable base is the only asset this team has, we have never valued it, and every campaign is a draw against it.”

3. Mechanics in depth: pricing a send

The pipeline is fixed, and competent teams skip steps three and six. One, trigger evaluation. Two, eligibility: the qualifying set, less suppression, less the cap, less the holdout. Three, arbitration: when two campaigns qualify and the cap allows one, absent an explicit chooser the loosest trigger wins by arriving first. Four, channel and window, constrained in India by the telecom regulator's 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. limit and the consent duties of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Five, outcome capture. Six, the ledger — not the funnel but the permission account: opt-outs, class mutes, uninstalls, store rating.

The formal treatment is one inequality. Send when

pc × m  >  po × Vperm  +  csend

where pc is the incremental conversion probability against a holdout, m the contribution margin, po the probability the message costs you the permission, Vperm the present value of holding it, and csend the channel cost. What is rare is computing Vperm, without which the apparatus collapses into open rates.

Palash computed it. Under the three-a-week policy the base of 7,13,000 produced 18,538 incremental transactions over four weeks against the holdout, worth ₹22 each, or ₹4,07,836 — ₹0.572 per reachable user per cycle. Treat that as a monthly yield, with the 1.0 per cent monthly opt-out that arm produced and a 36-month horizon: the sum of 0.572 × 0.99k for k from 0 to 35 is 0.572 × 30.36, or ₹17.37 per permission. Its fragility is the finding: at 24 months the same arithmetic gives ₹12.26, which alone moves the cap.

Figure 1. Compounding, not multiplication: 2.6 per cent a month leaves 72.9 per cent of the base after a year, 5,19,700 users, where multiplying by twelve predicts a loss of 2,22,500 instead of 1,93,300 — a 29,200-user error. Separately, the gap between the two curves plotted here, 5,19,700 against 6,32,000, is 1,12,300 users.

On this report push is the hero: 22,816 incremental transactions at no send cost, ₹5,01,952 net. Charge it for the 17,825 permissions it consumed at ₹17.37 — ₹3,09,620 — and push earns ₹1,92,332, almost exactly the ₹1,92,333 Table 1 shows at a cap of five; the ₹1 gap is rounding. A cap of three lifts push's true net to ₹2,83,989, a gain of ₹91,657 a cycle, while cutting opt-outs to 7,130 — 10,695 of 17,825 permissions saved, 60.0 per cent. The table also settles WhatsApp: 5,20,000 sends at ₹0.72 cost ₹3,74,400 and returned 4,940 incremental transactions worth ₹1,08,680, losing ₹2,65,720 before any permission charge; SMS loses ₹38,360. Both were defended on conversion rate — the highest of any channel, which on an expensive channel is no argument.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

Four testable conditions. The channel must be scarce and slow to refill. Volume must be large enough that a percentage point of opt-out rate is a real population. The incremental effect must be measurable, needing a holdout big enough for the effect size. And margin per conversion must be knowable, since the threshold is Vperm/m and an unknown denominator leaves it undefined.

All four hold at Palash: a user who declines runtime notification permission is not casually re-asked, 0.1 per cent of the base is 713 people, the holdout is ample, contribution is known to the rupee. At Pratidhwani the first holds emphatically — an operating-system mute is invisible and permanent — but the second and third fail: with 8,400 seats, withholding exception alerts from a holdout is negligence, not experiment. The framing applies; the apparatus does not, so Aniruddh substitutes acknowledgement latency per class.

It misleads twice. Where the message is the product — a monitoring tool — suppressing sends to protect permission destroys the proposition, and the design object becomes user-set thresholds rather than caps imposed by growth. Where a message discharges an obligation, the arithmetic does not apply at all, because the alternative to sending is not silence but harm.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product companies hit arbitration first. When one app holds four product lines with four growth owners, the cap becomes a rationing device and the loosest trigger fills the slot. Mature companies say a shared calendar solves it; the good ones run a bidding layer where each campaign declares an expected value per send and the highest bid takes the slot. The precondition is brutal: every team must expose its measurement to a system that can reject its sends.

Two-sided markets face asymmetric costs. Pagdandi Freight Exchange in Surat alerts operators to loads: annoying a shipper costs one booking, while driving an operator to mute the app removes capacity.

Regulated contexts turn design into compliance. Palash cannot push at 8.50 a.m. even if that is when it would work, so the 9 a.m. window becomes a congestion peak where every commercial sender competes for ten minutes. Hardware adds a second permission surface: at Peepal Wellness Devices in Mysuru a user who mutes the app still feels the wrist buzz, so opt-out data understates fatigue. The deepest seam is organisational: transactional messaging belongs to engineering, promotional to marketing, lifecycle to growth, and the fatigue they jointly create to nobody. Companies that handle it well give one owner the opt-out line and the store rating, with a veto.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The cost of a bad message is mostly not the opt-out. It is the discount the user applies to every later message, invisible in that campaign's report. The tell is transactional open rates drifting down in a quarter when promotional volume rose; the obvious reading, that flat opt-outs mean all is well, misses that habituation is a rate change, not an event.

Permission is class-scoped, not app-scoped. Notification channels let a user mute promotions and keep delivery alerts, so an expert asks which class was muted before asking how many left: a promotional mute is a pricing signal, a transactional mute an emergency that one aggregate number hides.

Email open rate is partly an artefact. Since mail privacy features began pre-fetching images, an open no longer implies a human; the tell is a step change dated to an operating-system release rather than to anything the team did. Experts moved to clicks and conversion years ago and treat an opens-optimised programme as unmeasured.

Incrementality decays and displaces. A reminder that lifts week one and dips week three moved demand rather than creating it, and a four-week holdout scores the shift as growth. The tell is a treated series oscillating around the holdout's trend instead of sitting above it — hence the six-to-twelve-month holdout serious programmes keep.

Opt-out is a depletion rate, and rates compound. Multiplying a monthly rate by twelve announces an unpriced asset: Palash's 2.6 per cent costs 27.1 per cent of the base a year, not 31.2, and the 29,200-user gap exceeds most target lists.

The most valuable message is one the product already owes. A failed mandate, a rider at the gate, a reply to a question: near-zero opt-out cost, highest conversion, built to a lower standard because no growth target depends on them. The tell is a transactional template unreviewed for a year beside a promotional one on its fourth test.

Suppression latency is the defect users notice. The gap between a state change and the segment refresh that reflects it sends a reactivation message to someone who reactivated yesterday. Measured in hours, it is the cheapest item here to fix and the least measured; the tell is tickets reducible to “I already did this”.

In business software the person who opts out is not the person who pays. A supervisor muting an alert class generates no unsubscribe and no complaint; the signal arrives months later as a renewal conversation, as at Pratidhwani. The diagnostic is acknowledgement latency by class and account.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the discipline is statistical: large bases, behavioural triggers, caps and arbitration, opt-out rate as the constraint. In business software it is relational: few named recipients, workflow triggers, email and in-product channels, acknowledgement latency and renewal as the metrics. The difference is not sophistication: consumer teams can learn by experiment and enterprise teams cannot. Marketplaces differ because their sides have different elasticities; hardware because permission lives on two surfaces, one of which cannot be silently revoked; AI products because message quality is a distribution, which makes a precision threshold a product control. Where the practice does not differ, say so: the inequality above is identical in all five, as is the need for a holdout wherever one is ethical.

Stage matters more than model. Before product-market fit, lifecycle infrastructure is a distraction: volumes are too small for a holdout and ten conversations teach more than a cohort table. In the scaling phase, where Palash sits, it repays within a quarter. At maturity the work is governance: arbitration, ownership of the opt-out line, and resisting the temptation to finance a revenue gap with a channel withdrawal.

8. Three worked examples

Pagdandi Freight Exchange: narrowing the broadcast. Pagdandi's 46,000 active truck operators received load alerts by broadcast: each of roughly 62,000 monthly loads notified about 1,200 operators: 7,44,00,000 alerts a month for 62,000 awards. Yuvraj Bhosale replaced it with a ranked top-60 match, cutting volume to 37,20,000, a 95.0 per cent reduction, while the bid rate within fifteen minutes rose from 4.5 to 21 per cent. Operators muting job alerts fell from 31 per cent to 12 per cent, and loads filled within thirty minutes rose from 54,808 of 62,000 (88.4 per cent) to 56,544 (91.2 per cent) — at ₹2,100 of net take per load, 1,736 extra loads worth ₹36,45,600 a month.

Peepal Wellness Devices: the failure and the recovery. Of 3,40,000 bands sold, 2,72,000 were paired to the app, and 1,90,400 of those 2,72,000 paired installs — 70 per cent — allowed notifications. Tanvi Marathe's team launched inactivity nudges with no holdout. Weekly app opens rose 9 per cent and the programme was declared a success. Over twelve weeks 12.4 per cent of the 1,90,400 revoked permission — reported as 4.1 per cent a month by dividing by three, where compounding gives 4.32 per cent, since 0.876 to the power of one-third is 0.9568. The metric that mattered fell: day-ninety wear of at least four days a week was 38.6 per cent against 44.2 for the prior cohort, because nudges fired during meetings and users took the band off. Recovery took a quarter — quiet hours, one daily digest, a permanent 4 per cent holdout — after which revocation over three months totalled 3.6 per cent, or 1.21 per cent a month compounded, and wear recovered to 43.9 per cent. Without a holdout, a programme that reduced the core behaviour reported a win for twelve weeks.

Pratibimb Agent Cloud: precision as a product control. Pratibimb's agent sends proactive findings to 26,400 seats across 4,800 paying teams, 1,64,000 messages a month. Zoheb Kantharia had 1,000 sampled messages rated: 712 of the 1,000 useful, 71.2 per cent, with 194 noise and 94 wrong. Raising the confidence threshold from 0.55 to 0.78 cut volume 41 per cent to 96,760 and lifted usefulness to 89.1 per cent, noise to 7.7 and wrong to 3.2. Useful messages fell from 1,16,768 a month to 86,213, a loss of 30,555; wrong ones fell from 15,416 to 3,096, 12,320 of 15,416 removed, 79.9 per cent. The exchange rate is 2.48 useful messages surrendered per wrong one prevented — defended by seats disabling proactive notifications falling from 1,795 of 26,400 (6.8 per cent) to 634 (2.4 per cent).

9. Failure modes, their early signs and the cost of lateness

Open rate as the scoreboard. Sign: campaigns win the weekly review while retention is flat. Diagnostic: what did the holdout do? Late, a team has optimised a mail-client artefact for years. No cross-team cap. Sign: nobody can state messages per user per week without a query. Diagnostic: run it. Late, the cost is a store rating, slower to rebuild than the opt-outs behind it. Promotional urgency in transactional clothing. Sign: click-through and opt-out rising together. Diagnostic: plot both on one axis. Late, users mute the class holding both, and the necessary message goes with the discount. Alert fatigue. Sign: acknowledgement latency rising with volume. Diagnostic: action rate per class — at Pratidhwani 2.1 per cent for stock-position variance against 62.0 for temperature excursions. Late, the cost is a missed severity-one event and the renewal after it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The permission-stock position rests on opt-in being a one-time gate and on dismal re-permissioning: once a user revokes, recovery runs through an in-product prompt most revokers never see. Its evidence is Table 1, and it is wrong if Vperm is smaller than estimated — exactly what a shorter horizon implies. At 24 months Palash's cap moves to four, and the position's own method hands the rival its answer.

The demand-shaping position notes that push is not the only reachability and the base is not fixed: installs arrive with fresh permission, email and inboxes reach users push cannot, and a lost permission costs the acquisition cost of a replacement, often less than a sentimental valuation suggests. Its evidence is the revenue of high-frequency programmes; it is wrong if habituation is cumulative, because then the harm is not confined to those who leave.

The attention-rights position is a measurement argument, not a moral one: every test measures a treated group against a control that also lives on a saturated phone, so within-app tests under-detect the cross-app externality, and the long-run equilibrium — notifications disabled wholesale, or demoted into summaries — is invisible to one company.

The sceptics hold that most lift is displacement, invisible to four-week holdouts; they are wrong if long-horizon holdouts show sustained separation. Few companies run one long enough to settle it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a cadence recommendation. Someone who has internalised it arrives with two questions: what is a permission worth here, and what is the margin on a conversion — because that ratio is the policy, and cadence falls out of it. The expert separates messages the product owes from messages it wants, holding the first to a higher engineering standard and arbitrating only the second. They treat the opt-out line as a balance-sheet item with an owner, and volunteer which assumption the answer turns on. Shown a large lift, they hunt for the dip that would reveal displacement before circulating the number.

12. What each of them decided

Sharvari approved the digest in a form the growth team had not proposed: opt-in, at the user's chosen time, inside a hard cap of three non-transactional pushes a week, arbitrated by declared expected value per send rather than by arrival order. She suspended promotional WhatsApp and SMS, recovering the ₹2,65,720 and ₹38,360 they lost every four weeks, and kept both for transactional use. She installed a permanent 3 per cent never-messaged holdout and a 0.5 per cent twelve-month holdout, and put opt-out rate and store rating on the weekly page beside incremental revenue. The cap alone gains ₹91,657 a cycle and preserves 10,695 permissions.

Aniruddh adopted the triage in Table 3: monthly alerts from 43,84,800 to 16,41,460, 17.4 per seat per day to 6.5, keeping an estimated 89.7 per cent of acted-on alerts, temperature excursions untouched and escalating to a phone call after ten unacknowledged minutes. He declined the Rajkot customer's request for a weekly summary to the plant head: a summary is what you add once you have given up on routing. Alert volume left his weekly review, replaced by acknowledgement within ten minutes by class, 41 per cent now, targeted at 75 by January.

One. Sharvari's cap of three becomes four if the permission horizon is 24 months rather than 36. What evidence would you require before letting that decide policy, and who chooses it?
Two. Pratibimb surrendered 2.48 useful messages per wrong one prevented. Argue from the figures given that the trade was too aggressive.
Three. Peepal reported a 9 per cent lift while reducing the behaviour the product exists to create. What would have caught it in week two, and at what cost?

13. Going deeper

  • Engagement loops and habit — what the loop must do for a notification to have anything true to say.
  • Push and notification strategy — permission timing, channel taxonomy, cadence governance, arbitration.
  • Growth loops vs funnels — why a campaign funnel hides the stock a loop view puts on the balance sheet.
  • Building a growth model — where Vperm and reachable base belong as terms.
  • Acquisition channels and economics — the replacement cost of a reachable user, the rival school's key number.
  • Activation and onboarding optimisation — where permission is granted, and so where the asset is made or wasted.
  • Retention strategy — separating pulled-forward demand from habit, what holdouts exist to measure.
  • Resurrection and win-back — the highest-opt-out corner, where the threshold rule bites hardest.

Daayra Fleet Telematics and the Price of a Nudge

An ambiguous case on notifications, email and lifecycle messaging

1. Sunday night in Sikar

On the night of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Sarita Shekhawat sat in the office of Daayra Fleet Telematics on Piprali Road in Sikar, Rajasthan, with two printouts that could not both be right. The board met by video at nine the next morning, and the item she owned was the January messaging plan for the freight peak. The deck she had written on Friday now looked indefensible.

The first was from her Chief Revenue Officer. The nudges sent through Umang Alert Desk had produced 11,520 credited app engagements in a four-week test; a coached driver was worth ₹1,850 a year; doubling volume would cost ₹3.76 lakh a month and protect crores of renewals. The second was from data science. Of those 11,520, about 2,520 — 21.9 per cent — would not have happened without the nudge; read eight weeks later the figure fell to 900; read per vehicle it cleared its interval by three-tenths of a point, and per fleet account it disappeared inside one.

Underneath both lay a note from Legal, dated Thursday, observing that the consent on which 33,300 of the company's 45,000 reachable drivers were being messaged had been given by their employers, in English, in a bundled tick-box, between 2019 and February 2024. Sarita had nine hours to decide whether the question she had been asked — how many nudges to send — was the question.

2. How Daayra came to be shaped this way

Daayra was founded in 2017 by Yogita Bagaria, who had spent nine years financing second-hand tippers in Shekhawati. The AIS-140 mandate for location tracking gave her a market: owners had to fit devices, and most resented it. Daayra sold the device near cost and made its money on the subscription and the dashboard where an owner in Sikar could see a truck outside Namakkal.

By September 2026 it had 2,10,000 connected vehicles across 4,300 fleet accounts, 9,400 of those vehicles and ₹3.20 crore of revenue in Kenya and Tanzania, sold from a two-person office in Nairobi. Revenue in the year to March 2026 was ₹73.00 crore: ₹45.36 crore of subscription (2,10,000 vehicles at an average ₹180 a month), ₹21.08 crore of hardware (62,000 devices at ₹3,400) and ₹6.56 crore of behaviour-data licensing to insurers and two truck makers. Daayra lost ₹4.10 crore and was preparing a Series B for February 2027.

One decision from 2019 shaped everything after it. To win a 1,800-vehicle contract, Daayra agreed that the fleet owner would consent for his drivers — one tick, covering "all communications including promotional" — and keyed its records to the vehicle and the account, because that was what the invoice needed. There was no stable driver identity until 2023. Coaching a driver, measuring a driver, asking a driver for consent: each has been retrofitted onto a model in which the driver was a field on a trip, not a person.

Taleem Driver Coach, the driver-facing Android app, launched in March 2023 with three message types. It now has fourteen, added by five teams, plus Mausam Route Alerts, a weather-and-diversion feed bought in for ₹34 lakh a year. Umang Alert Desk, built in 2024, credits any app open within twenty-four hours of a delivered message to that message, because that is what the vendor SDK did.

3. The industry around it

Indian commercial-vehicle telematics is crowded. Tata Motors ships Fleet Edge with its trucks and Mahindra has iMAXX; LocoNav, Fleetx and Intangles fight for the same mid-size fleets. Differentiation has moved from the map to the driver: fuel theft, harsh braking, document expiry, and the insurance premium behaviour data can move. Insurers such as ICICI Lombard and Tata AIG pay for scored behaviour, which is why the ₹6.56 crore data line grew fastest.

Four outside parties decide more about Daayra's messaging than Daayra does. TRAI's rules require every SMS header and template to be registered on a DLT platform and scrubbed against preference registers, so a wording change is a filing, not a deploy. Google Play governs what the app may do: notification permission has been a runtime grant since Android 13, full-screen intents and exact alarms are restricted, and a target-SDK deadline of 31 January 2027 sits in Lalit Dotasra's backlog. The handset makers govern whether a message arrives: Xiaomi, vivo and OPPO devices, two-thirds of the installed base, apply aggressive power management that delays or drops background notifications — a legitimate battery-life choice Daayra cannot appeal. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs whether the driver's data may be used for messaging or the insurer feed at all.

Diwali fell on 8 November 2026, and the January lane rates after it carry the renewal season.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 Sarita told the board that driver engagement was up 31 per cent year on year. It came from Umang Alert Desk and counted credited opens: app opens within twenty-four hours of a delivered message. Nobody asked what drivers would have done otherwise; no holdout existed to ask.

On Monday, 13 July, a template mismatch caused Daayra's SMS to be scrubbed at the DLT gateway. Over nine days to Tuesday, 21 July, 1,86,000 messages failed; the vendor dashboard reported them as submitted, so nobody noticed until a fleet owner telephoned. SMS delivery fell 86 per cent. App opens fell 2.1 per cent. On-time document renewals — the outcome the reminders exist for — were 61.4 per cent against 62.0 per cent in the preceding fortnight. Elakshi Pareek, in Warsaw, called it the cheapest experiment the company had run and the one it least wanted to read.

In August she ran a real one: all 45,000 push-reachable devices randomised, 36,000 treated and 9,000 into a silent holdout, from Monday, 3 August to Sunday, 30 August. Exhibit 4 supports opposite conclusions depending on the window and the unit.

On Wednesday, 2 September, a scheduling change made so Elakshi's batch jobs would finish inside the Warsaw working day sent 38,400 nudges at 02:10 IST. Six hundred and forty drivers disabled notifications within forty-eight hours. The same day produced 9,700 credited opens, the quarter's highest, because drivers woke, cleared the tray and opened up. The worst message Daayra has sent is the best-performing message in its dashboard.

In September an audit of delivery receipts produced Exhibit 3 and a number nobody had seen: only 62.0 per cent of a campaign arrives within fifteen minutes. On Thursday, 12 November, Shefali Jangid sent her consent note, prompted not by principle but by the insurer: the renewal due on 1 January 2027 carries an attestation that behavioural data rests on valid consent, and a clause cutting the fee 25 per cent — ₹1.64 crore a year — if consented coverage falls below 70 per cent.

5. The people

  • Sarita Shekhawat, Chief Product Officer, Sikar. Owns the January plan. Has not said that she wrote the 31 per cent slide herself and that the board remembers it.
  • Yogita Bagaria, co-founder and CEO, Sikar. Wants February's Series B raised on a clean data story and a growing insurer line; has not said which she would sacrifice.
  • Sohan Tibrewal, Chief Revenue Officer, New Delhi. Carries a ₹8.90 crore renewal quarter; values a coached driver at ₹1,850 a year. Has not said that this is gross contribution per contracted vehicle, not incremental value.
  • Elakshi Pareek, Head of Data Science, Warsaw. Costs ₹68 lakh a year against ₹26 lakh for the same seat in Bengaluru, which she knows is discussed. Has not said that her ₹610 per driver-year rests on a model she would not defend in court.
  • Lalit Dotasra, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Quotes 14 weeks and ₹64.00 lakh for consent and preferences. Has not said that his team has dropped low-priority nudges on power-managed devices since June to protect crash-free sessions.
  • Sumer Kaswan, Head of Driver Programmes, Jodhpur. Runs 240 field staff. Has not said that his team is paid on installs, which is why installs are 1,60,000 and activations 1,00,000.
  • Shefali Jangid, Legal and Data Protection Officer, Sikar. Believes the driver, not the fleet, is the data principal. Has not said that she approved the 2019 wording as outside counsel.
  • Lorna Wanjiru, Customer Success, Nairobi. Her fleets are on feature phones where push is theatre and SMS everything. Has not said that her largest account wants location alerts Daayra's policy would refuse in India.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1, the cost side, makes the January decision look small: 36.80 lakh messages a month for ₹5.98 lakh, a blended ₹0.16 a message, ₹71.76 lakh a year — just under 1 per cent of revenue. Push, the channel everyone argues about, costs ₹0.36 lakh.

On the device alone, the four weeks give three answers. Of the 13,680 treated devices that opened the app, Umang Alert Desk credited 11,520 opens to a nudge on its twenty-four-hour rule, 84.2 per cent. 7. Voices

"Twenty-one per cent of credited is still 2,520 drivers who did something they would not have done. I am asking for ₹3.76 lakh a month. What else buys 2,520 behaviour changes for that?" — Sohan Tibrewal, 6 November

"At eight weeks it is 900, and I have not put an interval on that read. The ±2.1 you keep quoting at me is drivers over four weeks. I am not saying the nudges do nothing. I am saying we do not know, and the dashboard says we do." — Elakshi Pareek

"We have dropped the low-priority queue on power-managed devices since June to keep crash-free sessions above 99.2. It is in the release notes. Nobody read them, and engagement went up anyway." — Lalit Dotasra, 11 November

"A driver at Jodhpur transport nagar will say the fitness-certificate reminder saved him a ₹10,000 challan and the coaching cards make him feel watched. Both are true. He cannot switch off one and keep the other." — Sumer Kaswan, 9 November

"Two men drive that truck; one installed the app. The score is on the truck, so when the night man brakes hard, the day man gets the message." — Lakhan Bhukar, fleet owner, 4 November

"The owner cannot consent for the driver, the notice is not in his language, and the behaviour-data licence sits in the same sentence as the promotional tick. I can write a defensible programme. I cannot write a defensible past." — Shefali Jangid, 12 November

8. The options as Sarita sees them

A. Ship the January plan. Push from 18.00 to 37.80 lakh messages a month and WhatsApp from 4.80 to 9.60 lakh, taking messaging cost from ₹5.98 lakh to ₹9.74 lakh, up ₹3.76 lakh. Nothing in Exhibit 4 supports Sohan's arithmetic; nothing refutes it, because the outcome he cares about is renewal, which the test did not measure.

B. Cut to the proven set. Retire the eight of fourteen nudge types with no holdout evidence, keeping document expiry, fuel-theft alerts and trip confirmation; saves perhaps ₹1.90 lakh a month. But the July failure suggests the tested ones may also do less than believed, and the message drivers value most is the one Legal is most exposed on.

C. Rebuild consent and preference first. Lalit's 14 weeks and ₹64.00 lakh: per-purpose toggles, notices in eight languages, IVR consent for drivers who do not read. Re-consenting the 33,300 drivers on an owner's tick or a missing record costs about ₹6.23 lakh — three IVR attempts each at ₹0.45, then field re-consent at ₹28 for the rest. At the 38 per cent IVR completion Sumer expects, push-reachable drivers fall to 24,354, 54.1 per cent of today: below the insurer's 70 per cent threshold, putting ₹1.64 crore a year at risk to protect a ₹71.76 lakh programme.

D. Give the fleet owner the dial. A console in which the owner chooses what his drivers receive. Owners ask for it, and it is the 2019 decision again in a better interface — except that Shefali believes the owner has no standing to choose.

Each option assumes the thing in dispute: that Daayra decides what arrives, that engagement is what it buys, and that the driver is a recipient rather than a party. Exhibit 3 contradicts the first, Exhibit 4 the second, Exhibit 6 the third.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board call is at nine on Monday, 16 November, and the January plan must be locked with the vendor by 30 November. Engineering is one team with three claims on it: the Play target-SDK deadline of 31 January 2027, the consent rebuild, peak-season load. The insurer renewal is 1 January 2027, with its 70 per cent attestation and ₹1.64 crore clause. Series B diligence begins in February and includes a data-protection review. Renewals worth ₹8.90 crore fall in the quarter to March.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 5, what does a notification cost Daayra, and which of those costs appear in a report?
  2. Exhibit 3 shows 62.0 per cent delivery in fifteen minutes and 77.0 per cent in twenty-four hours; its footnote adds 67.0 per cent displays from the app SDK. Which figure goes in the deck?
  3. Exhibit 4 gives four verdicts on one experiment. Which unit is right for a truck with two drivers and one handset, and who chooses it?
  4. Sohan's ₹1,850 and Elakshi's ₹610 describe the same driver. Is the gap a disagreement about value or about causation?
  5. If the 12,300 silent devices are the real cost of over-messaging, how would you make them visible, and what would you stop?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Sarita put to the board, what does she say about the 31 per cent she reported in January, and what would make her wrong?

At half past eleven she deleted the January slide and typed a new title, "What we do not know about our own messages," then deleted that too. Sohan would read it as an ambush; Yogita, as a Series B risk written into a board pack. Outside, trucks pulled out towards the Jaipur road, and in one cab a handset Daayra counted as reachable buzzed twice, in a language its holder did not read, and was laid face down.

Growth & Retention · Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation

Notifications, Email and Lifecycle Messaging

How do you message a user in a way that helps rather than nags — and how do you know, in numbers, which of those two you are actually doing?

1. The Monday the ratings dropped below four

On the morning of 15 September 2026, Devika Rane, Head of Retention Marketing at Taazgi Grocery Network, a quick-commerce grocery app based in Nagpur, opened three dashboards before her coffee was finished. Taazgi had 18,00,000 monthly active users, of whom 12,24,000 — 68 per cent — had push notifications switched on. That number used to comfort her. It no longer did.

Over the second quarter, chasing a board-mandated order-growth target, the marketing, retention and product teams had each, independently, added a notification programme: a cart-reminder flow, a discount digest, a "back in stock" alert, a win-back sequence. No one owned the total. The average push-enabled user went from 3 notifications a week in April to 9 by September. The monthly push opt-out rate — the share of push-enabled users who revoked the permission that month — rose from 1.2 per cent to 3.4 per cent, the Play Store rating slipped from 4.3 to 3.9, and tickets tagged "too many notifications" went from about 40 a week to 310.

Farhan Qureshi, her data scientist, had a proposal on her desk: a dormant-user win-back campaign was due that week, and he had built a propensity model that could shrink the target list from 5,00,000 users to a smaller, better-chosen 3,00,000 without simply cutting the campaign. Devika had two days to decide whether to send the broad list, send the modelled list, or shelve it — before her Friday update to a CEO who wanted Q3 order growth on track and had not yet heard about the opt-out trend.

2. The idea, defined precisely

Notifications, email and lifecycle messaging are the triggered, timed, personalised messages a product sends through push, email, SMS or in-app channels because a particular user has reached a particular state — distinct from a blast, one message sent to everyone regardless of where each person actually is. "Lifecycle" names the second layer: the sequence of such messages accompanying a user from signup through activation, habitual use, dormancy and, sometimes, win-back or churn, each stage with its own trigger logic rather than one campaign repeated on a schedule.

The idea has a traceable lineage. Marketing-automation platforms of the early-to-mid 2000s, Eloqua among the first, built the plumbing for "triggered" email keyed to a behavioural event rather than a send date, and Marketo and HubSpot generalised it through the 2010s. What changed the concept from a marketing tactic into a product discipline was the growth-loops thinking that spread through product teams from roughly 2015 onward, associated with writers such as Brian Balfour and Casey Winters: a notification is healthy only when it surfaces value the user already created or asked for — a reply, a price drop on a saved item — rather than manufacturing urgency the product did not earn. By the time Braze, Intercom and CleverTap became standard infrastructure in Indian product teams around 2018–2019, "lifecycle messaging" was the accepted term for this discipline.

The sentence Devika could say in the CEO's Friday review without sounding glib: "A good notification is information the user would have asked for, delivered before they had to ask — and the moment it stops being that, it is a withdrawal against a channel we cannot easily refill."

3. How it actually works, step by step

The mechanics run in a fixed order, and the steps experienced teams treat as obvious are the ones a newcomer skips. First, a trigger: event-based (a cart sits unpurchased two hours), time-based (day 3 with no first order), or state-based (a saved item's price crosses a threshold). Second, eligibility: who qualifies, minus anyone suppressed by a frequency cap, and — the step most teams skip — minus a small holdout group withheld from every campaign so its behaviour can be compared to the treated group later. Without a holdout, a team can report an open rate but never prove the message caused anything.

Third, the message is personalised. Fourth, a channel and time window are chosen: push for immediacy, email for anything searchable later, SMS or WhatsApp for unreliable connectivity, all constrained by India's Telecom Regulatory Authority rules restricting commercial communication between 9 p.m. and 9 a.m. Fifth, it is tracked through a funnel — delivered, opened, clicked, converted — alongside a second counter, opted out, the metric that moves the wrong way precisely when a campaign looks like it is succeeding. Sixth, results feed back into the eligibility model. Taazgi's win-back trigger was state-based: no completed order in 21 days for a user who had ordered at least three times before going quiet.

Figure 1. Four trigger families by urgency and whose value they carry. Devika's decision sits bottom-right: the quadrant with the highest opt-out risk after promotional sends.

4. A worked example: the same win-back budget, two ways

Devika asked Farhan to lay both options side by side using September's actual funnel rates, rather than guessing. Both draw from Taazgi's pool of dormant, push-enabled users; the difference is whether the list is the full eligible set or the subset his model flags as highest-propensity.

Read the broad column straight through: 5,00,000 sends at 92 per cent delivery reach 4,60,000 phones; 22 per cent of those open, 1,01,200 people; 35 per cent of openers click, 35,420; 20 per cent of clicks order, 7,084 orders, which at Taazgi's ₹640 average order value is ₹45,33,760, rounded to ₹45.34 lakh.
