The modelled column changes one input — who gets targeted — and every downstream figure moves with it, because Farhan's model selects for users statistically likelier to still want the message, raising both delivery and open rates. Same chain: 3,00,000 sends, 96 per cent delivered is 2,88,000, 30 per cent open is 86,400, 35 per cent click is 30,240, 20 per cent order is 6,048 orders, ₹38,70,720 in revenue, minus ₹0.42 lakh cost, netting ₹38.29 lakh — and only 864 opt-outs. The modelled send earns ₹12.76 net per message sent, against ₹8.93 for the broad send, while cutting opt-outs by 2,816, a 76.5 per cent reduction. The broad list earns ₹6.35 lakh more in net contribution this month; the modelled list keeps 2,816 more people reachable next month.

5. The nuances a learner has to sit with

Relevance is not the same lever as frequency

"Send more" and "send better" are not the same dial: a higher-frequency, lower-relevance programme raises short-run opens while raising opt-outs faster than revenue, exactly the pattern Taazgi's broad send showed against the modelled one.

An open-rate lift is not proof of an incremental lift

Without a holdout group — eligible users deliberately not sent the campaign — a team can only see that people who opened also ordered, not that the message caused it. Some of the broad send's 7,084 orders would have happened anyway; only a holdout comparison isolates the incremental effect.

Engagement lever and retention driver are different claims

A notification can lift a day's opens without moving the retention curve, because it pulls forward orders a user would have placed anyway rather than creating new habitual use. Messaging is an engagement lever within a broader loop, narrower than a claim about retention; the two should never be reported as interchangeable.

Opt-out is a leading indicator; open rate is a lagging one

Open rate describes what already happened to a message already sent. Opt-out describes the channel's future capacity to reach that person at all. A team that only watches open rate will not notice the channel eroding until it is already small.

Channel economics are not interchangeable

Push is nearly free but scarce in attention and permission; SMS costs real money and interrupts harder; email is cheap but easier to ignore. A frequency cap on one channel does not protect a user from fatigue on another.

What it cannot tell you

No trigger design or personalisation fixes a product that does not deliver what the message promises. If Taazgi's real complaint were late deliveries rather than volume, a better win-back message would only accelerate how fast reactivated users rediscover the same disappointment.

It is easily confused with personalisation

Personalisation is what the message says; lifecycle messaging is when and why it is sent at all. A beautifully personalised message sent at the wrong moment, or too often, is still a bad lifecycle decision.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace look genuinely different

At Taazgi, volume is high and most triggers are behavioural across a base too large to review individually; the main constraint is frequency capping across teams. Contrast Tantra Ledger Systems, a B2B reconciliation platform: notifications go to a few named users per corporate account, triggered by workflow events like an overdue invoice, sent mostly by email, and treated as a trust signal rather than a growth lever. Over-notifying one finance controller can cost Tantra Ledger Systems that whole account — a far larger loss than one consumer's opt-out.

A marketplace changes the picture again. Tijarat Home Services, connecting households with home-repair professionals, runs two lifecycle programmes at once: near-real-time push on the demand side for booking and arrival, where delay is itself the failure, and job alerts on the supply side, where over-alerting causes providers to mute the app and miss the one job they wanted, cutting the marketplace's fill rate. The same discipline, applied with consumer-side assumptions, breaks the supply side within weeks.

Stage matters as much as model. A pre-product-market-fit startup rarely has volume for a meaningful holdout, and is better served talking to users directly than building lifecycle infrastructure. The investment pays off once volume is large enough, as at Taazgi's 18,00,000 monthly active users, that a percentage-point shift in opt-out rate represents tens of thousands of real people.

7. Common mistakes, and the cheapest way to catch each one

The first is treating open rate as the scoreboard. Symptom: a campaign "wins" the weekly review while thirty-day retention stays flat; the error is mistaking curiosity for value delivered. Diagnostic: compare a holdout group's D30 retention against the sent group's.

The second is no cross-team frequency cap. Symptom: exactly what Devika found, a user getting 9 messages a week from three teams who each believe they are disciplined within their own campaign. Diagnostic: one audit of total messages per user per week, across every sender.

The third is borrowing promotional urgency — countdown timers, "just for you" language — for messages that are really transactional. Symptom: rising click-through alongside rising opt-out; diagnostic: track both trend lines on the same chart.

The fourth is stale suppression logic: a reactivation message to someone who already reactivated, or a cart reminder for an item already returned. Symptom: tickets saying some version of "I already did this"; diagnostic: the lag between a state change and the segment refresh meant to reflect it.

8. What good looks like

A year later, a mature version of Taazgi's retention programme runs on three disciplines absent in September 2026. Every campaign above a minimum size carries a permanent 5 per cent holdout, so the growth team reports incremental orders, not merely opens. A single shared "message budget" caps non-transactional notifications any user can receive across all teams in a rolling seven-day window. And opt-out rate sits on the same weekly dashboard as open rate, so an eroding channel is visible before it is small. None of this needs more cleverness than Devika's team already had; it needs treating the opt-out line as seriously as the revenue line.

9. What Devika decided

Devika approved Farhan's modelled list of 3,00,000 rather than the broad 5,00,000, accepting a projected ₹6.63 lakh less in this month's win-back revenue for 2,816 fewer users leaving the push channel permanently. Her reasoning for Friday's review: an opt-out is close to irreversible, and the 12,24,000 users still reachable by push are a stream of future campaigns this decision should not shrink for one month's number. She also asked every team sending notifications to Taazgi's users to report into one shared weekly total, and asked Farhan to build a permanent 5 per cent holdout into every lifecycle campaign, not just this one.

The natural next step is push and notification strategy proper: the platform-level questions of permission design, cadence limits and cross-team governance this single-campaign view sets up but does not answer. Two questions worth sitting with: first, if the holdout had shown the broad send's extra 2,00,000 messages produced no incremental orders beyond what the modelled 3,00,000 already captured, would your own team's habit of reporting open rate upward still feel honest? Second, where in a product you know well might a rising engagement number quietly be financed by a shrinking pool of people still willing to hear from you at all?
case20v1-growth.notifications:
Ilaaka Cricket Network and the Season-Opener Pushes

A decision case on notifications and lifecycle messaging

1. Opening

On Monday, 5 October 2026, Bimla Kandpal sat in the Haldwani office of Ilaaka Cricket Network, a laptop open to a dashboard she had been avoiding for a week. The winter cricket season across Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab would begin in earnest on the first weekend of November, just before Diwali on 8 November. On Friday, 9 October, Bimla, the Head of Product, had to present the board with a messaging plan for that month; the board would sign off on Monday, 12 October.

The dashboard showed that in September, 12,000 people had switched off notifications for the company's app, Padaav Scorer. The sales team had promised sponsors even more promotional pushes for November.

2. Company background

Ilaaka Cricket Network was founded in 2019 by Bhaskar Bisht, a former club opening batsman. Padaav Scorer began as a free ball-by-ball scoring app for tennis-ball and semi-pro leagues. It grew into league management: fixtures, points tables, registration and fee collection through UPI, with Razorpay handling cards. By September 2026 it had 18 lakh registered users, 6,00,000 monthly active users and about 3,600 active leagues.

CricHeroes is the best-known rival scoring app for amateur cricket, while Cricbuzz, JioHotstar and fantasy platforms such as Dream11 compete for the same evening minutes. Ilaaka covers the local match nobody else does. Revenue in the year to March 2026 was ₹14.4 crore, made up of ₹8.4 crore in organiser subscriptions, ₹4.8 crore in local and national sponsorship, and ₹1.2 crore from Fan Pass, a ₹150 monthly subscription for ad-free live alerts and match highlights.

3. The situation

Messaging at Ilaaka had grown by accretion: any team could add a push notification, and nobody removed one. Exhibit 1 shows the result. Push reaches 3,00,000 users, half the monthly active base, at about 30 pushes each a month, roughly seven a week. The company sends 111.9 lakh messages a month at a platform cost of ₹5.88 lakh, and push, at ₹0.02 a message, is the largest and cheapest channel.

Bimla asked Uttam Bahuguna, the data scientist in Melbourne, to break push down by purpose. Exhibit 2 is his answer. The first three types are triggered by something a user did or a match they follow. Promotional pushes (sponsor offers, Fan Pass promotions, contests) are scheduled by sales and marketing. They are 35 per cent of pushes, are tapped 1.6 per cent of the time, and account for 7,200 of the 12,000 opt-outs.

The global team saw the numbers differently. Ishwar Semwal, the engineering lead in Pune, said a proper preference centre would take about six weeks and cost roughly ₹12 lakh in engineering time. Ujjwal Rawat, the sales head in London, sold diaspora leagues to sponsors in Leicester and Birmingham and had learned that the 7 a.m. IST push arrived at 2:30 a.m. British time for about 30,000 users abroad. He wanted quiet hours by time zone, but he also owed sponsors their agreed exposure. Uttam asked one question repeatedly: what is a retained user worth?

His answer was that users who disabled push were retained at 22 per cent over the next 12 months, against 41 per cent for those who kept it on, a gap of 19 percentage points. Each retained user was worth about ₹300 over twelve months in sponsor exposure and Fan Pass. A lost push user therefore cost roughly ₹57 (19 per cent of ₹300). The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, was being phased in, and the company's lawyer had warned that purpose-specific, withdrawable consent would become the standard for marketing messages.

4. The people

  • Bimla Kandpal, Head of Product, Haldwani. She wants sponsor revenue to grow without shrinking the reachable audience.
  • Bhaskar Bisht, co-founder and CEO, Haldwani. He wants the sponsor contracts honoured; three run until March 2027.
  • Ujjwal Rawat, sales head, London. He wants more promotional inventory, and no more 2:30 a.m. pushes.
  • Uttam Bahuguna, data scientist, Melbourne. He wants the decision priced in retained users, not in sends.
  • Ishwar Semwal, engineering lead, Pune. He wants a defined scope, because November leaves no room for an open-ended rebuild.

5. What a promotional push earns

Exhibit 3 puts the promotional programme on one page. Fan Pass sales attributed to promotional pushes run at about 1,500 purchases a month at ₹150, or ₹2.25 lakh, and sponsors pay ₹4.50 lakh a month. Gross promotional revenue is therefore ₹6.75 lakh. From this, Bimla deducted the ₹0.63 lakh cost of sending and the ₹4.10 lakh of future value lost from 7,200 opt-outs at ₹57. What is left is ₹2.02 lakh a month, less than a third of the headline revenue.

The ₹57 is a modelled estimate: a 19-point retention gap applied to ₹300 of twelve-month value. It is a future cost, not this month's.

6. The options

Option A: Scale up. Keep every promotional push and add WhatsApp promotions for the 90,000 opted-in users, four a month, or 3,60,000 messages at ₹0.80. Ujjwal estimates sponsors would pay an extra ₹4.00 lakh a month. The added cost is ₹2.88 lakh, and Uttam expects about 1,400 users to block the number, a loss of ₹0.80 lakh.

Option B: Utility only. Stop all promotional pushes and send only triggered messages. This removes 7,200 opt-outs and the ₹0.63 lakh sending cost but forgoes ₹6.75 lakh of revenue and breaches sponsors' agreed exposure, forcing three contracts to be renegotiated mid-season.

Option C: A preference-led programme, tested. Build the preference centre so users choose the teams and topics they follow and whether they want offers. Cap promotions at one a week for the roughly 60,000 users who opt in, which is 2,40,000 promotional pushes a month. Move other sponsor exposure to email and in-app placements, and set quiet hours by time zone. Bimla estimates sponsors would keep 60 per cent of promotional revenue (₹4.05 lakh), because they pay for conversions, not sends. She expects promotional opt-outs to fall from 7,200 to about 600 and live-alert opt-outs from 3,000 to 1,800. It costs ₹12 lakh once and needs a six-week holdout test, in which a random tenth of users stay on the old regime, to prove the numbers.

Exhibit 4: Estimated monthly effect of each option against today (₹ lakh; positive is better)
OptionRevenue changeMessaging cost changeOpt-out value effectNet per month
A: Scale up+4.00-2.88-0.80+0.32

Option C also carries a one-time cost of ₹12 lakh. Opt-out effects use ₹57 a lost user: A, 1,400 extra blocks; B, 7,200 fewer opt-outs; C, 6,600 fewer promotional plus 1,200 fewer live-alert opt-outs (₹3.76 lakh and ₹0.68 lakh). At ₹30 a lost user instead, the nets become A +0.70, B -3.96 and C +0.22.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, which messages help users and which mainly serve the company? What does the tap rate alone fail to show?
  2. Why is net value in Exhibit 3 so far below gross revenue? How reliable is the ₹57?
  3. Using Exhibit 4, compare the three options. Why does Option A look positive, and what does it leave out?
  4. What would you recommend to the board on 12 October, and what result would make you change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

Triggered messaging helps when it is caused by something the user did or cares about, arrives when they can use it, and can be controlled by them. Exhibit 2 shows the difference: triggered types are tapped 14 to 31 per cent of the time, scheduled promotions 1.6 per cent. The lens also asks what a message costs in future engagement, not rupees per send. At ₹0.02 sending is nearly free; the cost appears in the opt-outs.

A well-reasoned answer prices the trade-off in retained users, respects the constraints (contracts, time zones, DPDP consent, the six-week build) and tests the key assumption. Option A looks attractive because lost users are hidden from monthly figures; Option B protects users but ignores the contracts.

One defensible path is Option C, sequenced to manage the risk. First, ship quiet hours by time zone immediately; it is cheap and answers the London complaint. Second, build the preference centre and run the holdout through November. Third, keep sponsor contracts whole with email and in-app placements. Fourth, set a clear kill criterion: if the holdout suggests a lost user is worth nearer ₹30 than ₹57, the net gain falls to about ₹0.22 lakh a month against a ₹12 lakh cost, and the company should shrink the programme to quiet hours and a promotional cap. At ₹57 the payback is about five months (₹12 lakh divided by ₹2.32 lakh a month). Promotion is not wrong; opted-in, capped and measured promotion beats blasting the whole base.
exp40v2-growth.loops:
Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Growth & Retention · Deep reading

Growth Loops vs Funnels

The funnel asks what a rupee of spend buys today. The loop asks what today's satisfied customer buys for you across the cycles still to come. Most companies that stall have answered only the first question well — and a good number that fail have answered only the second.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 4 February, in a room above a service road in Hyderabad's Gachibowli, Rohit Malviya, Head of Product at Maqta Systems, put four years of company history on one slide. Maqta sold billing, inventory and GST-return software to independent pharmacy chains at ₹2,400 per outlet per month through a field team of eleven: 4,900 paying outlets, ₹14.1 crore of ARR, net revenue retention of 112%. Over eight quarters the cost of acquiring an outlet had risen from ₹9,200 to ₹21,400 while quota attainment fell from 94% to 71%, even though every conversion rate in the pipeline had held or improved. Maqta was running out of pharmacies its outbound motion could cheaply reach, and the founder wanted six more reps. Rohit's counter-proposal, not yet costed, was that 38% of last quarter's new outlets had arrived through existing customers recommending Maqta to peers in the same distributor's network — and nobody owned that mechanism, measured it, or had spent a rupee improving it.

Nine days later and 1,700 kilometres north, Ira Deshmukh, co-founder of Roshnai Studio in Pune, faced the mirror image. Roshnai was AI-native: users uploaded photographs of a family event or a small shop's products, and the app returned post-ready images and captions in eleven Indian languages. Fourteen months old, 620,000 monthly actives, 41,000 subscribers at ₹299, almost no paid media. Every generated image carried a small, removable watermark, and watermarked images posted to Instagram and WhatsApp Status brought roughly 8,000 new users a week. But inference cost ₹1.90 per image, free users generated 6.2 images a month, and by her CFO's reading the loop that had built the company was burning ₹71 lakh a quarter to manufacture users who converted at 6.6%. The board asked her to consider removing the free tier; Ira believed the free tier was the channel, but could not prove it in a way that survived a spreadsheet. Both faced one question from opposite sides: leaky funnel, or self-reinforcing loop?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A funnel models growth as a directed sequence through which a cohort passes and shrinks — canonically Dave McClure's 2007 pirate metrics: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue. Its virtue is diagnostic: knowing 4% of visitors start a trial and 40% convert locates the leakage and prices the fix. Its structural assumption is that the top is refilled from outside, every period, by spend or effort.

A growth loop models growth as a closed cycle in which the output of one pass becomes an input to the next. The framing was sharpened around 2017 by practitioners including Brian Balfour and Casey Winters, as a critique of funnel-only thinking inside companies that had optimised every stage and stalled anyway. A loop has four elements: an input, the actions it performs, an output with acquisition value, and a re-entry where that output becomes the next period's input. The definition is stricter than it looks: if output does not become input, you have a channel, not a loop.

A funnel spends to acquire once. A loop reinvests what growth already produced in order to acquire again. Both describe the same business; they differ in what they treat as exogenous.

Three schools genuinely disagree. The loop-primacy school holds that the funnel is a reporting artefact and that any durable company runs one or two dominant loops whether it knows it or not, so strategy is choosing the loop to build the company around. It signs: "a company with no loop has no compounding and therefore no long-run advantage." It will not sign "every business must have a loop": an enterprise ERP vendor may grow well on a bought funnel and a strong brand.

The funnel-realist school, commoner among CMOs and in enterprise software, holds that loops are channel accounting that flatters companies with cheap virality and misleads everyone else. It signs: "most claimed loops are weak, saturating, and better modelled as an acquisition channel with a variable cost near zero." It will not sign "compounding does not exist" — word-of-mouth is real and often the largest channel; the claim is that loop framing adds no predictive power beyond measuring it as one.

The systems-dynamics school — older than both, descending from Jay Forrester's industrial dynamics and, popularly, Jim Collins's flywheel — holds that both camps under-model the balancing loops. Growth is never a single reinforcing loop; it is one wrapped in constraints — saturation, fatigue, unit cost, support capacity — that eventually dominate. It signs "every reinforcing loop is eventually governed by a balancing loop you have not yet named," and refuses both rival slogans.

3. Mechanics, worked rather than named

The formal treatment is simpler than most decks imply. Let b be the new users each active user produces per period through the loop, and c the fraction of the base lost per period. Then Bt+1 = Bt(1 + b − c) + P, where P is paid or sales-driven additions. Three regimes follow, and confusing them is the commonest error in growth reviews.

RegimeConditionBehaviour of the baseWhat paid spend does
Self-sustainingb > cGrows geometrically with no external inputAccelerates a curve that already rises
Subsidisedb < c, b > 0Decays to a plateau of P/(c − b)Sets the plateau; loop multiplies it by 1/(1 − b/c)
Pure funnelb ≈ 0Plateau at P/cIs the only thing holding the base up

The subsidised regime is where almost every real company lives. Rohit's peer-recommendation mechanism produced 0.021 new outlets per active outlet per quarter against quarterly logo churn of 0.034: the loop alone shrinks. But the multiplier 1/(1 − 0.021/0.034) = 2.6 was the number that mattered — each outlet the sales team added was worth 2.6 outlets of steady-state base over its life, so Maqta's true CAC was not ₹21,400 but roughly ₹8,230, which moves hiring six reps from reckless to obvious. The funnel-realist is right that this is channel accounting; the loop advocate is right that nobody had done it.

The loop Rohit had never costed, drawn with its inputs. Sales additions enter at the top; the balancing constraint — a finite number of peers per distributor catchment, plus churn — sits on the re-entry arc. Both arrows are needed to predict anything.

Four steps are routinely left implicit when teams "build a loop". First, name the unit that cycles — not "users" but a countable behaviour: for Maqta, a pharmacist mentioning the product to a peer, which Rohit proxied by asking every new lead who had referred them. Second, locate the trigger: Roshnai's was the instant a generated image was saved to camera roll, not the share button. Third, measure conversion inside the loop; its interior is funnel-shaped and the funnel toolkit belongs there. Fourth, verify re-entry — confirm that users the loop produced reach the same trigger at a comparable rate. That step is skipped almost universally, and it is what separates a loop from a referral programme: Roshnai's re-entry rate was 0.62, so the coefficient decayed 38% per cycle and the "loop" was a converging series, not a perpetual engine.

Two second-order effects deserve naming. Because b is per active user, any retention gain raises the base that produces output, which raises output, which raises the base: retention enters a loop model twice and a funnel model once, which is why loop-modelled companies fund it harder. And cycle time governs compounding as much as the coefficient does — b = 0.03 on a one-month cycle compounds faster than b = 0.15 on six. Rohit's cycle was five months; Ira's was eleven days. That difference is why loop thinking dominates consumer product culture and draws suspicion in enterprise software.

4. When the framing applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable claims, not aphorisms. One: the output must have acquisition value that needs no fresh spend. Roshnai passes cleanly — a watermarked image on WhatsApp Status costs nothing beyond inference already paid for. Maqta passes weakly: the mention is free, but converting it consumes a rep's day, so "free growth" is false. Two: re-entry must be non-trivial. Maqta's referred outlets referred onwards at 0.81 of base rate, Roshnai's at 0.62 — both pass, neither strongly. Three: the reachable population must be large relative to the base. Roshnai passes overwhelmingly; Maqta fails locally, because a catchment holds perhaps 120 pharmacies of which Maqta had 40, so the loop saturates after three cycles while the national market still looks vast. Four: cycle time must be short relative to the planning horizon. Roshnai passes; Maqta's five months against a quarterly board rhythm fails organisationally rather than mathematically.

The framing actively misleads in four situations. Where demand is genuinely one-shot — a home loan, a visa service, a wedding venue — customer re-entry is near zero and any loop runs through third parties, which is a referral channel and should be managed as one. Where purchase is gated by a regulator or a procurement process, the binding constraint is empanelment, not enthusiasm. In categories with strong negative signalling — sexual health, debt counselling, mental health — sharing is suppressed by the very thing that makes the product valuable, and loop targets borrowed from consumer apps are not merely unrealistic but insulting. And when the base is small, loop language is premature: 2% of 800 users is sixteen people, and a team that reorganises around sixteen people has confused a future engine with a present one.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product is where sophisticated companies live and the single-loop picture breaks. The honest question is whether product B sits inside product A's loop or is merely sold to the same base. Arhat Exchange, a marketplace matching mandi commission agents with truck owners for agricultural freight, learned this painfully: an insurance attach raised revenue per load 14% but sat outside the loop, because insured loads generated no additional supply or demand. Revenue rose; growth did not. If a product's contribution does not appear in b, it is a monetisation improvement — valuable, and different.

Two-sided markets have two loops with a shared constraint and must be modelled separately with a coupling term. Arhat's supply loop — more trucks listed, shorter waits, more agents posting loads — cycled in about nine days, its demand loop in three. Cross-elasticity mattered more than either coefficient: a 10% rise in listed trucks produced 3.4% more loads, while a 10% rise in loads produced 7.1% more listed trucks, which told Arhat to spend on demand and let supply follow. Marketplace loops are also local: every expansion resets the cold start.

Regulation changes what the output may be. A lending or insurance product cannot base an incentive on referral without meeting the regulator's view of who is acting as an intermediary; RBI and IRDAI rules on distribution are specific, and several Indian fintechs have restructured referral schemes after supervisory feedback. Regulated categories therefore tend toward content or data loops rather than incentive loops.

Hardware-plus-software puts a capital constraint on the re-entry arc. Saaz Instruments sells connected cold-chain monitors to dairy and pharma distributors with a subscription dashboard, and has a genuine loop — a distributor who sees spoilage fall recommends Saaz along the same corridor — but each new customer needs devices manufactured, financed and installed on a twelve-week lead time. Beyond the rate at which working capital recycles, the coefficient is irrelevant: Saaz's constraint is the balance sheet.

AI-native products carry two easily conflated loops: acquisition (watermarked outputs) and data (corrections improving the model, improving quality, improving retention and share rate). Their cycle times differ by an order of magnitude and the data loop's effect on b is hard to attribute. Worse, AI products carry a cost term classic software loops lack — inference — so a loop that grows usage also grows cost of goods, and can be positive in users while negative in contribution margin.

At the organisational seams the pattern is consistent and rarely said aloud: loops cross functions, budgets do not. Roshnai's watermark is owned by design, its removal is a pricing decision owned by monetisation, its measurement sits with an analyst reporting to marketing. Companies that claim to run on loops typically run funnels inside each function and show a loop diagram once a quarter. What works is narrow: one owner per loop with authority over trigger and output, a metric reported in cycles, and an explicit statement of which constraint currently governs.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Distinguishing a loop from a free channel. The competent practitioner calls anything free and recurring a loop; the expert asks whether output re-enters as input. Word-of-mouth from a fixed base of delighted users is a channel; word-of-mouth that grows because the base grew is a loop. The tell is a coefficient quoted per period rather than per user.

Reading the balancing loop first. When Rohit modelled Maqta properly, the useful insight was not b = 0.021 but that each catchment held about 120 pharmacies, making the loop saturating with a per-territory ceiling. The tell is a curve convex in early cohorts and concave in later ones within one geography. The obvious reading is that the loop is weakening; the correct one is that it works as before against a smaller remaining population.

Treating cycle time as a first-class variable. Competent teams optimise the coefficient; experts often find it cheaper to halve the cycle. Roshnai cut its cycle from fourteen days to eleven by pre-rendering a share-ready 9:16 crop at generation time, which did nothing to share rate but measurably raised annual compounding. The tell is a team reporting loop health weekly for a loop whose cycle is a quarter — that is noise, and they will act on it.

Knowing retention enters twice. Because b is per active user and the base is what churn erodes, a five-point retention gain raises both the multiplier and the population it multiplies, so experts price retention against loop leverage rather than direct revenue. The tell is whether a team can say what a one-point retention change does to steady-state base; most cannot, and the answer is larger than intuition suggests.

Watching for loops running in reverse. Every reinforcing loop can invert. Arhat saw it in Nashik when a fuel-price spike pulled trucks off the platform, lengthening match times, driving agents back to phone brokers, reducing load volume, pushing more trucks off. The tell is a decline that accelerates rather than flattens. The obvious reading is seasonality; the correct one is that the sign has flipped.

Separating the loop from its carrier. Practitioners fall in love with the referral screen, the watermark, the embed; experts treat these as replaceable carriers of a motive — status, reciprocity, getting something done with a colleague. When Roshnai removed the watermark for paying users their share rate fell only 9%, because the motive was pride in the output. The tell is a loop that survives removal of its supposed mechanism.

Distinguishing loop growth from loop-shaped reporting. Attribution will, if allowed, assign to the loop every user whose last touch was organic, so experts use holdouts. Maqta's first honest coefficient came from withholding the referral ask from 200 outlets for a quarter: referrals fell by less than the model predicted, revealing that a third of them were peers who would have arrived anyway. The tell is a loop never measured against a holdout.

Holding both models at once without fudging. The expert position is not that loops replace funnels but that the funnel diagnoses conversion within a period, the loop forecasts across periods, and the two must agree at the boundary. When they disagree for the same quarter, the gap usually locates an unmeasured re-entry or a double-counted channel. The tell is a company that maintains both and reconciles them monthly.

7. How this varies by product type and company stage

Consumer loops are fast, social and usually leased from a platform, so their coefficients are partly set by someone else's ranking algorithm and revocable without notice; the dominant risk is saturation of the sharer population. B2B loops run through organisations rather than social graphs — expansion from one team to the next inside an account, reference-based selling between peer firms — with cycle times in quarters and a human operating each arc consciously. The difference is not merely speed: a B2B loop can be managed, and therefore forecast, staffed and coached, whereas a consumer loop can mostly only be measured and nudged. In enterprise a third pattern runs through people rather than firms: practitioners carry a product from one employer to the next, a cycle with a two-to-four-year period, too slow to manage quarterly and too real to omit from a ten-year strategy.

Platforms and marketplaces run coupled loops and must decide which side to subsidise; the honest test is cross-elasticity, not ideology. Hardware loops are governed by working capital, the constraint sitting on the re-entry arc rather than on motivation. AI products add a data loop whose output is quality rather than users, plus a cost term — the only category where a stronger loop can worsen the P&L in the same quarter. Where the difference is not real, say so plainly: the arithmetic of b, c, cycle time and saturation is identical everywhere, and "loops don't apply to us" almost always means "our cycle is long and our coefficient small", which is quantitative, not categorical. Stage decides which engine gets the marginal rupee. Below roughly ten thousand actives no plausible coefficient produces meaningful volume, and the loop's only job is to prove it exists; in the scaling middle it is a multiplier on bought acquisition, and Rohit's CAC-divided-by-multiplier calculation is the central number; at scale the work shifts from proving the loop to defending it against saturation, fatigue and platform change.

8. Three worked examples

Sabaq Learning: a content loop that worked. Sabaq ran a test-preparation app for state-board students, where every solved question generated a public, indexable solution page. In month one it had 18,000 pages drawing 210,000 monthly organic sessions, converting at 2.1% to registration and 11% of those to paid; students produced roughly 0.9 new pages each per month. Over fourteen months pages rose to 141,000 and sessions to 1.32 million, while paid spend fell from ₹64 lakh to ₹19 lakh a quarter. The coefficient was unremarkable; the nine-day cycle from indexing to first visit made it compound. Tellingly, the team spent eleven months on page quality and internal linking rather than the share mechanism, because the binding constraint was the search engine's willingness to rank.

Arhat Exchange: a coupled loop with a local ceiling. Arhat's Nashik operation reached 640 active trucks and 2,900 monthly loads, with supply coefficient 0.11 per truck per month and demand 0.05 per agent. Expansion into four new mandis assumed the same numbers. In Guntur supply came in at 0.03, because a more consolidated commission-agent network meant fewer intermediaries and fewer informal recommendations. Arhat burned ₹4.1 crore over two quarters before recognising that its loop was a property of market structure rather than of the product.

Amrai Fresh: where the approach failed. Amrai sold produce from farmer collectives direct to urban households. Persuaded by a loop-primacy consultant, its leadership cut performance marketing 70% in one quarter to fund a referral programme paying ₹150 of credit to both sides, on a claimed b of 0.09 monthly. The model omitted that the coefficient had been measured during a festival promotion among early adopters in two Bengaluru pin codes with unusually dense social ties. Realised b was 0.026 against churn of 0.071. The base fell from 44,000 to 31,500 households in five months; margin worsened as credits went to low-basket households; and the reverse loop bit, as fewer households thinned delivery routes, raising cost per order, forcing a higher minimum order, raising churn again.

The recovery is the instructive part, and it was not a reversal. Amrai restored paid spend to about 78% of its old level, moved the referral trigger from the order-confirmation screen to the third successful delivery, capped credits by basket value, and reported net loop growth rather than referral volume. Churn fell as route density recovered. Eighteen months on, the loop contributed more households than it ever had under the aggressive programme, at a fifth of the credit cost — because the constraint had never been the incentive. It was the moment of asking, and the cohort asked.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Coefficient measured once, during a promotionOne impressive number with no time series behind itWhat is b across three consecutive rolling cohorts, excluding campaigns?Budget reallocated on a false premise — Amrai's 12,500 lost households

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is whether loops are a strategy or an accounting frame. Loop-primacy, steelmanned: businesses that compound do so because output re-enters as input, and organising roadmap, metrics and ownership around that arc produces decisions funnel-organised companies systematically miss — Rohit's uncosted referral channel being a textbook instance. Its evidence is the set of firms whose dominant acquisition is structurally free and whose margins show it; it would be wrong if those firms reached those economics through segment and pricing choices, the loop being an artefact of product-market fit rather than its cause. Funnel-realism, steelmanned: nearly all measured coefficients in non-network businesses are under 0.05 monthly and saturating, so the loop is a modest multiplier belonging to a channel owner with a budget, while the real levers are price, segment and sales capacity. Its evidence is the long list of loop reorganisations that changed no growth rate; it would be wrong if channel accounting systematically understates the multiplier on lifetime base — precisely what Maqta's 2.6× suggests.

The second disagreement is about incentives. One camp holds that paid referral corrupts measurement and attracts the wrong cohort, so any loop requiring payment is a channel in costume. The other holds that an incentive is simply a price for a transaction that would otherwise be hard to trigger. Amrai supports the first on cohort quality; plenty of Indian commerce and fintech companies have built durable bases on referral credit, which supports the second. It is an empirical question per product, answerable only with a holdout.

The third, and in 2026 the most consequential, is whether AI-native products have loops in the classic sense at all. One view holds the data loop is the real moat and user growth loops secondary. The other holds that data advantages in most applied products are shallow — foundation-model capability improves for everyone and fine-tuning on corrections yields fast-diminishing returns — so the only durable loop is distribution. Ira's board had members on both sides, which is why her decision was hard.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this draws loop diagrams, says flywheel, and asks teams to add a referral feature. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four ways. They ask for the holdout before the diagram, because an unmeasured coefficient is a hypothesis. They speak in cycles rather than months, and refuse to read a weekly movement in a quarterly loop. They name the balancing constraint unprompted, and can say what the ceiling is and what would raise it. And they keep both models running — funnel for this period's diagnosis, loop for next year's forecast — treating disagreement between them as the most informative signal available. The tell, in a review meeting, is that they ask what the base will be in four cycles rather than what last week's conversion rate was.

12. The decisions

Rohit took the hiring proposal forward unchanged in headcount but changed in reasoning. Six reps at ₹21,400 an outlet looked indefensible at face value; divided by the 2.6× multiplier the effective cost was ₹8,230, comfortably inside Maqta's payback threshold. He attached two conditions: a named owner for the referral arc with authority over when and how the ask is made, with the 5% holdout made permanent; and territory selection driven by remaining reachable population per catchment rather than absolute market size, because the loop saturates locally after about three cycles. He did not claim the loop would replace sales — only that it made sales affordable.

Ira did not remove the free tier. She proposed capping free generations at four a month rather than six, which modelled to a 31% cut in inference cost against a 12% fall in share volume, because the fifth and sixth generations came disproportionately from users who never shared. She also committed to two numbers the board had never seen: re-entry rate by cohort, so the decay from 0.62 would be visible, and contribution margin on loop-acquired users at ninety days. Her reasoning was that the free tier was neither charity nor a loop in itself — it was the price Roshnai paid for distribution, and a price should be negotiated, not abolished.

For discussion

1. Maqta's 2.6× rests on a coefficient measured in the territories it entered first. What evidence would persuade you it holds next year — and what changes if it falls to 1.4×?

2. Is Ira's free tier a growth loop with a cost term, or a paid channel whose currency is compute rather than rupees? Does the answer change what she should do?

3. Amrai's recovery came from changing the trigger and the cohort, not the incentive. When would the opposite have been true — and how would you have known before spending ₹4 crore?

13. Going deeper

Pirate metrics (AARRR) is the funnel this topic redraws as a cycle; precise stage definitions are what let you measure a loop's interior. Building a growth model is the next practical step, where b, c, cycle time and paid additions become one spreadsheet a board can argue with. Modelling and stress-testing growth loops breaks that model deliberately, the only way to learn whether your plan rests on a coefficient measured once during a festival. Acquisition channels and economics supplies the counterfactual: what growth costs when bought. Activation and onboarding optimisation governs how many acquired users reach the trigger at all, usually the cheapest lever on b. Engagement loops and habit covers the faster loops within a session that keep users in the base. Retention strategy is the c in the equation and enters twice, which is why it deserves more funding than funnel logic implies. Resurrection and win-back addresses lapsed users, ignored by most loop models and often a larger stock than the active base. Virality and the viral coefficient is the special case where the output is an invitation, unlocking the treatment of k, cycle time and the series that decides whether a loop converges or compounds.
case20v1-growth.loops:
Chaupal Group Payments: The Diwali Budget

A case on growth loops versus funnels

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 30 September 2026, Charu Mehrotra sat in the Jaipur office of Chaupal Group Payments with a one-page budget request and a deadline. The board would meet on Monday, 5 October, and Diwali fell on 8 November. As head of product, Mehrotra had up to ₹1.8 crore of incremental growth budget for October to December. She could spend it, or explain why it should be spent differently.

Three colleagues in three cities had given her three different answers, all from the same numbers.

2. Company background

Chaupal Group Payments, founded in 2019, builds an app that lets friends, flatmates and families share costs and settle them over UPI. A user opens a group for a Goa trip or a rented flat, adds expenses, and members pay their shares through any UPI app. Chaupal earns from merchant offers and a premium tier, with annualised revenue of ₹38 crore.

The company operated in a crowded lane. PhonePe and Paytm offered bill-splitting inside far larger payment apps, CRED had made group settlement part of its own experience, and Google Pay was a default on most Android phones. Chaupal's answer was depth: recurring groups, reminders and a shared ledger. It had about 62 lakh monthly active users, built up with performance marketing on Meta and YouTube and, more recently, unmeasured word of mouth.

3. The situation

Growth at Chaupal had always been managed as a funnel. The paid team bought installs, the product team improved onboarding, and success was read left to right. Exhibit 1 shows a typical recent month. Of 3,00,000 paid installs, 54,000 became activated users, meaning they had created a group with at least two members and completed one settlement. That is 18 per cent. On ₹60 lakh of monthly paid spend, an install cost ₹20 and an activated user ₹111.

Exhibit 1. The paid funnel, a typical recent month

Source: company dashboards. Cost per activated user is ₹60,00,000 divided by 54,000, rounded to the nearest rupee.

The funnel view missed something. Chinmay Rao, the data scientist in Toronto, had spent the summer tracing what activated users did next. Each one, he found, invited on average five people into a group. A quarter of those invitees installed the app and 32 per cent of the installers went on to activate. Exhibit 2 sets out the loop, and Figure 1 draws it.

Figure 1. The invite loop, first cycle from one month's paid cohort of 54,000 activated users.

Loop factor is invites x install rate x activation rate. Loop-driven activations equal 54,000 x k / (1 − k), the full tail of the geometric series; at k = 0.40 the first three cycles deliver 33,696 of the 36,000. Totals are rounded to whole users.

The loop factor was 0.40: 54,000 activated users produced 21,600 more, those produced 8,640, and so on. Summed over all cycles, a paid cohort of 54,000 became 90,000 activated users, so the true cost was ₹67 per activated user, not ₹111. Invited users were also stickier: at day 90, 41 per cent of invited users remained active against 22 per cent of those acquired through paid installs.

Because k was below one, the loop amplified paid acquisition but could not replace it.

From Berlin, the designer Vanessa Albrecht had watched session recordings. An invitee tapped a WhatsApp link, landed on the Play Store, and had to install, verify a phone number and find the group before paying a ₹450 share of a dinner bill. Her team had tested a web page where an invitee could pay a share through any UPI app with no install, followed by a prompt to save the group. In a pilot of 14,000 invites, 4,900 invitees joined, 35 per cent.

4. The people

Vikram Nair, head of growth in Bengaluru, ran the paid budget. He wanted to double spend, arguing that Diwali travel and gifting made this the cheapest quarter of the year to buy attention.

Chetan Joshi, engineering lead in Pune, managed a team of eleven with a committed roadmap for a merchant-offers module. A web pay-link meant eight engineer-weeks and a rework of the invite service. His costing came to ₹45 lakh, and the earliest release was 1 December. He also wanted consent screens reviewed for the DPDP Act.

Chinmay Rao, in Toronto, worked nine and a half hours behind Jaipur. He trusted the loop arithmetic but thought the pilot thin and feared rewards would attract users who joined only for money.

Vanessa Albrecht in Berlin wanted the friction removed, and distrusted incentives shipped before the invitee experience was fixed.

5. The options

Option A: buy more. Double monthly paid spend to ₹1.2 crore for October to December. Nair estimated the extra ₹60 lakh a month would buy 2,00,000 extra installs at ₹30 each, giving 5,00,000 installs and, at the same 18 per cent, 90,000 activations before the loop. With k at 0.40, that is 1,50,000 in total, an increase of 60,000 a month on the current 90,000. The upside is speed. The cost is the entire ₹1.8 crore, with nothing left behind once spending stops.

Option B: fix the loop. Spend ₹45 lakh on the web pay-link, live from 1 December, and keep paid spend at ₹60 lakh a month. If the pilot rate held, k would rise to 0.56 and each monthly paid cohort would deliver 1,22,727 activated users, an increase of 32,727 a month for no further spend. The cost is a two-month wait and a small pilot.

Option C: pay for invitations. Offer a ₹50 reward for each invitee who activates, launched within two weeks. Rao modelled invites rising to seven but activation falling to 26 per cent, so k would be 0.455. Chaupal would pay ₹50 on each of 45,083 loop-driven activations, or ₹22.54 lakh a month, for a gain of 9,083 a month. It needs little engineering, but the payout recurs and joiners may be weaker.

Exhibit 3. The three options compared over October to March
OptionCash cost (₹ lakh)Months of effectIncremental activationsCost per incremental activation

Incremental means over the current 90,000 a month. A runs October to December; B is live December to March; C runs all six months at ₹22.54 lakh a month. Costs per activation are cost divided by activations, rounded to the nearest rupee. The gains are eventual totals attributed to each month's paid cohort.

Exhibit 3 shows why the choice was not obvious. Over the quarter alone, Option A delivered 1,80,000 extra activations and Option B about 32,727, one month of effect from its December release. Over six months A still led on volume, 1,80,000 against 1,30,908, but at ₹100 per activation against ₹34, and B left ₹1.35 crore unspent and kept delivering after March.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1 only, what would you conclude about the cost of an activated user? How does Exhibit 2 change that conclusion?
  2. Why is a loop factor of 0.40 valuable even though it is below one? What would it mean for Chaupal if k reached 1.0?
  3. Which single number in Exhibit 2 is least certain, and what would you do this week to reduce that uncertainty?
  4. Choose among A, B and C, and state what would need to be true for you to change your mind.

7. A note for the learner

A funnel counts what each rupee of acquisition buys once. A loop asks what the output of one cycle does to the input of the next. Chaupal was already a loop business, and its funnel dashboard priced users at ₹111 when the loop-aware figure was ₹67. The useful question is which stage of the loop has the most leverage per rupee.

In Exhibit 2 every stage multiplies the others. Raising the invite-to-install rate from 25 to 35 per cent lifts k by 40 per cent, from 0.40 to 0.56. Because the total is 1/(1−k), that moves the multiplier on a paid cohort from 1.67 to 2.27. Doubling spend, by contrast, raises installs by two-thirds at a higher marginal price. The retention gap also matters, since invited users stay active at almost twice the rate.

One defensible path is Option B, with discipline about its weak point. Approve the ₹45 lakh and the December release, but ask Rao to re-run the pilot on a larger and more varied sample before 15 October, including festive-season invites. Keep paid spend at ₹60 lakh a month; Option A buys more volume in the quarter, but B is about three times cheaper per activation and its gain outlasts the spend. If Nair can show that a smaller increase, perhaps ₹15 lakh a month, keeps buying installs at ₹20 to ₹22, take that from the remaining budget rather than the full ₹1.8 crore. Reject Option C for now: it pays for behaviour the design fix would create free, and its lower activation rate suggests weaker users.

The path is defensible because it improves the mechanism rather than renting volume: B costs more per activation than A over six months if the pilot rate falls below about 29 per cent, testable before the board meets. A well-reasoned answer names that condition.
case40v1-growth.loops:
Aamantran Booking Cloud: The Badge, the Directory and the Dubai Contract

A case on growth loops and funnels. Ahmedabad, October 2026.

1. Sunday night, 4 October 2026

Anuradha Deshpande had the board pre-read open on one screen and, on the other, a spreadsheet that would not settle. It was almost eleven at night. The board of Aamantran Booking Cloud met at nine, and the decision before it was how to deploy the ₹11 crore ring-fenced for growth to March 2027.

As chief product officer, Deshpande owned the recommendation. She had four proposals from four people in four time zones, each internally consistent, each reading the same telemetry differently. The disagreement, she suspected, was not about which number was right but about what kind of machine Aamantran was.

For seven years the company had described its growth as a funnel: buy a click, win a trial, activate a workspace, convert a subscription. In April, a data scientist in Toronto had begun instrumenting what activated workspaces did to the population around them, and the picture that came back ran in a circle. Three methods of measuring it gave three answers, and two of its strongest arcs were about to be cut — one by a contract signed in 2021, the other by a statute.

2. Company history

Aamantran was founded in Ahmedabad in 2018 by Eshan Bhatt and a co-founder who left in 2023. A small service business — a clinic, a salon, a chartered accountant, a tutor — created a public booking page, published the link on WhatsApp and Google Business Profile, and took appointments with reminders and, after 2022, prepaid UPI deposits through Razorpay. It competed with Zoho Bookings, Practo in clinics, Justdial, and the free calendar links every customer already had.

One decision from that period shaped everything available in 2026. In March 2021, with 9,400 paying workspaces and eleven months of cash, Bhatt signed an original-equipment agreement with Ekatra Merchant Services, a payments firm with a large offline merchant base, which bundled a co-branded Aamantran into its merchant app. Ekatra's lawyers asked for one thing that seemed costless: no Aamantran branding on pages created through Ekatra. Nobody objected, because nobody was measuring what the branding did.

By 31 August 2026 Aamantran had 4,12,000 published booking pages and 64,000 paying workspaces, 11,400 of them through Ekatra and 4,000 outside India. Monthly recurring revenue was ₹479.58 lakh, an annualised ₹57.55 crore. Cash was ₹41 crore against a monthly operating loss of ₹31.32 lakh, so runway was not the constraint. Growth was: revenue rose 45.0 per cent in the year to August 2025 and 22.0 per cent in the year to August 2026, and the Series B lead wanted it back above 40 per cent before a Series C.

Three forces bore on the product. UPI had made prepayment normal, so a booking carrying a ₹200 deposit no longer felt exotic. The Reserve Bank's e-mandate rules made auto-debit workable but cost a fifth of renewal attempts on the first pass. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act bore on the part of the product that generated free traffic: a public booking page for a diagnostics centre listing practitioner names and open slots would, in counsel's September note, need fresh consent to remain indexed after 1 January 2027. Of 4,12,000 published pages, 1,93,640 — 47 per cent — were in flagged categories.

Competition had also become more expensive. Cost per click rose from about ₹9 in early 2025 to ₹14 by August 2026 as Zoho pushed its bundle and entrants bid on Indian keywords; blended cost per activated workspace rose from ₹812 to ₹1,333, up 64.2 per cent. Abroad, 4,000 paying workspaces in the UAE, Singapore and the United States paid an average of ₹1,800 a month. In August, Esha Krishnan in Singapore brought in an approach from Ehtimaad Medical Group, a Dubai clinic chain of 140 locations wanting a white-labelled deployment.

Growth Loops vs Funnels

Is our growth a leaky funnel or a self-reinforcing loop? The question sounds academic until the marketing budget runs out and the answer decides whether the company keeps growing at all.

1. A board meeting in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of March, Ananya Rao, VP of Growth at Rasoi Club, opened the monthly board deck with a chart she had been dreading. Rasoi Club sold weekly recipe-kit subscriptions — pre-portioned ingredients and printed cards for regional Indian dishes, delivered to homes in six cities. Eighteen months in, the company had 31,000 active subscribers and had just closed a ₹40 crore Series A. Customer acquisition cost had climbed from ₹540 to ₹850 over two quarters, while new-subscriber volume had flattened at roughly 2,600 a month despite a 35% increase in performance-marketing spend on Instagram and Google.

Every stage of Rasoi Club's funnel still looked healthy in isolation: 4.1% of visitors signed up for a trial box, 46% converted to a paid subscription, and 61% were still active after month two. Ananya's team had spent a year optimising exactly these numbers, and each optimisation had produced a small, real lift. Yet total new subscribers had not moved in five months. The board's question was blunt: if every conversion rate is improving, why has growth stopped compounding? Ananya's answer, given hesitantly because she had only recently worked it out herself, was that Rasoi Club had been measuring a funnel while its actual growth engine — a handful of customers who photographed their finished dishes and tagged friends — ran on its own, unmeasured and unfed. Her decision was whether to keep pouring new funding into the funnel she understood, or redirect a share of it into a loop she had only just noticed.

2. The idea

A funnel is a model of growth as a one-way sequence of stages — typically Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue, the "AARRR" pirate metrics that Dave McClure popularised around 2007 — in which a cohort of prospects enters at the top and a shrinking fraction survives each stage. A funnel is useful because it isolates where people are lost, but it treats every new customer as the result of a fresh injection of attention at the top: run the ads, buy the impressions, start again next month. A growth loop is a different model, popularised roughly a decade later by growth practitioners such as Brian Balfour and Casey Winters as an explicit critique of funnel-only thinking: it describes growth as a closed cycle in which the output of one round of the cycle becomes the input to the next round, so that the system can, in principle, keep running without a continuous fresh injection from outside. A referral loop is the simplest example — an existing customer shares the product, the share produces a new customer, the new customer (once retained and satisfied) eventually shares too — but loops also run on content, on data, or on reinvested revenue, not only on invitations. The problem the loop framing was invented to solve is precisely the one Rasoi Club had: a company can improve every stage of its funnel and still stall, because a funnel by construction resets to zero every cycle, while a loop compounds on the base that came before it. The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this.

A funnel spends to acquire once; a loop reinvests what growth already produced to acquire again.
The funnel drains into a fixed pool once; the loop's fourth stage regenerates the first stage of the next cycle.

3. How it actually works

Practitioners usually leave four steps implicit when they talk about loops. First, identify the unit that cycles — not "users" in general, but a specific behaviour: at Rasoi Club it was a subscriber photographing a plated dish and tagging a friend. Second, name the trigger — the moment that prompts the behaviour. This is the step teams skip most often: a share prompt fired at checkout, before the customer has tasted anything, has almost no power, while the same prompt fired forty minutes after delivery, alongside a four- or five-star rating, catches the customer proudest of what they made. Third, measure the conversion inside the loop — of the people who receive the shared content, what fraction become new subscribers, with the same stage-by-stage rigour a funnel would apply, because internally a loop is still made of funnel-shaped steps. Fourth, confirm that the new subscribers the loop produces eventually reach the same trigger themselves, closing the cycle rather than dead-ending. A team that instruments only the first three steps has built a referral programme; a team that instruments all four has built a loop, because only then can it tell whether the system sustains itself across cycles rather than just the one.

4. A worked example, twice

Ananya's team pulled the numbers for March. In that month, 1,000 subscribers were shown the "share your plate" button at the post-delivery trigger point, and 20% — 200 people — actually shared. Each share reached enough friends, through WhatsApp and Instagram Stories, that 0.15 new sign-ups resulted per share: 200 × 0.15 = 30 sign-ups attributable to the loop. Of those, 40% converted to a paying subscription, the same rate the funnel achieved on paid traffic: 30 × 0.40 = 12 new subscribers, produced without a rupee of media spend, from a base of 1,000 exposed subscribers — a monthly loop contribution of 1.2%.

The team then changed one input: they replaced the generic "invite a friend" button with a one-tap sticker template pre-filled with the dish photo, shown only to subscribers who had just rated a meal four stars or higher. Nothing else changed. The share rate rose from 20% to 35% — 350 sharers instead of 200 — while per-share conversion held at 0.15: 350 × 0.15 = 52.5 sign-ups, and at the same 40% trial conversion, 21 new subscribers, up from 1.2% to 2.1% of the exposed base.
