After the redesign it needed only 379 (₹3,22,150) plus ₹2,100 in credits: ₹810.60 — a modest 2% saving in a single month. What mattered to the board was not that saving but that the loop's 21 subscribers joined the base the loop draws from next month, so the same 2.1% rate would produce more absolute subscribers in April without any further redesign, while the funnel's ₹850 cost would not fall by a rupee no matter how many months it ran.

At 2.1% monthly on a growing base, loop-sourced subscribers rise even with zero change in tactic; paid volume at a fixed budget does not.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

A loop still contains funnel-shaped stages

Loops do not abolish conversion-rate thinking; they change what the last stage's output is used for. Every loop, examined closely, has a trigger, an action, a conversion event, and a resulting state — the same anatomy as a funnel — so stage-by-stage measurement is not wasted, only nested one level deeper.

Loop coefficient is broader than viral k-factor

The classic viral k-factor — invitations per user, times conversion rate of each — is one special case of a loop coefficient. Content loops (a review page indexed by search engines), data loops (usage improving a model that improves retention), and paid loops (reinvesting a share of revenue at a return that funds itself) all have their own coefficients; confusing "loop" with "viral" causes teams to overlook loops that never involve one user inviting another.

Compounding is directional, not automatic

A 2.1% monthly loop contribution only compounds the visible base if it exceeds the rate that base is lost to churn. Rasoi Club's month-two retention was 61%, meaning roughly 3% of subscribers lapsed each month at that stage; a loop contributing 2.1% against 3% churn is still net-shrinking alone and needs the funnel, or a retention fix, to stay net-positive.

Cycle time defeats short dashboards

A loop's cycle time — the gap between a subscriber's first delivery and their referred friend reaching the same trigger — was close to six weeks for Rasoi Club. A weekly dashboard built for funnel campaigns reads this as noise; loops need cohort tracking measured in cycles, not calendar weeks.

"Loop" is routinely confused with "viral"

Most durable consumer loops are not viral; they are content or retention loops that never need k above 1, because they are not trying to grow the population exponentially alone — they are trying to lower the marginal cost of growth the company is already buying.

What a loop can never tell you

A loop framing describes the mechanics of compounding; it says nothing about whether the underlying product deserves to compound. A well-instrumented loop around a mediocre recipe-kit will compound complaints as faithfully as referrals — loop analysis assumes retention quality and unit economics are already sound, it does not substitute for them.

Funnels remain the right tool in several places

Enterprise leads from a trade show, or a one-time regulatory approval, have no natural cycle to close; forcing loop language onto them is cargo-cult vocabulary. Funnels also remain the correct lens for diagnosing exactly where inside a loop's own stages the leakage occurs.

Questions worth asking before relying on a loop

What is the cycle time, and can the organisation tolerate results lagging that long? Is the input capped by something finite, such as the size of a customer's own social graph? And critically: does the stated coefficient come from a single burst campaign, or a rolling measurement across at least three full cycles?

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and stage of company

In consumer products like Rasoi Club, loops tend to be fast and social: sharing, user-generated content, search-indexed pages, with cycle times of days to weeks and a large, loosely connected population to draw on. In B2B software, the natural loop is slower and travels through organisations rather than social graphs — one team's adoption produces internal advocates who pull in adjacent teams, or a satisfied account becomes a reference a salesperson uses to close a peer company — with cycle times of months, consciously operated by a sales team rather than running automatically in the product. In a marketplace, the loop runs between the two sides: more supply improves selection for demand, more demand improves earnings for supply, and the model can seize up with a cold-start problem if either side is seeded too thin; marketplaces must also watch for loops that work in one city or category but do not transfer to a new one, resetting cold-start at every expansion.

Stage of company changes which engine should get the marginal rupee. An early-stage company's base is too small for any coefficient, however good, to produce meaningful volume — 2.1% of 1,000 is 21 people, useful but not enough to found a company on — so paid acquisition remains primary, with the loop's job simply to prove the coefficient is real before it is trusted with more base. A large company's base is big enough that the same coefficient produces thousands of subscribers a month at near-zero marginal cost, which is when loops genuinely move blended CAC, and when the discipline shifts from proving the loop exists to guarding it against saturation — referral fatigue, or a market where most plausible sharers are already reached.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting a one-time viral coefficient as a sustained loop. Symptom: a growth deck cites "k = 1.3" from a single referral push. Misunderstanding: a burst campaign measured once is not evidence of a repeating cycle. Diagnostic: recompute the coefficient across three separate rolling cohorts and see whether it holds.

Growth stalling despite a reportedly healthy loop. Symptom: the loop coefficient looks stable but total subscribers are flat or falling. Misunderstanding: the loop's addition rate is being netted against churn nobody is tracking in the same unit. Diagnostic: compute net loop growth as loop-driven adds minus churn-driven losses over the same base and period.

A referral feature that does not move the number. Symptom: engineering ships a share button and usage of it is negligible. Misunderstanding: the trigger is placed at a moment of low product satisfaction rather than immediately after the customer's best experience. Diagnostic: measure the time lag between a customer's peak satisfaction event and the first share prompt they see.

Treating "build a growth loop" as a mandate to build something new. Symptom: leadership asks the team to "add a loop" and a costly feature ships with no lift. Misunderstanding: the team looked for a loop to build rather than a loop already occurring informally in customer behaviour. Diagnostic: audit existing user journeys for any repeat or sharing behaviour that already happens unprompted before commissioning new engineering.

8. What good looks like

Six weeks after that board meeting, Ananya's team had not built anything new; they had found the "plate photo" behaviour already happening among roughly 14% of subscribers with no prompt at all, moved the existing share button to fire only after a four-or-five-star rating, and set up cohort tracking with a six-week window rather than the weekly dashboard the funnel team used. They deliberately kept the paid budget roughly flat rather than cutting it, treating it as the primer that put new subscribers into the loop's base in the first place, and reported two numbers to the board every month from then on: the loop's rolling three-cohort coefficient, and net loop growth after subtracting churn. Neither number was dramatic on its own, but both were visibly compounding by the second quarter, and blended CAC had a believable, if unglamorous, downward trend that did not depend on any single campaign working.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya did not ask the board to defund paid acquisition — with only 31,000 subscribers, Rasoi Club's loop was still too small to carry growth alone, and cutting the funnel would have starved the very base the loop needed. Instead she reallocated roughly 15% of the new funding toward instrumenting the loop properly: cohort-based tracking with a six-week window, a redesigned trigger at the moment of peak satisfaction, and a monthly net-loop-growth number reported alongside CAC. She reasoned that a funnel and a loop answer different questions — the funnel tells you what a rupee of spend buys today, the loop tells you what today's satisfied customer is worth over the cycles still to come — and a company that only ever asks the first question will keep paying full price for the same growth forever. The natural next readings for anyone who has followed Rasoi Club this far are building a full growth model that combines both engines with realistic assumptions, and then stress-testing that model against the inputs most likely to be wrong — churn creeping up, a share rate that fatigues, a channel cost that keeps rising. Two questions are worth sitting with before that next reading. First: what behaviour is already happening in your own product, unprompted and unmeasured, that might already be loop-shaped? Second: if the paid budget were switched off entirely tomorrow, would your loop sustain positive net growth on its own, or is it, honestly, only a subsidy that makes the funnel cheaper?

Sit with these:
1. What behaviour already happening in your product, unprompted, might already be loop-shaped?
2. If paid acquisition stopped tomorrow, would your loop alone sustain positive net growth — or is it only a subsidy multiplier on top of the funnel?
exp20v2-growth.onboarding:
Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation › Growth & Retention

Activation and Onboarding Optimisation

How do we get users to the aha moment faster?

1. A board call that ran forty minutes long

On the second Monday of September 2026, Kavya Menon, head of growth at Qatra Laundry Works, sat through a board call that ran forty minutes longer than scheduled. Qatra's app connected households across Thrissur to a network of 34 partner laundries, promising pickup within two hours and delivery within 48. Installs for August had come in at 18,500, comfortably ahead of plan, and 11,100 of the 18,500 installs — 60% — had converted into signed-up accounts with a saved address and a payment method on file. Girish Warrier, Qatra's co-founder and CEO, pulled up the number that mattered most to the investors on the call: only 23.5% of new signups were still placing a second order sixty days after they joined. Growth spend had bought installs; it had not obviously bought customers who stayed.

The board wanted an answer within six weeks, and Qatra had roughly eight months of runway left to show its Series A investors a clearer path to durable growth. Kavya's working hypothesis was that Qatra was measuring the wrong moment: the team had been treating "signup" as success and "retention" as a downstream mystery, with nothing in between to explain why some new users stayed and most did not. If she could find the specific early action that separated the two groups — and redesign onboarding to push more people toward it, faster — Thrissur's retention number, and the case for expanding into Alappuzha the following year, would rest on evidence rather than hope.

2. The idea: finding the moment that predicts the rest

Activation is the specific, observable action a new user takes that predicts whether they will keep using a product — distinct from signup, which only proves they arrived, and distinct from long-term retention, which is what activation is trying to predict. The "aha moment" is shorthand for the point at which a user has experienced enough of a product's real value that continuing to use it becomes the natural choice rather than an effortful one. Onboarding is the deliberate design work — the screens, nudges, defaults and incentives shown between signup and that moment — aimed at getting more users there, faster.

The idea has a specific parentage. In 2007, investor Dave McClure proposed "AARRR" — Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue — as a simple funnel for locating where a startup's growth problem actually lived, placing activation between a user's arrival and their return. Facebook's early growth team made the idea concrete a few years later with an internal finding that a new user who reached seven friends within ten days was dramatically more likely to stay active — a single, testable definition discovered by studying data rather than guessing. By the mid-2010s, growth researchers including Brian Balfour and Casey Winters had generalised the method into a repeatable discipline: find the action, in real cohort data, most correlated with long-term retention, and treat getting users to it as a design problem in its own right. The sentence Kavya could repeat in the boardroom without sounding glib: "Activation is not the first thing a user does — it's the earliest thing that predicts they'll do it again."

3. How it actually works, step by step

Finding and using an activation definition follows a sequence that is easy to state and, under deadline pressure, easy to skip steps in.

First, establish the retention baseline you are trying to explain — for Qatra, the share of new signups placing a second order by day 60, a blended 23.5%. Second, list candidate activation events: completing signup, adding an address, browsing the partner-laundry list, scheduling a first pickup, and completing a first order — pickup collected, cleaned, and delivered back. Third, and the step teams most often skip, segment a real cohort of past signups by whether and when they reached each candidate event, and compare each segment's actual retention rather than assuming which event matters; a plausible-sounding candidate such as "opened the app three times" often predicts nothing once tested. Fourth, choose the event and the time window together — an event with no window is too loose to design onboarding around, while a window applied to too small a population becomes statistically unreliable. Fifth, once a definition is chosen, instrument every step leading to it; Qatra needed visibility into where new users dropped out between scheduling a pickup and receiving clean clothes back. Sixth, ship an onboarding change aimed narrowly at the activation event, and re-measure the same cohort comparison rather than a vanity metric like app opens.

4. A worked example: four days that explained the number

Kavya pulled a cohort of 1,000 signups sampled from Qatra's August 2026 accounts and asked one question of the data: did completing a first order within four days of signup — before the free trial credit and the novelty of a new app wore off — predict who reordered by day 60? The cohort split into three groups.

The gap was too large to be noise: 132 of the 220 fast starters (60%) reordered by day 60, against 80 of the 320 slow starters (25%) and just 23 of the 460 no-shows (5%). Blended, the cohort's overall reorder rate was exactly the 23.5% the board had seen — 235 of 1,000 users. Kavya now had her definition: activation at Qatra meant a first order within four days of signup, and onboarding could aim squarely at moving users out of the slow-starter and no-show groups and into the fast-starter group.

The second pass tested what a specific onboarding change was worth. Qatra's product team proposed a same-day-pickup nudge — a push notification and a modest discount, shown within an hour of signup, prompting the user to schedule a pickup before closing the app. Modelling its effect on the same 1,000-person cohort, and assuming each segment kept its own underlying reorder rate, moving 100 users from the slow-starter group into the fast-starter group produced the result below.

Blended reorder rate rose from 23.5% to 27.0% — a 3.5-point gain, worth 35 retained customers per 1,000 signups, roughly 15% relative — for a change touching only the first hour after signup.

5. The nuances a learner must become aware of

Activation is not satisfaction

A user can be delighted by good service and still never reorder because their circumstances changed — they moved city, or hired a full-time domestic helper. Activation measures a behavioural pattern correlated with retention, not a verified cause of it, and needs periodic re-testing as the product and market shift.

Speed alone is not the point

It is easy to collapse activation into "time to first value" defined purely as speed. A user who orders within an hour but receives stained clothes back is not activated in any useful sense; the event must capture a complete, successful experience, not merely the fastest click.

Definitions do not transfer

The four-day window belongs to Qatra's own cohort and cannot be borrowed by another laundry app, let alone a different category, without repeating the segmentation. A grocery app's activation window is measured in hours; a B2B tool's, in weeks — because the decision cycle differs.

A clean number can still be gamed

An onboarding flow can be tuned to push users toward the event without the underlying value behind it. Auto-scheduling a pickup a user never asked for would inflate the fast-starter count while destroying the retention the definition was built to predict.

Sample size is easy to overrate

With only 220 fast starters in the cohort, splitting that group further — by payment method, say — would produce segments too small to trust. A definition tested on one month should be re-validated on a second before it is treated as settled.

It explains who, not why

Activation cannot say why the no-show group failed to act — only that it did not reach the event. Whether pickup availability was thin, pricing felt unclear, or checkout crashed requires separate qualitative work, not a better metric.

Three questions before trusting one

A thoughtful newcomer should ask what time window was tested, how large and recent the cohort was, and whether anyone has re-validated the definition since the last major product or pricing change. An activation definition goes stale silently, not with a warning.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early stage versus scale

The mechanics travel, but what counts as the aha moment does not. In a consumer app like Qatra, activation is usually a single completed transaction experienced end to end — the clothes come back clean and on time. In a B2B product, activation more often requires a team, not an individual, to reach value together: a project-management tool might define it as three teammates completing five tasks in a shared workspace within two weeks, because one person's action rarely predicts whether the account renews. In a marketplace, activation has two sides that must both clear: Qatra's model depends not only on a household reordering but on a partner laundry fulfilling enough orders to stay engaged, and a growth team that optimises only the consumer side can activate demand a thin supply network cannot serve.

Stage changes the picture too. An early-stage company like Qatra must define activation from thin, noisy cohorts and hold the definition loosely, revisiting it every quarter. A large consumer company with millions of monthly signups can afford several activation definitions for different segments — new-to-city users, gift-order users, corporate accounts — each validated on its own large cohort, a precision Qatra will not have for years.

7. Common mistakes

Treating signup as activation. The symptom is a growth team celebrating signup numbers while retention stays flat; the cheapest diagnostic is plotting retention for signed-up users against retention for whichever later event is proposed as the real activation point.

Picking the event by intuition, not cohort data. The symptom is an onboarding redesign that improves the chosen metric without moving retention; the diagnostic is the segmentation Kavya ran — if "activated" and "non-activated" groups show no meaningfully different reorder rate, the definition is wrong.

Optimising the event until it goes hollow. The symptom is a rising activation rate alongside a flat or falling retention rate; the cheapest diagnostic is checking, month over month, whether the two numbers are still moving together.

8. What good looks like

Six months later, Qatra's onboarding screen no longer asked new users to "explore the app." It asked for a pickup address and offered same-day collection with a modest first-order discount, shown before the user could navigate away, with one follow-up notification for anyone who had not scheduled within two hours. Girish reported that the fast-starter share of new signups had grown from 22% to just over 30% of each monthly cohort, and day-60 reorder rates were tracking toward the 27% Kavya's model had projected. Nobody claimed victory on installs; the board slide that mattered now showed cohorts split by activation speed, re-measured monthly, with onboarding treated as a live surface rather than a screen shipped once and forgotten.

9. What Kavya decided

Kavya's recommendation to the board was narrow: adopt "first order completed within four days of signup" as Qatra's activation definition, redesign onboarding around the same-day-pickup nudge, and fund the Alappuzha expansion only once the fast-starter share had crossed 30% in Thrissur for two consecutive months — proof the model, not just the market, would travel. Growth spend on installs was cheap to defend and easy to mistake for progress; a validated activation definition turned onboarding from a matter of taste into a measurable design problem.

What she asked to study next was cohort-based retention analysis itself — the tool that let her test candidate activation events against real behaviour instead of intuition, and the natural foundation for the onboarding and platform-adoption problems Qatra would face as it grew. Two questions worth sitting with: what would your product's version of "seven friends in ten days" turn out to be, if tested against a real cohort instead of assumed? And how would you know if your activation definition had quietly gone stale?
case40v1-growth.onboarding:
Vardaan Wheels Exchange: Four Activations and One Base

A case on activation and onboarding optimisation, set in Tiruchirappalli, October 2026

1. Sunday night on Williams Road

At a quarter past ten on Sunday, 11 October 2026, the floor above the Williams Road yard in Tiruchirappalli held only Mathivanan Sethuraman and a generator. Below him, under tarpaulin, stood ninety-odd used two-wheelers waiting for Ayudha Pooja, when half of Tamil Nadu buys a vehicle. He was Chief Product Officer of Vardaan Wheels Exchange, and on Monday morning he had to send the founder one number.

The number was the dealer activation rate, and the reason it had become a Sunday-night problem was that Vardaan had four of them. Growth put it at 68.0 per cent. Dealer operations put it at 36.0 per cent. His own data science lead put it at 14.0 per cent. Warisan Capital Finance, the lender behind a third of every month's sales, put it at 8.0 per cent. All four came from the same 2,400 dealers who opened an account between April and June, and none was wrong.

Thursday's board call would treat whichever figure he sent as a fact. Gomathi Natarajan wanted the highest defensible one, because ₹22 crore of the Series A sat undrawn behind a milestone worded as "a dealer activation rate of not less than 60 per cent". Mathivanan had concluded that the sentence meant nothing until somebody chose a definition, and that whoever chose it was choosing the money.

He had also, in the course of the weekend, stopped being sure that the thing he was supposed to shorten the distance to actually existed.

2. How Vardaan got here

Vardaan Wheels Exchange began in 2019 as two yards, in Tiruchirappalli and Salem, buying used Hero Splendors, TVS Jupiters and Honda Activas from owners and reselling them with a paper guarantee. Gomathi had run her family's hire-purchase office and knew the trade's constraint: a buyer in a tier-three town pays ₹4,000 more if somebody credible says the engine has been opened, and pays in instalments if somebody will lend.

The platform came in 2021. Dealers — single-owner shops with fifteen to sixty vehicles — got the Vardaan Dealer Console to list stock. Vardaan took a transaction fee, sold subscriptions, and added two things that made it more than a classifieds board: the Vardaan Assurance Label, a six-month engine-and-gearbox cover issued off a forty-two-point physical inspection, and financing.

The decision shaping every option open to Mathivanan was taken in April 2023. Vardaan signed a five-year exclusive origination agreement with Warisan Capital Finance, a Mumbai-headquartered non-banking lender, running to 31 March 2028. Warisan gave it a dealer floor-stock line, a 2.5 per cent origination commission, and branch officers who already knew every two-wheeler shop in eleven districts. In exchange Vardaan accepted clause 7.4, which fixes the order: the dealer's trade certificate, GST registration and CKYC record on file, and a physical inspection report carrying photographs of the engine and chassis numbers, before Vardaan may originate a loan lead. Exclusivity means there is no second lender to fall back on.

By March 2026 it had 5,860 dealers who had listed at least once, 2,600 paying subscriptions, 96 inspectors and 84 field executives under Franklin Chelladurai. It had raised ₹92 crore across two rounds and drawn ₹70 crore. FY26 revenue was ₹13.04 crore on GMV of ₹150.80 crore (Exhibit 6); net burn was ₹2.30 crore a month against cash of ₹38.10 crore.

3. The trade Vardaan sits in

India sells roughly four used two-wheelers for every new one, almost all of it cash, local and undocumented. The organised end is crowded: CredR and Droom have been at it for years, OLX is where most private sellers still start, CARS24 and Spinny have shown in four-wheelers what certification is worth, and TVS, Hero MotoCorp and Honda dealerships run their own certified pre-owned exchanges. Vardaan's nearest rival, Ankur Gaadi Bazaar, works the same districts out of Salem with a thinner inspection and a lower fee.

Regulation touches every step. Transfer of registration needs Forms 29 and 30 at the RTO; insurance must move within fourteen days; the Assurance Label is underwritten by an insurer and sits inside IRDAI's product rules, which is why the administrator can void a claim on an uninspected vehicle. Lending sits under the RBI's KYC Master Direction and the digital lending guidelines, which clause 7.4 echoes: Warisan cannot delegate customer due diligence to a marketplace. Under the DPDP Act every identity image Vardaan holds is a consented, retention-limited liability.

The company is also, awkwardly for a Trichy firm, globally staffed: engineering in Bengaluru under Ganapathy Marimuthu, data science in Dublin under Zoheb Irani, hired in April 2026 at four times the Bengaluru band for the same title. The Series A was led by a Japanese strategic investor whose portfolio director, Kenji Furukawa, attends from Osaka.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Figure 1 sets out the sequence. Through 2025 Vardaan reported dealer activation as profile completion plus a first listing carrying three photographs and a price, within fourteen days of sign-up. On that definition the October–December 2025 cohort activated at 53.9 per cent — 949 of 1,760 sign-ups — and everybody agreed it was too low.

In February 2026 the growth team shipped Onboarding 2.0: fewer sign-up fields, vernacular help, a listing form that saved automatically. Reported activation moved from 54.5 per cent to 68.0 per cent. The Q4 FY26 bonus pool of ₹18 lakh was paid against it, and the figure went into the Series A tranche conversation.

Zoheb Irani joined in April and spent two months rebuilding the event layer from raw logs. In June he circulated Exhibit 2. Besides the design, two things had changed in February: the dealer_activated event now fired on a first listing saved, drafts included, rather than on one carrying three photographs and a price; and the window had widened from fourteen days to thirty. Recomputed on the April–June cohort, the old definition gives 1,308 of the same 2,400 — 54.5 per cent. Against the previous cohort's 53.9 per cent, dealer behaviour had moved six-tenths of a point. The rest of the thirteen-and-a-half points was arithmetic.

Franklin Chelladurai's field reports had been saying something adjacent since May: listings created were climbing fast, listings live, priced and inspected were not. Exhibit 4 puts January beside September: creation up 41.0 per cent, inspected-and-live up 1.9 per cent, units sold up 6.1 per cent. Vardaan had got very good at producing the event it was measuring.

In September the problem acquired a counterparty. Warisan audited 812 loan files from April to September and found 61 incomplete — 7.5 per cent — mostly missing the engine-number photograph or carrying an inspection dated after disbursal. Gnanavel Murugesan withheld commission on those files, ₹73,200, and served a cure notice. The money is trivial; the notice is not. Repeated clause 7.4 breaches let Warisan terminate on thirty days, and there is no second lender.

Nobody has established whether the incomplete files came from a leak in the flow or from field executives moving fast. During a release defect between 14 February and 27 March, 214 dealers listed without passing the inspection gate. Their disputes ran at 9.8 per 100 sales against 3.2 for gated dealers — just over three times — on a sample too small and too self-selected to settle anything.

5. The people

Gomathi Natarajan, co-founder and chief executive, Tiruchirappalli. Wants one number on Thursday's slide, beginning with a six; her incentive is the ₹22 crore tranche behind it. Unsaid: she treated the milestone wording as settled when she signed, and has not asked counsel whether "measured consistently with the Company's reporting" means November 2024's or today's.

Malarvizhi Kathiresan, vice-president, growth, Tiruchirappalli. Owns the 68.0 per cent: a first listing is the first moment a dealer does anything at all, and every later definition measures the market, not the onboarding. Her targets and last year's bonus are in that currency. Unsaid: she signed off the February event change in a release note she did not read closely, and its author has left.

Franklin Chelladurai, head of dealer network operations, Tiruchirappalli. Eighty-four executives, eleven districts, paid a commission on "productive" dealers — five listings and one answered buyer lead — which is where his 36.0 per cent comes from. He believes the inspection gate is all that separates Vardaan from Ankur Gaadi Bazaar. Unsaid: 148 of the 864 productive dealers had a first listing created from a field executive's tablet, 17.1 per cent of his own number.

Zoheb Irani, head of data science, Dublin. Activation must mean a completed sale within thirty days, the first event correlated with a dealer still being present in month six. His overlap with Trichy is four hours; his salary is a standing irritant in Bengaluru. Unsaid: the window is thirty days partly because it smoothed the retention curve, and it excludes 27 dealers whose first sale landed between days 31 and 38.

Ganapathy Marimuthu, director of engineering, Bengaluru. The event layer can carry one definition well or four badly; four properly is a seven-week refactor costing ₹46 lakh, landing after Diwali. Unsaid: the February change bypassed his review because growth had its own deployment path, granted in January at his suggestion.

Mekala Ravichandran, counsel, Tiruchirappalli. The inspection and document capture cannot move after the sale — not for the loan, because of clause 7.4 and the KYC direction behind it, and not for the Assurance Label, because the administrator voids claims on uninspected vehicles. Unsaid: she has not told the board that the 61 files are already a breach rather than housekeeping.

Gnanavel Murugesan, head of credit and risk, Warisan Capital Finance, Mumbai. His definition — a financed sale, buyer KYC complete, disbursal within forty-five days — is the only one attached to money moving, and he notes, correctly, that his own branch-referral channel is its best performer. Unsaid: Warisan has a dealer-facing app in internal testing, and the exclusivity runs only to March 2028.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"A dealer who has put one bike on the console has crossed the line. Everything after that is whether the market wants his bike. You are asking onboarding to carry demand."Malarvizhi Kathiresan, product review, 6 October
"There is no moment. I have looked. There is a listing, and sometimes weeks later a sale, and the only channel where the two sit close together is the one where a Warisan loan officer already knew the man. We are not measuring an aha. We are measuring who vouched for him."Zoheb Irani, chat thread, 7 October, 02:14 IST
"Clause 7.4 is not a constraint you can negotiate with a prototype, and the Label is an insurance product. Please stop calling the inspection friction in documents I sign."Mekala Ravichandran, email, 8 October
"Sixty-one files. I am not making a point about your funnel. My auditor made one about mine."Gnanavel Murugesan, call from Mumbai, 30 September
"Send the November 2024 basis, the current basis, and the bridge. If the bridge is large, send it anyway."Kenji Furukawa, email, 9 October, 06:02 IST

8. The options as Mathivanan sees them

He has written four. The first is to pick one definition — Zoheb's — restate the last three board packs on it, and tell Kenji Furukawa before Thursday. It costs almost nothing to build and everything else: the tranche milestone becomes unmeetable, the ₹18 lakh bonus becomes a story, and growth loses its unit of account.

The second is to keep 68.0 per cent as the reported figure, disclose the basis, and run the other three internally as a quality ladder. It is the cheapest peace, and leaves four teams optimising four things with no shared answer to whether any change helped.

The third is to treat the inspection gate as the binding constraint and rebuild the first-run flow around it: inspection booking inside the listing form, document capture with on-device guidance, a progress state the dealer can see. Seven weeks, ₹46 lakh, live on 30 November — after Ayudha Pooja and Diwali both. Mekala's position is that the gate's content cannot move at all; the most this can do is make it faster and better explained.

The fourth is to buy the gate down: forty more inspectors, ₹15.20 lakh a month, live by 9 November, cutting the median wait for a slot from 2.4 days to under a day. It is the only option that lands inside the season and the only one raising fixed cost in a business burning ₹2.30 crore a month.

Reading his own list, Mathivanan noticed that all four assume there is a moment to arrive at and that the work is to shorten the road to it. Exhibit 3 does not say that. The channel with the highest first-listing rate loses ₹2,500 a dealer; the best financed-sale rate belongs to the channel where a lender's branch officer made the introduction; and 47.0 per cent of the cohort arrives self-serve, behaves unlike the rest, and drags the blended figure to a number describing none of the four populations. If activation is mostly a property of who vouched for the dealer, shortening the flow is not the project.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The number goes to Gomathi on Monday, 12 October, and to the board on Thursday the fifteenth. Warisan's cure notice expires on 30 October. Ayudha Pooja falls in the third week of October and Diwali on 8 November; September's 2,314 units will roughly double across those weeks, and engineering is on release freeze from 16 October. Cash is ₹38.10 crore against ₹2.30 crore of monthly burn. The ₹22 crore tranche turns on a sentence nobody has construed. Clause 7.4 runs to 31 March 2028 and admits no substitute lender, and Mekala will not sign a flow that defers the inspection.

At half past eleven he typed a message to Zoheb, deleted it, and wrote a note to himself instead: which of our four numbers would I bet the tranche on, and what would I have to believe. The generator cut out. Below, under the tarpaulin, ninety-one vehicles waited for a festival, each inspected, each belonging to a dealer who counted as activated on at least one of the four definitions and, on the one that mattered to the lender, mostly did not.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, say what decision each of the four definitions is fit to support. Which, if any, measures onboarding rather than market demand?
  2. Exhibit 2 attributes 13.5 points to measurement and 0.6 to behaviour. What did Vardaan learn in February 2026, and what should it do about the ₹18 lakh already paid?
  3. Exhibit 5 shows time-to-activation falling from 11.6 days to 4.1. Explain to Kenji Furukawa why the chart is true and misleading at once, and what would make it decision-grade.
  4. Exhibit 3 ranks the channels in nearly opposite orders on two definitions. If the funnel is four populations, what becomes of a single activation rate, a single onboarding flow and a single milestone?
  5. Mekala Ravichandran and Gnanavel Murugesan both say the inspection step cannot move. Take that as absolute and rebuild the case for each option. Which survive, and what is left of the claim that onboarding is a design problem?
  6. It is Monday morning. What number, with what caveats, does Mathivanan send Gomathi Natarajan, and what does he tell the board about the gap between what Vardaan measured and what it changed? What must be true by 31 December for him to know he was right?
exp40v2-growth.onboarding:
Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation › Growth & Retention

Activation and Onboarding Optimisation

Near-expert treatment: the mechanism under the heuristic, the measurement traps, and where the standard advice quietly stops being true.

1. Two desks in Siliguri, one week apart

On 8 September 2026 the board of Farmaan Trade Systems gave Raima Ghoshal, its vice-president of growth, eighteen months to lift gross logo renewal from 41.8 per cent to 60 per cent. Farmaan sells customs-documentation software from Siliguri to exporters and licensed customs brokers in the north Bengal corridor: 2,150 paying accounts at a blended ₹42,000 of annual contract value, ₹9.03 crore of recurring revenue. Onboarding means capturing an Importer-Exporter Code, an authorised-dealer code from the exporter's bank and a digital signature registered on ICEGATE, then migrating a year of shipping bills and a cleaned HS-code master. Raima's team proposed paying Farmaan's document centre in Malda to migrate that data for the customer: sixty-five extra renewals per six hundred new accounts, her model claimed.

Six days later, Lopamudra Sanyal put a different problem to Bandobast Trade Cloud's investors. Bandobast is self-serve: it turns an exporter's invoice into a packing list, a certificate-of-origin application and a pre-filled shipping-bill draft, free until the first filing and ₹300 a month after, with 2,900 paying accounts and ₹1.04 crore of recurring revenue. Her August cohort activated at 42.0 per cent against 38.0 per cent in June, and the deck called it the product team's best quarter. Lopamudra doubted the number described her product rather than her traffic.

2. The idea, and the four camps that fight over it

Activation is a predicate: a named, observable event, completed inside a named window, that partitions new users into a group whose later retention is high and one whose is low. It is not satisfaction, not signup, and — the distinction on which most confusion turns — not necessarily a cause of retention. The construct exists because retention is measured too late to manage: a twelve-month renewal number describes a cohort acquired fourteen months ago.

The lineage is short. Dave McClure's 2007 AARRR framework placed activation between acquisition and retention; Sean Ellis popularised the aha moment and the habit of hunting it in cohort data; Brian Balfour and Casey Winters turned the hunt into a method. The canonical illustration — Facebook's new user reaching roughly ten friends in an early window — travelled much further than its evidence, and an expert treats its numbers as folklore rather than results. A separate literature had named the hazard: surrogate endpoints in trials, and Goodhart's and Campbell's laws, all hold that an intermediate measure adopted as a target stops behaving like the measure it replaced.

Four camps disagree substantively. The predictive-threshold camp signs “activation is one numeric event-plus-window threshold, found in cohort data and reported weekly”; it will not sign “the threshold is causal”. The experiment-first camp signs “only a randomised holdout measures what an onboarding change is worth”; it will not sign “the activated-versus-not gap tells you the value of moving a user across the line”. The friction-removal camp signs “every field and gate before first value costs users”; it will not sign “front-loading configuration raises eventual value”. The commitment camp signs the inverse, citing effort justification, the IKEA effect, and the retention of migration-heavy accounts.

3. Mechanics: find the threshold, then distrust it

Raima began with a mature cohort: the 600 accounts contracted between January and June 2025, all past their renewal decision, with onboarding laid out as a state machine.

Next came the retention comparison every growth team produces. Its numbers are correct and its usual reading is wrong.

Before trusting the ten-bill threshold, an expert sweeps it. The question is not which threshold maximises separation — one always does — but whether separation is flat nearby. A plateau means a genuine regime change; a lone spike means the analyst fitted one cohort's noise.

Raima's team then stopped treating Exhibit 2 as a valuation. The 87.8 per cent belongs to accounts that reached ten bills unaided, self-selected by intent: an exporter shipping twice a week clears ten bills inside the window because that is simply their volume. What an investment needs is the marginal rate, the retention of accounts pushed across the line. Farmaan randomised 400 new accounts in May, offering concierge migration to 200 and business as usual to 200. Activation reached 84 of 200 treated accounts, 42.0 per cent, against 60 of 200 controls, 30.0 per cent.

Renewal could not be observed; those accounts were four months old. This is the field's structural problem: a 45-day window plus a twelve-month renewal decision is a fourteen-month loop, so every programme runs on a surrogate. Farmaan's was “filed at least one bill in month four”. In the control arm 52 of the 60 activated accounts cleared it, 86.7 per cent, and 52 of the remaining 140 also cleared it, 37.1 per cent — 104 control accounts, 52.0 per cent. Applying those rates to the treatment mix predicted 116 accounts, 58.0 per cent; treatment delivered 112, 56.0 per cent, an eight-account lift rather than the twelve those rates predicted. Surrogate lift over activation lift is the marginal sustain rate: 8 of the 24 induced activations, 33.3 per cent, against 86.7 per cent for the average activated account.

Rebuilding the model with both rates makes the naive assumption's cost legible. Suppose the concierge moves ninety of the 312 never-migrated accounts to activation. The naive model applies 87.8 per cent to them. The ratio of 33.3 to 86.7 is 0.38, putting the marginal account's renewal probability near 34 per cent — the link Farmaan's memo called weakest, transporting a month-four ratio onto a month-twelve outcome.

The distance between 65 and 17 decides the programme once cost enters. Concierge migration costs ₹4,500 per account — nine hours of analyst time in Malda at ₹400 an hour plus ₹900 of retrieval and checking — and must be offered to every unmigrated account, not only the ninety who respond. Contribution per retained account-year is ₹29,400, being ₹42,000 of contract value at a 70 per cent gross margin.

Targeting recovers almost the whole benefit — 16 incremental renewals against 17 — for 30.8 per cent of the cost. When marginal returns vary sharply by segment, the onboarding question is rarely whether to invest in a step but whom to invest in, and an aggregate activation rate cannot say.

4. Five conditions, stated as tests

One: a threshold exists with a wide, flat separation. Sweep it. Farmaan passes — 65.7 points, within 0.6 of its neighbour. Bandobast passes numerically and fails in substance, which is the second condition.

Two: the event measures onboarding, not qualification. Bandobast's event is “profile completed with a valid IEC”. Most who fail it are not failing at onboarding; they are aspiring exporters without an Importer-Exporter Code from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade, and no screen conjures a licence. The tell: the denominator holds a population the product cannot serve.

Three: induced users behave like self-selected ones. Only a holdout tests this. Farmaan tested and failed: 33.3 per cent against 86.7.

Four: the cohort matures fast enough to close the loop. Farmaan fails, and must validate a surrogate. The standard borrowed from trial statistics is not that the surrogate correlates with the outcome but that the treatment's effect runs through it. Almost nobody tests that.

Five: acquisition mix is stable enough that the metric reflects craft. Bandobast fails. June was 4,000 organic signups at 46.0 per cent plus 2,000 paid-social at 22.0 per cent; August, 6,300 organic and 2,100 paid, the paid rate having improved to 30.0 per cent after a landing-page rebuild.

Where is the idea actively misleading? Where usage frequency is lower than any tolerable window — an annual duty-drawback reconciliation has no 45-day signal. Where the signer is not the user: Farmaan's contract is signed by a proprietor and used by a documentation clerk. And where slowness is the design: the shortest path to a first filing can optimise away the configuration that makes filing number forty accurate.

5. Hard edges: gates, pairs, tokens and models

Regulated gates. Of the 108 accounts that captured licence details but never validated ICEGATE credentials, an audit found 71, or 65.7 per cent, waiting on a bank's authorised-dealer letter or an expired digital signature certificate. They had not dropped out; they were queuing behind an institution. A funnel with no blocked state reports a queue as a leak, and removing friction has no purchase on a bank's turnaround. What works is resequencing: let the account draft bills before the gate.

Two-sided dependence. Of the 246 accounts that filed a first bill, 198 — 80.5 per cent — filed through a customs broker already using Farmaan. The unit of activation is the exporter-broker pair, so the fastest lever is broker-side supply in the corridor, invisible in an exporter-side funnel.

Hardware in the loop. Digital signature tokens are physical. Accounts receiving their pre-registered token kit within three days activated at 40 per cent; those waiting eight days or more, at 25 per cent. A third of kits went out inside three days, reconciling to the cohort's 30.0 per cent.

Multi-product. Eighty-four accounts adopted a second module and 78 renewed. The finding is nearly worthless: 79 of the 84 were already activated, so adoption follows the same intent. Conditioning on a downstream variable manufactures effects that evaporate under intervention.

AI-native onboarding. Farmaan's extraction model fills shipping-bill fields from scanned invoices. With twelve months of migrated history it reaches 94 per cent field-level accuracy; with none, 71 per cent, and below roughly 85 per cent clerks reported that typing was faster. The aha moment is therefore a product state the user's own data unlocks — a cold-start dependency that inverts the friction-removal prescription, because the tedious migration is the value.

Organisational seams. Growth owned the funnel, implementation owned migration, a compliance desk owned licence validation; the number crossed three budget owners, none of whom could move it alone. Mature companies make one executive accountable and move the migration cost line into the growth budget, which is what makes the Exhibit 5 decision worth taking.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

The gap in the chart is selection, not treatment

The tell is a slide quoting the activated-versus-not retention gap as the value of activation. The obvious reading assumes the gap is causal when it mostly measures who was already committed: Farmaan's 65.7 points became a negative marginal effect under test.

A plateau is evidence; a peak is overfitting

When a team quotes eleven bills rather than ten and cannot say what nine or thirteen looked like, the number was fitted to noise. Sweep, prefer the round number inside the flat region, and re-run on a later cohort.

The metric you can move fastest is measured last

A dashboard showing this month's activation rate for a 45-day window reports an immature cohort, which always looks worse than it will finish. The obvious fix — shorten the window — trades predictive power for measurability.

Most month-to-month movement is composition

If activation moves in step with channel spend, the product team is being praised for the media plan. Half of Bandobast's four points was mix. A decomposition costs an afternoon; without one, quarters cannot be compared.

A surrogate needs mediation, not correlation

Teams validate a leading indicator by showing it correlates with renewal, which every plausible candidate does. What matters is whether the intervention's whole effect passes through it. A concierge that lifts month-four filing while teaching customers that Farmaan does the work overstates durable value.

Onboarding changes propagate upward and sideways

Easier setup lets sales close accounts it once disqualified, so activation rises as cohort quality falls; assisted setup stops support learning where the product confuses people. Treat a large activation gain with everything else unchanged as an artefact.

Power-feature findings are usually colliders

“Accounts using feature X retain twice as well” is nearly always a statement about who chooses X. Ask what share of its users were already high-intent; if most, as with Farmaan's second module, it cannot support a nudge.

Speed can destroy what the event represents

The event is a claim that value was experienced. Remove a step protecting that value and the proxy rises while the value falls. The tell is divergence: activation up, and an error or quality metric up with it. Faisla Trade Systems is the worked case.

7. Across product types and stages

The mechanics are invariant; the content is not. In self-serve micro-business products like Bandobast, activation is a single-user event measurable in days and the binding constraint is qualification. In mid-market B2B like Farmaan it is a multi-person, multi-week configuration achievement constrained by work done outside the product. In enterprise it is deployment depth, and the honest statement is that a few hundred accounts give no threshold sweep enough power; judgement dominates, and pretending otherwise is theatre. In marketplaces the predicate must be two-sided; in hardware it is partly logistics; in AI products, partly data.

Stage changes what the number is for. Bandobast's 8,400 monthly signups support segment-level definitions and weekly experiments; Farmaan's 600 semi-annual contracts support one. At large scale the risk inverts: rival definitions drift until nobody can reconcile activation with the retention curve.

8. Three worked examples

Farmaan's targeted concierge is covered above: 1.36 times cost on the naive model, 0.36 on the tested one, rescued to 1.09 in year one and 3.27 over three years by restricting the offer to 96 accounts with real prior volume.

Bandobast against a qualification gate. August ran 8,400 signups to 3,528 profiles completed with a valid IEC, 42.0 per cent; 1,764 first invoices, 50.0 per cent of those profiles and 21.0 per cent of signups; 588 document packs used on a real consignment, 33.3 per cent of the invoice group and 7.0 per cent of signups; and 147 paid conversions inside sixty days, 25.0 per cent of the 588 and 1.75 per cent of signups. Paid social bought 2,100 signups at ₹210 each, ₹4.41 lakh, producing 630 activations at ₹700 apiece. At the same downstream rates those signups yield about 37 paying accounts: ₹11,919 of acquisition cost against ₹3,600 of annual revenue.

Faisla Trade Systems, where the approach failed. Labanya Jena's team in Siliguri defined activation as a first shipping bill filed within fourteen days. The winning experiment pre-filled each account's first declaration from its most similar past bill and removed the mandatory HS-code confirmation screen.

Activation rose 27 points and month-six retention fell 9. An inherited HS code produced a customs query, the query a delay at the port, and the delay an exporter who concluded the software was a liability. The recovery was not a rollback: Faisla reinstated confirmation as a one-tap accept of a suggested code, added staff review of each account's first three filings, and accepted a lower activation rate for a query rate near the original. A change that raises the event while degrading the value falsifies the claim rather than improving the number.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Valuing a correlation as a causal effect. Sign: a business case built from segment retention rates with no holdout. Diagnostic: what is the marginal retention of an account we push across the line? Late cost: ₹14.04 lakh committed against ₹5.00 lakh of benefit.

Mistaking composition for craft. Sign: activation and channel mix moving together. Diagnostic: hold last quarter's within-channel rates and recompute. Late cost: a roadmap justified by a gain the product never produced.

Optimising the event past the value. Sign: activation and an error or query metric rising together. Diagnostic: what step did we remove, and what was it protecting? Late cost: Faisla's nine points.

Treating a queue as churn. Sign: re-engagement campaigns with high open rates and no conversion. Diagnostic: what share of stalled accounts are blocked on a third party? Late cost: months aimed at accounts already trying.

Letting the definition drift. Sign: two decks in one week quoting different activation rates. Diagnostic: which cohort, which window, which denominator? Late cost: a board that believes no growth number.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Metric or mechanism? The threshold camp argues that a single legible number aligns an organisation, that most onboarding work is too small to power a clean experiment, and that teams adopting a validated threshold outperform teams arguing about causality. It would be wrong if marginal and average retention diverged so routinely that the number misdirects more than it aligns. The experiment-first camp holds that Farmaan's result is the norm, and would be wrong if holdouts usually confirmed the observational gap.

Defer setup or front-load it? Friction removal has the stronger general evidence: completion falls with every added field, and most products have no cold-start dependency. Commitment has the stronger evidence where migration creates the value — 94 per cent extraction accuracy with history against 71 per cent without is a fact about Farmaan's product, not a taste in design.

Is assisted onboarding a product answer or a subsidy? One view: unscalable work by hand is how you learn what to automate, so Malda is a research instrument. The other: a service line absorbing a product failure keeps it invisible and reappears as gross-margin erosion.

One definition or many? Segment-specific definitions are more accurate and less governable. Practitioners burned by reconciliation prefer one company-level definition plus diagnostic sub-metrics; those burned by a blended average prefer the portfolio. Both describe real damage.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this arrives with a definition and a plan to raise it. Someone who has internalised it arrives with three questions: what is the marginal retention of an induced user, how much of last quarter's movement was composition, and who is blocked rather than lost. They sweep thresholds instead of quoting one, label immature cohorts, and will recommend a lower activation rate when the event has been hollowed out.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Raima recommended funding concierge migration only for accounts with thirty or more prior-year filings, 96 of the 312 unmigrated, at ₹4.32 lakh; retaining the ten-bill threshold as a reported definition but never again using it to value an intervention; requiring a holdout above ₹5 lakh; and treating the token-kit logistics gap as the next target. She told the board that 60 per cent renewal was not reachable from onboarding alone, and that the rest must come from qualification at the point of sale.

Lopamudra took the harder decision. She replaced “profile completed” with “document pack used on a real consignment”, accepting that the headline rate would fall from 42.0 per cent to 7.0 per cent of signups, and cut the paid-social line. A metric whose denominator is full of people without an Importer-Exporter Code measures marketing's reach; a smaller honest number is something her team can move.

Three questions. If Farmaan's surrogate is the weakest link, what would a defensible validation cost, and is Raima right to act before it exists? Lopamudra's new definition makes her product look nine months worse overnight: under what governance does a growth leader survive that? And when is a lower activation rate the correct target, as it was at Faisla — and how would you see that case coming?

13. Going deeper

Defining activation (the aha moment) — the threshold-discovery craft this page assumes. Onboarding and first-run design — the sequencing choices that move the predicate, including resequencing around gates. Consumer onboarding and first session — where activation collapses into minutes and qualification does the work. Driving adoption of internal platforms — the same mechanics with a captive population. Growth loops vs funnels — why a funnel understates the compounding broker-side supply gave Farmaan. Building a growth model — where Exhibit 4's two models belong. Acquisition channels and economics — the ₹11,919 problem. Engagement loops and habit — why the habit school disputes the threshold framing. Retention strategy — the outcome activation is a surrogate for. Resurrection and win-back — the home for accounts blocked rather than lost.
case20v1-growth.onboarding:
Pankh Skill Exchange: Where the Riders Disappear

A case on activation and onboarding optimisation

1. Opening

On Monday 5 October 2026, Venkat Penmetsa sat in the glass-walled product room above a sweet shop in Rajahmundry, watching a funnel chart that refused to improve. He was Chief Product Officer of Pankh Skill Exchange, an app that trains gig-economy delivery riders and warehouse workers and matches them to shifts. By Friday 9 October he had to tell the founder-CEO, Phani Chekuri, where the next quarter's engineering money would go.

The urgency had a date attached. Diwali fell on 8 November, and the festive hiring surge would begin within weeks. Employers would post more shifts than Pankh had ever seen. Whatever he chose had to be live by the end of October. Of every hundred people who installed the app, only about six were doing what the company called activated.

2. Company background

Pankh Skill Exchange was founded in 2021 by Phani Chekuri, a former logistics supervisor, and a small team of engineers from Kakinada and Rajahmundry. A rider delivering for Zomato, Swiggy or Zepto earns by the delivery and has no way to prove skills that would earn more; a warehouse picker in a Flipkart fulfilment centre faces a similar wall. Pankh offered short vernacular modules (safe driving, handheld-scanner use, basic inventory counts, customer conversation) and a Lakeer Kaam Score, a portable record of completed modules and verified documents that employers could read.

Revenue came from employers. Pankh charged ₹2,000 for each worker placed and retained for ten shifts, paid by hiring partners, among them Vishwaas Fleet Partners, a Vijayawada fleet operator that supplied riders to several quick-commerce dark stores. Competing for the same worker were job boards such as Apna and WorkIndia and Skill India programmes run through NSDC. Workers were paid by UPI and were increasingly aware of e-Shram registration. Under the DPDP Act, every document collected was a liability.

In August 2026 the app took 2,40,000 installs at ₹60 each, an acquisition spend of ₹144 lakh.

3. The situation

Pankh's data scientist, Jagadish Vegesna, had spent the summer defining activation. After several rounds with Venkat, the team settled on this: a new user counts as activated when she has earned at least one skill badge and applied to a matched shift within seven days of install. Users who applied within seven days were far likelier to complete ten shifts. That was the aha moment: seeing a real shift, nearby, that her badge had unlocked.

Exhibit 1 shows the August cohort. The largest absolute loss was at sign-up, but the step Jagadish flagged was the second: 57,600 people who finished sign-up gave up when asked to upload a driving licence or identity proof before seeing a single module. They had not yet been shown any benefit. From Austin he sent an annotated chart with one sentence: "We ask for the most sensitive thing at the moment they trust us least."

The designer, Jyothsna Kakarla, worked from Lisbon and had a different reading. She had watched fifteen riders complete the flow on cheap Android phones. Many photographed a licence in poor light, or typed Telugu or Hindi names in English spelling to match the document. "They do not fail because they are unwilling," she said. "They fail because the app punishes them for being honest." Reordering, she argued, was a partial fix.

Exhibit 2 splits the same cohort by worker type. Warehouse workers, who arrived through hub supervisors with documents in hand, activated at 9.0 per cent. Riders, who came mostly from paid social ads, activated at 5.4 per cent. Riders were seventy per cent of installs, so the headline was mostly a rider story.

4. The people

Phani Chekuri, founder and CEO, in Rajahmundry, wanted a result before the year-end fundraise. He had raised ₹6 crore in 2024 and wanted to show investors placements, not downloads.

Pallavi Nallamilli, head of partner operations in Vijayawada, managed the hiring partners. A fleet operator such as Vishwaas would drop Pankh the first time an unverified rider caused a problem at a dark store, so she distrusted any change that delayed identity checks.

Jagadish Vegesna, the data scientist in Austin, wanted a design that could be measured cleanly. He preferred one change at a time with a holdout group, and warned that the team's earlier pilots had been too small to settle anything.

Jyothsna Kakarla, the designer in Lisbon, wanted the experience rebuilt around the worker's phone, language and patience. Her hours overlapped with Rajahmundry's only in the late afternoon.

5. The options

Venkat had drawn up three courses of action. The first, Option A, was to reorder the flow so that the user starts a module and earns a first badge before documents are requested, and verification happens when she applies for a shift. Engineering estimated three weeks and ₹18 lakh, so it could ship on 30 October. It also suited the DPDP Act's data minimisation, since Pankh would hold documents only from people who showed intent. The cost was risk. Pallavi expected extra manual review of about ₹4 lakh a month, and a small risk that unverified users would see shifts they could not take.

Option B, the Bhor Pehla Hafta programme, meant an assisted first week: voice notes on WhatsApp in three languages, plus paid ambassadors at rider hubs to help with document photos and the first badge. It cost ₹20 lakh to set up and ₹36 lakh a month to run, and would reach only the hubs where ambassadors were placed. The evidence was a two-hub pilot in Rajahmundry and Kakinada, too small to trust and possibly flattered by unusually motivated riders. Ambassador hiring would take five weeks, missing most of the Diwali surge.

Option C was to leave onboarding alone and buy more traffic, lifting installs by 25 per cent to 3,00,000. Marginal installs, however, were costing ₹90 rather than ₹60, because the cheap audiences were exhausted.

Exhibit 3 puts the three side by side, holding the current step rates fixed for Option C and using stated assumptions for the others. Option A assumes activation rises by a quarter; Option B by 37.5 per cent. Each placed worker earns Pankh ₹2,000 and half of activated users are placed, as in August.

Option A pays back its ₹18 lakh in about half a month at the modelled gain. Option B pays back its ₹20 lakh in under a month, but its gain is smaller and rests on an untested assumption. Option C loses money on every extra install. The comparison holds only if the assumed lifts are right, which is why Jagadish wanted a holdout.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, where does Pankh lose the most users, and where does it lose the users it can most plausibly recover?

2. Why define activation as a badge plus a shift application within seven days, and what does Exhibit 2 tell the CEO?

3. In Exhibit 3, which figures are measured and which are assumptions? How sensitive is the ranking of A and B to the assumed lifts?

4. Which option, or sequence, should Venkat present on Friday, and what evidence would make him change course by the end of November?

7. A note for the learner

Activation work begins with a definition, not a tactic. Once activation is defined as the moment a worker sees a real shift her badge has unlocked, onboarding becomes the task of shortening the distance to that moment. Every step before it is a cost the user pays before receiving value. Here the documents step asks the most sensitive thing of the least persuaded user, exactly the friction this topic teaches you to move later.

One defensible path is to ship Option A now and treat Option B as a staged experiment. Option A is the cheapest, it is the only plan that lands before Diwali, it is reversible, and it is consistent with data minimisation. Run it with a ten per cent holdout on the old flow so that Jagadish can measure the real lift rather than the assumed twenty-five per cent. Meanwhile, put ambassadors at four rider hubs only, since Exhibit 2 says riders are where the loss is, and compare them with matched hubs.

Pallavi's concern should be built in: verification required before a shift is accepted, and partners like Vishwaas Fleet Partners never seeing an unverified worker. Option C should be declined: it pays more for the same weak funnel, and the ₹15.12 lakh monthly loss shows the funnel, not the traffic, is the constraint. At the end of November, if the holdout shows a lift well below the assumed 25 per cent, Venkat should re-open the case for B with better numbers.
